EventDetail:
The programme includes a component on disaster preparedness and response

Programme highlights

The course will provide you with an opportunity to:
  • understand your role in educating students and colleagues about conservation, sustainable development, issues related to your environment and natural and human made disasters;
  • understanding your and others’ roles in creating a sustainable and safe environment for all;
  • contribute towards sustainable development; disaster planning, preparedness and response; infusing environmental education, natural and human made disaster preparedness and response education in policy, teaching, learning, curriculum and assessment;
  • partake in field visits; and
  • network with a range of fellow learners/organizations in the field, including AKU-IED’s MEd students as classroom peers.
Programme Facilitator

Ms Unaeza Alvi is a faculty member at AKU-IED, Pakistan. She has contributed in areas of
environment/science education, assessment and textbooks and curriculum development through
policy bodies, development projects, capacity building programmes, networking with public and
private sector organizations, voluntary work, research and dissemination. She has been involved
in the development of the ‘Situational Analysis Report on Environment Education in Pakistan’,
the ‘Integrated Environmental Education Curriculum’, the ‘Environmental Studies Curriculum’
and is the lead author of ‘Teaching and Learning Materials for Environmental Studies’. Her
research interests are in contextually relevant and innovative textbooks/teaching and learning
material development, assessment and learning, technology leadership, interactive and engaging
pedagogies in science, cultural studies, environment education, education in emergency and
education for sustainable development.

Who should attend?

Teachers and teacher educators, educational managers/leaders, curriculum developers, students or representatives of NGOs who are interested in environment and disaster preparedness education

Programme highlights
The course will provide you with an opportunity to:
  • explore key definitions around health promotion through schools;
  • critically examine the international, national and local responses to major development issues relating to health and education;
  • determine the implications for curriculum planning and content selection of using a broader definition of health;
  • practice the Child-to-Child approach as a child-centered methodology that links the learning place (school) with the living place (home and community), in a school through teacher development workshops;

Programme Facilitator
Dr Sadia M Bhutta is an Assistant Professor at AKU-IED, Pakistan. She earned her doctoral degree from the University of Oxford, Department of Education (UK) with a specific focus on health education classroom practices in the context of Pakistan. She had the opportunity to work with school health experts and practitioners around the world. Who should attend?
School teachers from urban and rural contexts, representatives from NGOs and INGOs who are responsible for implementing school health programmes

  • articulate the need for inclusive education system in your context

The course will provide you with an opportunity to:
  • Enhance your strategic thinking and involving skills, such as scenario planning, forward thinking, seeing the bigger picture, developing long-term vision, understanding the longterm implication of decisions etc.;

Programme facilitators
Dr Kulsoom Jaffer serves as Head, Outreach and Assistant Professor at AKU-IED. She holds a doctoral degree in Education from the Institute of Education, University of London and a masters degree in Arts, Educational Management and Administration, from the Institute of Education, University of London. She teaches Educational Leadership and Management courses at the graduate level. Her research interests include monitoring and review of school performance and institutional leadership and management.

Dr Sajid Ali is an Assistant Professor and Coordinator of Doctoral Programmes at AKU-IED. He holds a PhD in Policy Studies from University of Edinburgh, an MEd in Leadership and Policy from Monash University and a Masters in Sociology from the University of Karachi.   • A.R. Kiyani Gold Medal 1997, Australian Development Scholarship 2003, Commonwealth Youth Leadership Award 2003
  • Edinburgh Research Scholarship 2006
  • South Asian Visiting Fellowship at Oxford 2011
Dr Ali has also taught at Hamdard University, Karachi University and University of Edinburgh. He is the current General Secretary of Pakistan Association for Research in Education (PARE). His research interests include globalization and education policy, new forms of educational governance, policy networks, education reforms, privatization of education and role of knowledge resources in shaping policy.

EventDetail:
Synopsis
In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, movement around the Indian Ocean was invigorated by new economic and imperial realities. However, connections around the rim of the Indian Ocean themselves were not new. For many centuries before the arrival of the British, we have evidence of interaction and exchange between Persia, India, Indonesia, East Africa, and many places in between. The combination of long-distance and short-distance trade over time is what wove these societies together both economically and culturally. Until now however, scholarship on the Indian Ocean has mostly used 19th and 20th century realities to focus on long-distance movements towards economic centres, and failed to capture shorter migrations that infused small Indian Ocean ports with a cosmopolitanism of their own over many centuries.
In looking at migration between the south of Iran and Kuwait in the early 20th century, this lecture will highlight the ways in which the current ways of framing Indian Ocean connections fail to capture shorter migrations outside of major economic centres. Stephenson will critique the explanatory power of the language of both "foreland and hinterland” and “littoral societies,” and argue for a third way of conceptualising relationships between port cities.  

About the speaker
Lindsey Stephenson is a doctoral candidate in the Department of Near Eastern Studies at Princeton University. Her research focuses on migration of Persians and Arabs from the south of Iran and their settlement in Kuwait in Bahrain in the early 20th century. She graduated from the ISMC in 2012.

EventDetail:
The aim of this exploratory and informal workshop is to reflect on methodologies, research agendas, and case studies for investigating history writing in Arabic in the Middle East and North Africa in any period from the seventh century to the present.  

Through what practices of writing or otherwise encoding the past and of remembering and forgetting, have different groups in the Middle East and North Africa viewed their pasts? At different times and places, how have the significant contours, events and actors in their histories been seen? Was the significant past the same for court historians as for literary historians; for bureaucrats as for the military; for Sufis as for Muslim lawyers and Traditionists? How did non-Muslims and Muslims, men and women, adherents of different sectarian or juristic traditions, or speakers of different languages, within societies that became “Islamic” imagine the shape and meaning of their specific societies’ own pasts, and their relation to the universal history of the Islamic community? More recently, how have urban and rural people, workers and peasants, the religiously educated and the technocratic elite, developed different ways of writing, remembering, or commemorating particular events in, or the broad sweep of, local, national, or “Islamic” history?

Contributions are invited that will consider the practical and conceptual challenges of working on history writing in the region, as well as offering examples of themes, me​thods, and case studies of recent research that might elucidate these questions. Contributions are invited from scholars at all career levels, addressing any period and any part of the Middle East and North Africa, broadly defined.

Please send by 20 April an abstract of 300 words or less to sarah.savant@aku.edu. There is a small budget to provide some travel assistance for scholars outside of London.

The workshop will take place in London on 25 September 2015 and is co-hosted by the Aga Khan University, Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations and SOAS, University of London.​

Organisers
Hugh Kennedy and Konrad Hirschler (SOAS), James McDougall (Oxford), and Sarah Bowen Savant (AKU-ISMC)

EventDetail:
Synopsis
The Israeli-Palestinian conflict is arguably the most intractable dispute in international politics today, and opinion on this dispute is often polarized (one is either firmly pro-Israeli, or firmly pro-Palestinian). How did students at an American university in Iraq react to a careful historical study of this conflict? Opinion among the students was to some extent polarized, but for reasons that are very different than one would find in a North American university. Why were Kurdish-Iraqi students more sympathetic to Zionism than Arab-Iraqi students? What misconceptions did the students have about Zionism and Jews? How did they view Iraqi Jews who had emigrated to Israel? How did they view Hamas (the class took place in August 2014, during Operation Protective Edge)? How did these opinions change in the course of an intensive four week course (the class met for about three hours a day, four days a week)? Was there a difference in opinion between Sunni and Shia students? In this paper Dr Samad will outline his surprising findings while teaching this class, and report on his experience teaching this conflict in a Muslim-majority country.

Biography
Dr Joy Samad is an Assistant Professor at the American University of Iraq (AUIS). His academic interests include political philosophy, American politics, and Middle East politics. Prior to joinin AUIS he taught political philosophy and American politics at several universities in America and Bangladesh. He has published studies of Plato and Aristotle in Polis: The Journal for Ancient Greek Political Thought, and Acta Philosophica. He has also published a review essay on Egypt under Mubarak in The British Journal of Middle Eastern Studies, and an essay titled “John Locke and Muslim Liberalism” in the Journal of Church and State.

EventDetail:
Synopsis
Central Asia’s Ferghana Valley has historically been a mosaic of social groups and identities. The emergence of international boundaries with the break-up of the Soviet Union imposed a new political geographical logic on the social fabric of the Valley. This talk explores the tensions between these two logics of ordering territory, and the effects on inter-communal relations. Focussing on ethnically-mixed rural villages along the Uzbekistan-Kyrgyzstan boundary, it traces the fate of communities whose existence challenged both the new ideologies of nationalism and the analytical narratives of inter-communal tension.

Biography
Nick Megoran is a lecturer in a political geography at Newcastle University, and has been visiting these border communities for two decades.

This lecture is part of the 2014/2015 lecture series:Communalism and Sectarianism in a Globalised World

EventDetail:
Synopsis 
For years, the significance in the history of al-Andalus of the Great Mosque of Cordoba (Madīnat Qurṭuba) has overshadowed any other archaeological discovery in the city. In addition, the study of the palatine town of Madīnat al-Zahrā, founded in 936 just a few miles away from the Andalusian capital, has also eclipsed the past of the ancient Qurṭuba. However, due to the urban growth since the last two decades, new excavations in the city have provided with a huge amount of archaeological data, especially from the Umayyad Caliphate (929-1031). As a result, knowledge of the Islamic Cordoba has considerably increased in a very short space of time.

The most relevant findings came from the western area, where thousands of square metres of medieval suburbs have been excavated and found in a good state of conservation. During the 10th century, according to its status as capital of the Caliphate of Cordoba and the consequent increase in population, new districts were built in this part of the city, consisting of domestic habitats, mosques, artisanal installations, cemeteries and agricultural areas. The principal features of each of these spaces will be described during the lecture.

Biography
Belén Vázquez Navajas (BA in History of Art and MA in Archaeology and Heritage) is a member of the Sisifo Research Group of the University of Cordoba (Spain), where she has taken part in several archaeological activities. She is currently completing her PhD on water management in the Umayyad Cordoba.

Aim

It allows insight into why and how research is actually done, including the rationale, methodology and conclusions, and encourages careful consideration of the value of published research studies. Speaker
Dr. HR Ahmad, Professor of Physiology, Department of Biological and Biomedical Sciences

Learning Outcomes
What is education? Let us invite Noam Chomsky to introduce Bertrand Russell. His humanistic conception should be understood in context of a gardener nurturing a young tree. It will develop into an admirable form, given proper soil, air and light. This analogy refers to an individual human’s growth which for too many seems to be difficult because the soil and the freedom required for it are immeasurably difficult to find or provide. The solution may lie in Bertrand Russell’s libertarian concepts of education. 

He defines education as an activity directed towards the world that we want our efforts to create. It should not aim at passive awareness of dead facts. Its goal should be to elicit and fortify whatever creative energy a human possesses. In the modern world, the principle of growth in most of us is hampered by tradition imbibed by laws of the simpler age and institutions built around it. Therefore, the reconstruction of a society must search for ways to liberate the creative energy but not to establish new forms of authority. Russell would have agreed with Wilhelm von Humboldt that “to inquire and to create” are the centres around which all human pursuits more or less directly revolve. 

The session is open to all.

EventDetail:
A talk by Dr. Murad M. Khan, Professor of Psychiatry
Pakistan is lost. Not lost as in being finished but lost as in not knowing where it is and where it is going. A rudderless ship, floundering on the high seas, the captain and the crew clueless where they are and what they need to do. And the ship is taking water.
It is said that as we shall sow, so shall we reap. In the 67 years since independence we have sown a lot: religious intolerance, ghost schools, corruption, nepotism, bribery, rigged elec-tions, military coups, weak judiciary, weaponization, and neglected healthcare. Add to this incompetence, greed and mismanagement and you have a perfect recipe for disaster. And no one should be surprised at the disasters- whether it is the systematic destruction of our state institutions or the horrific massacre of the Army Public School in Peshawar- all are part of the same process that has allowed the growth of the multi-headed hydra that is now trying to swallow us whole.
Now schools in Pakistan have been directed to increase their security and raise their walls. But how high should the walls be? Should they be so high that no terrorist can build a lad-der long enough to climb over them? And what if, instead, the terrorists decide to target hospitals? Or shopping malls? Or public parks? Or even an open bazaar? Should we build walls around all of these places too?
What is the psychological impact of living in such adverse conditions? How does one keep a positive attitude and face the tribulations without breaking down? How can we turn adver-sity into triumph?
How can we build more bridges instead of higher walls?

We are delighted to announce the details for our popular Summer Programme. This year, the two-week course will take Education and Muslim communities as its theme. Held at ISMC’s central-London location at 210 Euston Road, the programme will run from 6-17 July 2015 and will be in two parts.
Each week can be taken separately and will feature content carefully designed to support and develop professionals and those with an interest in Muslim societies.
The first week will be devoted to introducing some key aspects of the historical and contemporary experience of Muslim communities and cultures in different contexts worldwide, both where Muslims are a majority and in a minority.  The second week will focus on issues around education for and about Muslims.
In the first week, the course will include visits to major UK museums such as the British Museum and Victoria and Albert, featuring talks by museum curators. In the second week, participants will visit schools with special interests in Muslim education. An optional excursion outside London will be arranged for the weekend between the two parts of the programme.

Course outline
Week 1
• Cities as centres of cultural production in the Muslim world
• Music and art historically and in the contemporary world
• Debates on the origins of Islam
• Cities in the modern Muslim world

Week 2
• Traditions of education in Muslim contexts
• Current educational issues in Muslim contexts
• Teaching about Islam and Muslim cultures in the UK

• Comparative European and North American perspectives

The Provost and the AKU Network of Teaching and Learning invite you to:

A talk by Fiona Deller, Research Director, Higher Education Quality Council of Ontario

Abstract: We often claim our programmes produce students who are critical creative thinkers, problem solvers, ethical global leaders, good communicators, lifelong learners and environmentally aware citizens. How do we know our graduates have attained these attributes? Learning outcomes are the game changer in higher education, but they're only meaningful if they're measurable. Hear from a leading world expert as the session explores the importance of generic learning outcomes and the value of creating a common language when designing, teaching and assessing learning outcomes. The talk will address why you should care about assessing learning outcomes and how to think about them in a practical way. The speaker will cover how to write learning outcomes and how to create assessment tools to measure them.

About Fiona Deller: I am a research director at HEQCO where I focus on issues related to accessibility, accountability and pathways for under-represented students.  Prior to coming to HEQCO, I worked as the postsecondary education coordinator at the Council of Ministers of Education, Canada where I focused on federal/provincial/territorial relations in postsecondary, quality assurance, government funding of PSE, student financial assistance and credit transfer, among others. I have also worked for both the provincial and the federal governments in PSE-related positions.  Previously, I have held advocacy positions with the Federation of Canadian Municipalities and the Canadian Alliance of Student Associations. I am a doctoral candidate at OISE/University of Toronto in the field of theory and policy of higher education.

About the book 
Claims abound that Saudi oil money is fuelling Salafi Islam in cultural and geographical terrains as disparate as the remote hamlets of the Swat valley in Pakistan and sprawling megacities such as Jakarta. Similarly, it is commonly assumed that Iran and the Sunni Arab states are fighting proxy wars in foreign lands. This empirically grounded study challenges these assumptions. Focusing on case studies of three of the most influential international centres of Islamic learning, the book traces how ideas are transmitted from one locale to another and how this process often influences those ideas.

Synopsis
Following the 2011 Arab uprisings, foreign policies of state/non-state actors and the international relations of the Middle East appear at the current historical juncture to be in the throes of sectarian conflict.The wars in Syria, Yemen and Libya and the region-wide confrontation between an Iran- and Saudi-centred axis are increasingly being represented in terms of a Sunni-Shia rivalry which goes back to the beginnings of Islamic history.The idea of sectarian conflict is indeed gradually becoming a self-fulfilling prophesy which, by framing the 'enemy' in religious identity terms, arguably hinders reconciliation and conflict-resolution. 
While not denying this emerging new reality in the Middle East region, the lecture will suggest that sectarianism must be placed in its proper context and given its proper measure. It will unpack the meanings of sectarianism and define it carefully so as to be able to distinguish it from ideology. It will also juxtapose the two, ideational drivers of the international relations of the region, with material considerations of power and interest. 

About the speaker
Dr Katerina Dalacoura is Associate Professor in International Relations at the London School of Economics and Political Science. Her main areas of expertise include human rights, democracy and democracy promotion in the Middle East; political Islam; culture and religion in International Relations. She has published in the Review of International Studies, Millennium, International Affairs, Democratisation, International Studies Notes, Third World Quarterly and International Relations, and has authored a number of chapters in edited books. Her latest book, Islamist Terrorism and Democracy in the Middle East, was published by Cambridge University Press in 2011.

EventDetail:
Flow cytometry is an important technique used routinely in diagnostics and research. The field is ever growing and several advancements have been made in simplifying this technique for more user friendly protocol for routine use in research and diagnostics.

The flow cytometer has not only reduced in size in terms of platforms but multiple panels of antibodies with wide spectral range are being used. The protocols are simplified so that they can be easily followed without any hassle.

In Pakistan, very few labs are equipped with flow cytometer and expertise is limited only to diagnostics labs. It is therefore important to introduce basic concepts of flow cytometry at national level whereby young researchers, students, technicians and research faculties can acquire first-hand knowledge from experts in this field.

Learning outcomes:
To enable the participants to understand:
  • Basics of flow cytometry, interpretation and analysis of results
  • Application of flow cytometry in research and diagnostics
  • Diagnosis of malignant haematological disorder (leukaemia & lymphoma) using flow cytometry
  • Diagnoses and immunophenotyping of haematological malignancies (Leukaemia / Lymphoma and non hematopoietic malignancy) by immunohistochemistry (IHC) on Bone Marrow Trephine Biopsies
  • Immunophenotyping of lymphocytes (Total T & B cell, CD4, CD8, CD4/CD8 & NK) in immunodeficiency states with particular reference to HIV
Course Directors:
  • Dr Najeeha Iqbal, Assistant Professor, Departments of Paediatrics and Child Health and Biological and Biomedical Sciences

EventDetail:
About the session
The session will discuss the overlap in the system of reason that focuses on teaching, learning, childhood, and curriculum and the problem of change. This way of reasoning will be deliberated in the following four parts:
  • Outlining the characteristics of each research program as strategies of change;
  • Considering research as salvation themes about the Desired Future Teacher (and Society) To Actualize by the research;
  • Exploring the research less about improving practices but as making kind of persons. These people entail the desired capabilities and characteristics of not only the teacher but connect the teacher to changing the trilogy of the child/family/community of those who come to school;
  • Concluding with how research on practice is not a theory of change but conserves the existing framework of schooling and its hierarchies that compares, divides and excludes/abjects in its efforts to include.
Presenter
Professor Tom Popkewitz
Curriculum and Instruction (CI)
School of Education University of Wisconsin-Madison

Professor Tom Popkewitz’s studies are concerned with the knowledge or systems of reason that govern educational policy and research related to pedagogy and teacher education. His research includes historical, ethnographic, and comparative studies of national educational reforms and the education sciences in Asia, Europe, Latin America, Southern Africa, and the US. Scholarship: He has written or edited approximately 30 books and over 200 articles in journals and as book chapters. Two of his books (Paradigms and Ideology in Educational Research and A Political Sociology of Educational Reform) have won awards for their contribution to educational studies. 

He has conducted national and comparative studies of teacher education and curriculum reforms in the US, Europe, Latin America, and Asia, particularly as they relate to questions of social inclusion (e.g., The Myth of Educational Reform, and Struggling for the Soul). Professor Popkewitz has also co-directed a ten-country European Union-funded research project on educational governance and social exclusion (1999-2002), and (co)directed comparative projects in the history and contemporary contexts of educational reforms. These studies appear in edited books (e.g., Educational Knowledge; Changing Patterns of Power; Educational Restructuring; Inventing the Modern Self and John Dewey: Modernities and the Traveling of Pragmatism in Education; and The Child, the Citizen, and the Promised Land: Comparative Visions in the Development of Schooling in the Long 19th Century).

EventDetail:
PROVOST'S SPEAKER SERIES
 
It's Not All About the Student - Find Out Why!
 
With Professor Winnie Mucherah
Ball State University, Muncie, Indiana, USA
Visiting Carnegie African Diaspora Fellow

  
ABSTRACT: 
Winner of the American Educational Research Association’s Best Published Paper Award, this study examined classroom climate and student goal structures in high school biology classrooms in Kenya. Participants included 891 students and their teachers in Form 2 and 3 from two same-sex boarding schools—one for boys and the other for girls. School differences were found on all classroom climate aspects except teacher support and competition. Relative to Form 2 students, Form 3 students perceived their classrooms to be higher in teacher support, task focus, competition, rule strictness, and innovation. There were school and form level differences in students’ goal structures, with School 1 students, relative to School 2 students, perceiving more personal performance approach goals and their teachers as encouraging performance-approach goals. Form 3 students reported more performance-approach goals at both the personal and teacher levels. Teachers perceived their classroom climates more positively than their students. Observation data provides interpretative information.
 
ABOUT THE SPEAKER:
Winnie Mucherah is Professor of Developmental Psychology in the Department of Educational Psychology at Ball State University, Muncie, Indiana, USA. She earned her doctoral degree in Human Development in 1998 from the University of Maryland. She teaches graduate and undergraduate courses in human development and serves as the director of the Minor in the Psychology of Human Development.
 
ABOUT THE CARNEGIE AFRICAN DIASPORA FELLOWSHIP (CADF) PROGRAMME:
CADF is an innovative fellowship programme aimed at facilitating engagement between scholars born in Africa who are now based in the United States or Canada and scholars in Africa on mutually beneficial academic activities, including curriculum co-development, research, graduate teaching, training and mentoring.  Professor Winnie Mucherah is one of 110 African diaspora scholars who have been awarded fellowships to travel to Africa over the first two years of the program.  The projects span an impressive range of fields across the arts and humanities, social sciences, education, sciences, technology, engineering and mathematics. The program is managed by the Institute of International Education (IIE) in collaboration with Quinnipiac University and is funded by Carnegie Corporation of New York.

EventDetail:
Synopsis
Pakistani politics is shaped  by the interactions of four powerful elites which include in their number oligarchs, feudal lords, military officers, ulama, and civil servants: wealthy landowners, religious groups, the military and politicians. Each of these sectors have competed or allied with each other for control of the country. 
 
Recent years have seen religious and feudal elites allied with the military elite to topple Bhutto’s regime; General Zia ul-Haq has allied himself with the religious elite mainly Jamaat-i-Islami; and even General Musharraf who initially tried to enforce secularism has found himself allied with Islamists. 
 
This lecture will argue that these elites were careless about the people's demands and focused only on keeping the status quo to maintain their power.They have impeded the developments of institutions, and have succeeded in strengthening central government to oppress ethnic and sectarian demands.
 
The speaker will interrogate key areas in the debate, including the impact of this structure on establishing a consolidated democracy in Pakistan, and what impact this situation will have on sectarian violence in Pakistan.

EventDetail:
Abstract
The lecture will focus on the diverse attempts made by Muslims in British Columbia to realise ummicity (the quality of being part of a larger Muslim community and identity) through the construction of institutions such as the mosque and school. Is there any conflict between the practices and conceptions of ethnic or national forms of Islam brought to Canada and, if so, how are they reconciled within built Muslim spaces? Is there an identifiable Canadian way of knowing and practicing Islam or can one identify a regional experience, dependent on the timetable of arrival and composition of Muslims? How are institutions of knowing Islam constructed within the different Muslim communities of British Columbia and how do they overlap? Special attention will be drawn to the importance of 'double diaspora' Muslims in the Vancouver context.

About the Speaker
Derryl Maclean is the founding Director of the Centre for the Comparative Study of Muslim Societies and Cultures at Simon Fraser University.  A social historian of religion with a focus on Islamic Studies, his research spans Abbasid and Fatimid history on the eastern frontier, millennial movements in the early modern Persianate world, and diasporic Muslim communities in British Columbia. He is the author of numerous scholarly articles and the book Religion and Society in Arab Sind and the co-editor of the recently published Cosmopolitanism in Muslim Contexts: Perspectives from the Past.

EventDetail:
Conference theme: Engaged Teaching for Engaged Learning

The Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL) promotes teaching as a scholarly endeavor where “the work of the classroom [becomes] a site for inquiry, asking and answering questions about students’ learning in ways that can improve one’s own classroom and also advance the larger profession of teaching” (Huber and Hutchings, 2005). SoTL engages individuals in designing, conducting, and publishing research on teaching and learning. It also creates a community of practitioners who contribute to the body of knowledge about teaching and learning as well as benefit from the SoTL of others. 

The Network of Teaching and Learning will host the 1st bi-annual SoTL conference aimed at enabling AKU faculty and Aga Khan Development Network/AKU partners to join in conversations and collaborations on SoTL with one another from the regions AKU serves across Asia, Africa and the UK.

The conference will run over two days in Karachi with participants joining in from other campuses via WebEx and videoconference.  There will be three plenary keynote sessions beamed via videoconference, concurrent sessions of face-to-face paper presentations and poster presentations on site in Karachi.

EventDetail:
Successive Pakistani governments have struggled to provide good-quality, accessible education.  Literacy levels are still low and standards in education vary enormously across the country.  

Organised by City Circle, this important event will examine where those in charge at governmental level have repeatedly gone wrong, if there is a way back to setting in place a State-led high quality education system or is the private and third sector the only way forward? How can we ensure that attaining an education doesn't become the privilege of the affluent few but the right of the many?

Speakers 

Dr David Taylor  is the Director of the Aga Khan University Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations in London. He holds a PhD in Politics from the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS), University of London. He graduated in History in 1966 from the University of Cambridge and completed his MA in Area Studies from SOAS. Dr Taylor was Vice Provost of the Aga Khan University in Karachi from 2002-2008. Prior to that, he was a faculty member at SOAS, where he became Dean and then Pro-Director with responsibility for teaching. He has been a Visiting Fellow at Panjab University in Chandigarh (India), Jawaharlal Nehru University in Delhi, and the Zentrum Moderner Orient, Berlin, and was a Senior Research Fellow at the Institute of Commonwealth Studies, University of London. His research interests focus on contemporary politics in India and Pakistan.

Shezad Abediis one of the founding members of CARE in the UK. Shezad has worked in the energy and finance sectors for almost 20 years. Having held senior positions in EDF Trading, TAIB Yatrim Bank and Carron Energy Ltd, he has worked in locations as diverse as Turkey and Bahrain. Shezad is currently Chairman at PDF Corporate Finance in London.

Zahabiya Karimi graduated in International Relations and Journalism from Monash University, and has since been working in the charity sector. Before she joined the Citizens Foundation in the UK, she was working at the Head Office in Karachi, managing the charity's volunteer programmes across the country, and prior to that worked in fundraising at WWF-Pakistan.

This course will provide you with an opportunity to:

EventDetail:
Dear Colleagues & Friends,
 
The Department of Continuing Professional Education (DCPE) in collaboration with the Department of Community Health Sciences (CHS), Aga Khan University (AKU), Karachi, Pakistan is pleased to announce a short course on Qualitative Research Methods and Analysis (QRMA) scheduled from July 27-August 1, 2015. This course is part of CHS’s Continuing Education Programme.  The brief course information is given below for your reference and course registration form is attached. For more detail of QRMA and other short courses please visit http://www.aku.edu/mcpk/chs/cep

About the Course:

Witnessing a gradual paradigm shift in the research from quantitative studies to mix methodologies, and worldwide acceptance of conclusions based on qualitative scientific inquiries, researchers are expected to conduct qualitative research with greater scientific rigor in their data collection methods and analysis. A comprehensive understanding of qualitative research with this perspective is thus essential for people involved in research particularly in Pakistan.  

The Qualitative Research Methods and Analysis course is designed to introduce participants to key features and issues in conducting qualitative research focusing on content analysis both manually and using software. This course will also provide a rich experience including pros and cons of methodologies, the basic techniques of data collection and analysis such as interviews, observation, and coding, and concepts related to ethics, and trustworthiness. 

Goal:

This course is designed to provide sound understanding of fundamental qualitative research concepts by using hands-on approach on the analysis softwares.

Objectives:

By the end of the course, the participants would be able to: 
  • Apply knowledge about the applications of Qualitative Research Methods and Analysis in their projects, especially related to community settings
  • Understand different types of qualitative study designs, and be able to select what is relevant and important in their own project(s)
  • Comprehend different analytical techniques used for qualitative research
  • Develop skills, gain hands-on experience about qualitative data analysis softwares (NVIVO and Open Code), and interpret the results 
Putting Theory into Practice:

This course provides each participant with a practical opportunity to apply concepts and skills learned towards addressing research issues related to their work setting(s). Participants will also be encouraged to select at least one project that each of them will pursue after completion of the course.

Educational Strategies:

QRMA is a full-time one week course.  A participatory method of teaching and learning is followed which includes interactive lectures, large and small group discussions, group presentations, field exposure for data collection, and hands-on experience on analysis software.

Participants bring with them a breadth of experience from different backgrounds and learning is encouraged through a mutual sharing of experiences. Pre and post-course tests are conducted to evaluate the performance of the course and the value of the programme to its participants.

Medium of Instruction:

As English is the exclusive language of instruction, participants must be comfortable to read, write and speak in English language.

Who Should Attend:

The course is designed mainly for Junior and mid-management level personnel of public and private organisations and individuals interested in developing an understanding of basic concepts in Qualitative Research Methods and Analysis.

Duration of the Course:

The duration of the course is six working days. The scheduled dates are from July 27-August 1, 2015, both days inclusive.

Course Fee: 

The course tuition fee is Rs 16,000 (US$ 200/= applicable for international participants), which covers classroom instructions, course material, refreshment, and simple lunch during working hours. 

Submission Date of Applications: 

Participants will be selected on first come first serve basis, and criteria set by the programme.  Kindly send brief CV along with filled registration form latest by July 20, 2015 to Ms Nadira Ashraf, Assistant Manager, Continuing Education Programme; Department of Community Health Sciences, Aga Khan University, P.O. Box 3500, Karachi 74800, Pakistan; Telephone: +92-21-34864802; E-mail: nadira.ashraf@aku.edu; chs.cep@aku.edu

EventDetail:
Throughout the Middle East, cultural heritage is being destroyed faster than we can document it.  Dr Smith’s paper examines the processes and praxes necessary to capture information documenting material and visual culture – from monumental to ephemeral - for future generations.

Dr Sharon C. Smith is Program Head at the Aga Khan Documentation Centre at MIT, and Co-Director of Archnet. She earned her PhD from Binghamton University, SUNY, in 2009. Her areas of specialisation include Middle Eastern art and architecture, and Early Modern Italian art and architecture. Sharon sits on several boards, including the Middle East Outreach Council (MEOC), and was recently named a Fellow of the Institute, Tangier American Legation Institute for Moroccan Studies (TALIM). In addition, Sharon serves as image editor for Muqarnas: An Annual on the Visual Cultures of the Islamic World. She has presented widely on issues of documentation, digitization, and the dissemination of knowledge, as well as on art historical topics primarily focused on visual and material culture in the Early Modern Mediterranean.

About the event

Ratish Nanda (CEO, Aga Khan Trust for Culture, India) will share his experience leading AKTC India’s work on the Urban Renewal project in the Nizamuddin Conservation area. The project includes the conservation of over 50 monuments, environmental development of over 300 acres in the heart of the city and an extensive socio economic development programme leading to the improvement of the quality of life for more than 15,000 residents of Nizamuddin Basti. 

In addition to this, he will also speak about his work at the head of the Qutb Shahi Heritage Park in Hyderabad, a project which includes the conservation of over 80 monuments belonging to the 16th century Qutb Shahi dynasty as well as 108 acres of landscape development.

About the speaker

For AKTC, Mr Nanda has also led the Baghe Babur restoration, a 16th century enclosed garden in Kabul, Afghanistan. His work also includes the Garden Restoration of Humayun’s Tomb in Delhi and several projects for INTACH, including the conservation of St James Church, the ruins adjacent to Sultan Garhi and unprotected monuments in the Mehrauli Archaeological Park.

Mr Nanda has received a number of awards including the Eisenhower Fellowship 2007, the Sanskriti Award for ‘Social and Cultural Achievement’, the Prince Claus Fund’s ‘Urban Hero’ the Aga Khan Foundation International Scholarship and the Charles Wallace Conservation Fellowship.

EventDetail:
By Dr Konrad Hirschler

Abstract
The Cairo Geniza, a collection of more than 300,000 documents dating from the 9th-19th is well known. However the Geniza was not the only depository for 'sacred trash' in the Egyptian and Syrian lands. A wide variety of social groups deposited their documents in the Damascus Dome of the Treasury. 
Dr Hirschler will present an attempt to reconstitute documents (marriage contracts, bequest-related legal disputes, and private letters) from this depository which were recycled in late Mamluk manuscripts. 
The talk will also address issues of access to Damascene manuscripts while the Syrian war is ongoing. 

Speaker
Dr Konrad Hirschler is Professor of Middle Eastern History at SOAS, University of London. He is the author of Medieval Damascus: Plurality and Diversity in an Arabic Library – The Ashrafīya Library Catalogue (forthcoming 2016), The Written Word in the Medieval Arabic Lands (2012) and Medieval Arabic Historiography: Authors as Actors (2006) as well as co-editor of Manuscript Notes as a Documentary Source (2011).

This seminar, organised by the Strengthening Teacher Education in Pakistan (STEP) project of IED will focus on knowledge sharing and deliberating on recommendations around issues of gender equity in education in Pakistan, highlighting lessons learnt from STEP intervention districts from Sindh and Balochistan as well as broader research on the theme. Researchers and practitioners will share their learning based on their research, observations and experiences and will discuss post 2015 possibilities and challenges for ensuring gender equity in education. In particular the focus will be on exploring the link between equality and quality in classroom and schools.

The STEP project has worked extensively in incorporating gender equity in its Whole School Improvement Programme and Cluster Based Mentoring Programme models as well as other interventions resulting in significant change in perceptions and practice. It would be helpful to share these practices and models that have worked successfully not only with relevant sector stakeholders but also with the general public to make these models accessible to be applied on a broader level. It would also serve as an advocacy tool to raise awareness on practices that promote gender equity in education.

This dissemination of ideas will be done through relatable real life case studies making the information crisp and understandable for all audiences. In addition, it will be supported by research on the theme.

EventDetail:
A non-deferential and indeed a rebellious society in a sectarian religious environment, the Emerald Isle was the ultimate test ground for those who wished to reconcile democracy with minority rights. The Third Home Rule Bill, passed but not enacted in 1912-14, had tried to enshrine a series of guarantees for the Unionist and predominantly Protestant minority in both Ulster and the South. However, the regions where the Protestants represented a local majority refused to countenance a Dublin-based, Catholic nation-state, effectively claiming that they had a right to self-determination too.

Ireland was 'typical' of the situation in Europe, where from 1875 multi-ethnic states reeled under the impact of democratic nationalism. The latter rejected the traditional politics of deference and the marginality of peripheral social, economic and ethnic groups and cultivated the revival of subaltern languages to assert their cultural autonomy, claiming sovereignty on behalf of the people. In this context, popular violence played an important political role because it involved the claiming of sovereignty by 'the people', through self-selected groups who claimed to speak on their behalf. In the religious sphere this went together with the revival of sectarianism, which, Biagini argues, must be distinguished from religion as much as popular sovereignty must be distinguished from parliamentary sovereignty.

Prof. Biagini will argue that sectarianism has to be seen as a biproduct of secularisation, where the loss of clerical power allowed lay community leaders to claim the slogans and symbols of religion for their own political purposes. The talk will be followed by a wide-ranging discussion, which will attempt to explore how far Irish models of sectarianism might be applied to Asian contexts, such as Syria, Bahrain, India or Malaysia¹.

EventDetail:
The partition of colonial India that led to the emigration of Sindhi Hindus from Sindh and the immigration of Urdu-speaking Muslims from across India to Sindh, created a need to defend Sindhi language and culture amongst the locals.

In this talk, Ms Hemani will argue that the post-partition Sindhi nationalism that developed in response to Pakistani state’s policy to suppress ethnic differences enabled a supposedly “little tradition” of Shah jo Raag to emerge from the Sufi shrine of Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai in Bhitshah in Sind. The shrine became the central stage for musicians from both the supposedly “greater tradition” of Gwalior gharana in Sindh, as well as rural musicians from musical communities such as manganiyaar and non-musical communities.  These groups in turn became the presenters of “Sindhi culture” locally and internationally.
Whereas British writers such as the 19th century author H.T Sorley elevated the status of Shah Latif as a “classical poet” of Sindhi, similar to Milton or Shakespeare, the post-colonial Sindhi revival of the musical renditions of Shah Latif led Sindhi scholars such as Dr. N.A Baloch to argue that Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai was the “pioneer of new musical era” elevating his status to the founder of a “classical musical tradition” of Sindh.
The attempt to transform a supposedly “little” tradition to a “great” tradition reflects the distinctive experience of processes of modernity in Sindh, whereby “Sindhi music” constructed from the sonic culture of Muslim shrines makes us re-assess the place of the so-called “little traditions” in post-colonial Pakistan. 

Speaker
Shumaila Hemani is a PhD student in Ethnomusicology at the University of Alberta in Canada and studies Sufi music of the Shah jo Raag, the sung poetry of Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai in Sindh, Pakistan and across the borders of Pakistan and India.
She was recently awarded the State of Kuwait Doctoral Award in Islamic Studies (2015) and in the past has been recipient of Flore Shaw Graduate Scholarship in Music (2014), Paine Music Scholarship (2010), and the Institute of Ismaili Studies' (IIS) Graduate Scholarship in Islamic Studies and Humanities (2006-08), and PhD Scholarship (2013). Her publications include her MA thesis “Representing Pakistan through folk music and dances,” submitted to University of Alberta in 2011, and she has also received an invitation to contribute an entry on women's music of Pakistan for “Women and Islamic Cultures” (published by Brill).

Mary is a very signiﬁcant character in the Qur’an. A whole Qur’anic chapter (Sura19, “Maryam”) even bears her name. Professor Dye will first focus on the meaning and sources of the beginning of this particular chapter (19:1-33) in order to show how its content echoes a number of Late Antique Christian traditions related to the celebration of Mary’s role in the Nativity, especially the liturgical practices of the Kathisma Church, which was located half-way between Jerusalem and Bethlehem (and which, incidentally, provided the architectural model for the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem). He will then study the relative chronology of Q 19:1-33, Q 3:33-63, and Q 19:34-40.

Speaker 
Professor Guillaume Dye teaches Islamic Studies at the Université libre de Bruxelles (ULB), where is he is a member of the Centre interdisciplinaire d’Étude des Religions et de la Laïcité (Interdisciplinary Centre for Study of Religions and Secularism). His main research area pertains to Qur'anic studies, considered methodologically and thematically, as a part of Biblical studies. He is the co-founder and co-director of The Early Islamic Studies Seminar: International Scholarship on the Qur’ān and Islamic Origins. 

He is the author of several articles on Quranic studies and he recently published Partage du sacré: transferts, dévotions mixtes, rivalités interconfessionnelles, edited by Isabelle Dépret et Guillaume Dye, Bruxelles-Fernelmont, EME, 2012, and Hérésies: une construction d'identités religieuses, edited by Christian Brouwer, Guillaume Dye et Anja van Rompaey, Bruxelles, Editions de l'Université de Bruxelles ((Problèmes d'Histoire des Religions), 2015.

EventDetail:
A strand in current scholarship examines early Islam and the Caliphate against a late antique backdrop of Sasanid-East Roman tension, dogmatic strife in the Church, and the maturation of rabbinic Judaism. Gibbon long ago insisted there had been more than one road out of Antiquity, not just the formation of Latin Christendom – Papacy, German Empire and Italian Renaissance – but also Greek Christendom and the rise of Islam. Yet this aspect of Decline and Fall remains unappreciated, especially in John Pocock’s monumental Barbarism and Religion.

This lecture traces the origins of Gibbon’s eastward turn in his reading of seventeenth and eighteenth-century Arabists, historians and travellers, and his decision to follow East Roman history down to 1453. Not only Voltaire but also the Universal History (London, 1736-66) encouraged Gibbon to look beyond Europe and its Christian narrative.  While attitudes to Islam had softened in the decades around 1700 thanks to greater familiarity with its literature and the weakening of theological prejudice, Gibbon achieved a powerful, empathetic portrait of Muḥammad as political leader as well as prophet. His account of the Muslim empires from Medinan origins to the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople offers revealing comparisons with ancient Iran and Rome. Although his classical Greek and Roman criterion of cultural and historical value forced him to conclude that Islam too was, in the end, tyranny and imposture, nevertheless the weight Gibbon accorded the Muslim world anticipates the more inclusive methods of global historians in our day.

Speaker
Professor Garth Fowden is Sultan Qaboos Professor of Abrahamic Faiths and holds the position of Senior Research Associate, Peterhouse College in the Faculty of Divinity at the University of Cambridge. He read Modern History at Merton College, Oxford, and there also wrote his doctoral thesis, under the supervision of Henry Chadwick, on Pagan philosophers in late antique society, with special reference to Iamblichus and his followers (1979). Between 1978 and 1983 Professor Fowden held research fellowships at Peterhouse and at Darwin College, Cambridge. From 1983 to 1985 he taught Byzantine and Modern Greek History at Groningen University in the Netherlands,moving  to a position at the National Research Foundation, Athens, and then to the Sultan Qaboos Chair in 2013. He has held visiting appointments at Princeton University; the Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton; the Institute for the Humanities, University of Michigan; the École des Hautes Études en Sciences Sociales, Paris; and most recently (2012-13) the Wissenschaftskolleg zu Berlin.

EventDetail:
Part of DIALOGUES 2016: A thought-provoking series of seminars on Governance and Constitutions in Muslim Contexts

This presentation proposes a structure for Islamic constitutionalism that is inspired by pre-modern Islamic jurisprudence and Muslim history, yet designed for contemporary realities. This structure is conceptually different from the typical ‘Islamic state’ imagined by modern political Islam movements because it is built on legal pluralism rather than legal centralism. 
Unlike the centralized European nation-state systems inherited by most Muslim-majority countries, the constitutional structure presented here is built upon the separation of law making power that characterised Muslim legal and political systems for centuries: a separation between (1) siyasa laws made by rulers in furtherance of the public good (maslaha) and (2) fiqh laws articulated by religious legal scholars based on scriptural interpretation and existing in a diversity of legal schools. Understanding sharia as an Islamic rule of law (rather than merely a collection of rules) encompassing both fiqh and siyasa, this presentation proposes a three-part structure for modern Islamic constitutionalism.  This structure would allow Muslims to have sharia as the ‘law of the land’, but is not theocratic because it does not allow a state to impose its preferred religious doctrine upon the entire population. It also opens up new solutions to longstanding conflicts between secular and religious forces in Muslim-majority countries today, such as the purported incompatibility of Islam and democracy and apparent conflicts between sharia and human rights. These solutions have been missed in global discourses about Islamic government so far because Eurocentric concepts of law (especially religious law) currently dominate the field. 
This paper challenges these concepts by showing how an Islamic constitutionalism that is not secular and not theocratic is not impossible.

Speaker
Dr Asifa Quraishi-Landes holds a doctorate from Harvard Law School and other degrees from Columbia Law School, the University of California at Davis, and the University of California at Berkeley, and has served as law clerk in the United State Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.  She is currently on the governing board of the Association of American Law Schools' Section on Islamic Law, the National Association of Muslim Lawyers (NAML), and Muslim Advocates.

Drafting a Basic Law for the Palestinian Authority, established following the Oslo Agreements, was a long and hard process. The output was interestingly one of the most ‘liberal’ constitutions in the Arab world. 
In this paper Dr Khalil will argue that the Palestinian Authority passed to a second level, i.e. from a legal text to a text-based institutional practice (and back). This passage has consequences for the Palestinian Authority itself, the place and role of the Basic Law, and the future of Palestine. In wider perspective, using Palestine as a working example interrogates us on the under-explored relationship between constitutional text and governance practice.

Speaker
Dr Asem Khalil is an Associate Professor of Public Law, H.H. Shaikh Hamad Bin Khalifa Al-Thani Chair in Constitutional and International Law, Birzeit University.

About the Series - Dialogue 2016
ISMC’s Governance for the Public Good in Muslim Contexts Programme aims to address the deeply rooted religious and cultural sensitivities prevalent in matters of governance. By making outputs accessible to wider audiences, the programme is committed to encouraging healthy and informed debate among scholars and the public alike. The Dialogues series is a key part of this commitment.

This year the series will focus on the oft-neglected issues surrounding governance in constitutions. We will explore what specificities Muslim contexts offer on governance, given that most of the key issues in constitutional design, forms of government, or decision-making are not necessarily defined by religious beliefs. The full programme is available here.

EventDetail:
In writings and drawings, the Parthenon’s early modern viewers portrayed the Athenian built environment using interpretative tools ranging from the Qur’an, to Arab geographers and hagiographers, to ancient Greek and Latin authors, to European costume albums created in Istanbul and local legends colored by an inventive mix of myth and history. This talk will not only discuss material remains of the mosque, but also consider how European scientific impetus and Ottoman universalising historiography confronted a building infused over many centuries with the mirabilia and legends that had given it life. The Parthenon and its famous sculptures lay at the heart of an Athenian landscape populated by philosophers and prophets, where wonder and history were intertwined.

About the Speaker

Dr Elizabeth Key Fowden is currently Gerda Henkel Stiftung Senior Researcher in the Faculty of Asian and Middle Eastern Studies at the University of Cambridge. Sparked by an early interest in Renaissance Italy, she studied Classics, specialising in late antique history and material culture in the Eastern Mediterranean and Middle East. Her PhD thesis, supervised by Peter Brown at Princeton University and later published as The Barbarian Plain: Saint Sergius between Rome and Iran (Berkeley 1999), examines religious, political and architectural crosspollination in late antique and early Islamic Syria. The after-life of artistic forms and religious ideas freed from their original contexts is a dominant theme throughout her teaching and research. In her current book project, The Parthenon Mosque, Fowden applies her interest in Islamic re-formulation of the Classical and Christian inheritance to the early modern conjunction of Greek, European and Ottoman views of Athens’ most celebrated building.

EventDetail:
The presentation seeks to explore how youth negotiate the relationship between their self-identity and communal identity in globalising contexts.

The analysis will be drawn from qualitative field-studies conducted in three countries: Canada, Tajikistan & Pakistan. The data discussed here was generated through in-depth interviews and focus group discussions with young people, parents and grand-parents. From a theoretical standpoint, Dr Datoo has employed the conceptual metaphors of roots and rhizomes, filiations and affiliations, global and local to illuminate how the discourses of tradition and community are viewed, interpreted and maintained between generationally. Furthermore, the analysis will highlight some noticeable ‘ruptures’ in the sense of continuity and change in tradition, and how these inter-generational understandings in turn shape debates about changing notion of ‘community’ in globalising societies.

Speaker
Dr Al-Karim Datoo has a PhD (McGill, Canada): in Cultural-Sociology of Education, and an MSc in Educational Research Methodology (University of Oxford), Graduate Program in Islamic Studies and Humanities (Institute of Ismaili Studies, London). He works as a research coordinator, in the Constituency Studies Unit, Institute of Ismaili Studies, London. He is an ethnographer with special research and teaching interests in: globalisation, education and identity, globalisation and youth values and sociology of curriculum. He is a co-editor of a book titled: (delete) Globalisation, culture and education in South Asia: Critical excursions, Palgrave: USA.

Chair
Dr Philip Wood

EventDetail:
Segregation is often seen as the result of the behaviour of ethnic minorities, but here, Goodhart investigates the role of the behaviours and preferences of the ‘white’ ethnic majority. In particular he uses recent research to address how far American experience in the 1950s and 60s can be used to explain the contemporary British experience. 

Speaker 
David Goodhart is a British journalist, commentator, author and director of the Integration Hub as well as the Demography, Immigration, and Integration Unit based at Policy Exchange. He is the former director of the London based think tank Demos. He is also founder and former editor of Prospect magazine, which he set up in 1995, and he remains the magazine’s editor-at-large. 

David is a prominent figure in public debate in the UK, who regularly writes for the national press. He has also presented several BBC Radio 4 Analysis programmes. Before Prospect, he was a correspondent for the Financial Times for 12 years – including a stint in Germany during the unification period. In 2013 David published a book, The British Dream, about postwar multiculturalism, national identity and immigration. It was short-listed for the Orwell Book Prize in 2014.

Introduction
The PGME Conference is organised each year with the objective to provide its audience with an opportunity to listen and interact with national and international experts in related fields according to the selected theme of the conference.  The conference provides a platform to share experiences and recommend ways to improve the standards of postgraduate medical education in the country. 

This year’s PGME Conference will focus on innovations in technology and teaching/learning methods.  Additionally, participants will learn how to capitalize on opportunities and to cope with the challenges during and after postgraduate training.  Renowned national and international speakers will share their knowledge and experiences of the latest technological advances in health care. EventDetail:
The Network of Teaching & Learning is pleased to announce the offering of the Teaching and Learning Workshop for AKU East Africa faculty in Dar es Salaam on 25th – 27th July, 2016.

Objective of the workshop:

The workshop aims to support participants develop increased competence and confidence as facilitators of learning as well as provide them with resources to be more reflective about their teaching. It will engage faculty in real teaching experiences within the training so as to provide them with the opportunity to translate their knowledge about teaching into practice. 

The programme

The workshop will target faculty from across all disciplines in AKU therefore providing a rich multi-disciplinary context within which to learn about teaching. For further details on the workshop please click here. 

The programme is modelled along the well-recognised Instructional Skills Workshop (ISW) programme offered in many universities, largely in Canada and the USA, but also around the world, including Asia and Africa (http://iswnetwork.ca/). It will be facilitated by facilitators drawn from AKU faculty who will be specially trained by experts from Western University to facilitate the workshop. A certificate for successful completion of the workshop will be awarded to participants by ISW.

If you are interested in participating in the programme, please contact your entity head as entities are required to cover travel and accommodation costs of participating faculty who are not based in Dar es Salaam. No fees will be charged for faculty participating in the training. Lunch and tea will also be served during the workshop days.

Deadline: Please confirm your participation not later than 20th June 2016 through your Dean or Director

Facilitator
Professor The-Hung Bui, Senior Consultant Clinical Geneticist & Fetal Medicine, Dept of Clinical Genetics & Center for Fetal Medicine Karolinska University Hospital, Sweden

Dr The-Hung Bui’s interest is in the field of clinical genetics and prenatal diagnosis and therapy, especially of genetic disorders and congenital malformations. An area of expertise is stem cell transplantation in utero, another is in prenatal genetic diagnostics (cytogenetics, molecular cytogenetics, molecular genetics, clinical genomics) and fetal ultrasound. A graduate of the Karolinska Institute, Stockholm, Sweden he is board certified in both clinical genetics and obstetrics and gynaecology. He is a Prof/Senior consultant in clinical genetics and a Senior Consultant in fetal medicine, and director of the prenatal diagnosis programme at the Karolinska University Hospital, the largest medical centre in the Nordic countries. He serves on a number of editorial boards of scientific journals, and he has published extensively in the fields of interest. He is a member of numerous scientific societies, a past President of the Swedish Society of Medical Genetics, past Secretary General of the European Association of Perinatal Medicine (EAPM) and a frequent invited speaker at national and international meetings.

About the Programme
In 2011, a university-wide Faculty Professional Development Program (FPDP) for blended learning was started. The overall aim of the program is to enable faculty members at AKU to design, teach and evaluate courses offered in a blended learning mode and provide opportunities for collaborative course design, teaching, and research across AKU entities. Thus far, the program has been offered four times, supporting fifty-eight faculty members to redesign and offer thirty courses through blended learning approaches. Thirteen of these courses have been offered more than once. This year the programme starts on July 25th 2016 and ends on March 31st 2017.

Duration
The program cycle runs for nine months. However, given the situated nature of the program, the end date for each faculty member is agreed upon at the start of the program. Cohort 5 of the FPDP will start on July 25th 2016 and end on March 31 2017. The next Faculty Professional Development Program (FPDP) for blended learning will be offered in 2018. For more information about this programme please click on Details for AKU Blended Learning Faculty Development Program

The workshop aims to support participants develop increased competence and confidence as facilitators of learning as well as provide them with resources to be more reflective about their teaching. Entry to the seminar is free. To register, please contact the Research and Policy Studies Office.


About the Seminar

This online seminar presents research by academics belonging to the Global Education Research and Teaching Team (GERT) at the University of Newcastle, Australia. This group works primarily with pre-service teachers to build teaching skills to develop more inclusive and collaborative curriculum and pedagogy. The term Global Education in the Australian context is linked to a framework of five different emphases (Curriculum Corporation, 2008);  interdependence and globalisation; identity and cultural diversity; social justice and human rights; peace building and conflict resolution; and sustainable futures. However these are not necessarily explicit in the Australian curriculum or in the pedagogy used in classrooms. The team has worked to enhance teacher classroom practice that can lead to better understanding these areas of global focus and to promote peaceful community building within the constraints of current curriculum. Although the group could theoretically cover a huge range of interests this paper will elucidate some of the team research associated with children’s sense of place and their mapping of the world; the value of cooperative learning and the difficulties in learning to use it in classrooms situations; the value of using children’s literature as a teaching tool particularly in achieving sustainable living; staff and student interpretations of intercultural understanding and how to achieve that; grouping strategies for equity in classrooms; international perspectives on global education and what that actually means; and the role of the teacher educator in developing global perspectives in curriculum.

Presenter

Dr Ruth Reynolds is an Associate Professor in the Faculty of Education and Arts at the University of Newcastle. She is editor of Journal of International Social Studies, the journal of the International Assembly of the National Council of the Social Studies (US) and is team leader of the Global Education Research and Teaching group (GERT) at the University of Newcastle, a group which focuses on teaching global education across disciplinary areas and on researching the success of their various initiatives https://global-education.net/. She has been a program convenor in Social Education in Early Childhood, Primary and Secondary teacher education for over twenty five years; has been past President of Social Educators Association of Australia [SEAA], past national conference convenor for SEAA, committee member of History Educators Network of Australia, and member of the editorial committee for The Social Educator. She has published six books in teacher education and primary teaching pedagogy, and ten books for teachers in teaching Social Education as well as numerous refereed articles, chapters in books and conference papers in the areas of pedagogy, humanities and social science curriculum and pedagogy, peace education and social justice issues. In 2010, as a result of conducting cross cultural research into intercultural understandings in young children she was awarded an International Understanding Award by the National Council for the Social Studies in USA. In 2013 she was awarded an Australian Award for University teaching with a citation for Outstanding Contributions to Student Learning for contribution to the Humanities and Social Sciences area of the curriculum. She was a guest editor for Educational Sciences (Basel) with a special edition on Global Citizenship in 2012. http://www.newcastle.edu.au/profile/ruth-reynolds

Guest Speaker
Dr Margaret Gyapong (PhD), Director, Dodowa Health Research Centre, Accra, Ghana; and  and Consultant World Health Organization: Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases (TDR)
 
Profile of the Speaker
Dr Margaret Gyapong has a PhD in Cultural Epidemiology from University of Basel,  Switzerland. In the last 20 years, Dr Gyapong has risen through the ranks of the research ladder from a research assistant to become a seasoned and internationally renowned scientist. Since 2005, Dr Gyapong has held the joint position of Deputy Director for Research and Development within the Ghana Health Service and Director of the Dodowa Health Research Centre. From humble beginnings with only a few partners, she has been able to attract several funders and grants to the institution on projects related to Neglected Tropical Diseases (NTDs), Malaria, TB and maternal health. In the last 24 years, she has worked at the intersection between health research and practice taking a key leadership role both in Ghana and globally and building research capacity in Ghana and abroad.  She has demonstrated international leadership through serving on several task forces, steering committees and working groups for the World Health Organization, the Task force for Global health, The standing committee of the National Institute of Health (NIH) Washington DC to mention a few. She is lead author and facilitator of the recently launched WHO/TDR toolkit on Implementation Research and a member of the team that put together the Global Technical Strategy for Malaria Control. She chairs the Social Working Group of the INDEPTH NETWORK and is a member of the African Social Research Initiative (ASRI) and the Partnership for Social Science in Infectious Diseases of Poverty (PSSIDP). Dr Margaret has demonstrated academic excellence with adjunct professorial positions in Georgetown University and the University of Ghana, has supervised several masters and PhD students, is a reviewer and Associate editor for several international journals and has 70 publications in peer reviewed journals to her credit.

Dr Syed Rizwanuddin Ahmad, MD, MPH, FISPE, FCP
Independent Consultant, Pharmacovigilance and Regulatory System Strengthening
Associate Professor (adjunct), Rutgers University School of Public Health, NJ, USA
Assistant Professor (adjunct), Georgetown University School of Medicine, Washington, DC, USA

Dr Syed Rizwanuddin Ahmad has been trained in drug regulatory science, pharmacovigilance, pharmacoepidemiology and clinical pharmacology.  He has over 25 years of experience in civil society organizations/non-profit groups and the United States Food and Drug Administration-FDA where he worked for 15 years (1998-2013). He is a medical graduate of  Dow Medical College; did a fellowship in clinical pharmacology and drug regulation at Georgetown University Medical Center, Washington, DC; and has a public health degree from the Johns Hopkins School of Public Health, Baltimore.

Dr. Ahmad has provided technical assistance to national medicines regulatory agencies/Ministries of Health in Asian and African countries.  He has academic appointments at Georgetown University School of Medicine (Assistant Professor) and at Rutgers School of Public Health (Associate Professor).  He has been invited to give lectures/workshops in several international meetings.

Course Aim
Psychiatric disorders are a major cause of disability in all segments of society. They affect the low income countries with the same impact as high income countries. Despite extensive reported research conducted on psychiatric disorders, there has not been any significant progress on developing definitive treatment for them. A possible reason for this could be sub-standard quality of research. Therefore, it is important to ensure that the participating scientists are well informed about latest research on psychiatric disorders and well trained in how to conduct human and animal-based research on psychiatric disorders.

Basic scientists, students and other allied and mental health professionals.

The University of Johannesburg, in collaboration with colleagues at other South African universities, including UWC, CPUT and RU, will host an international conference, which focuses on the scholarship of teaching and learning in the global South. EventDetail:
The presentation gives an overview of manuscript and wall paintings from the Tajik Museum and archive collections that portray subject matter from the Persian Shahnama epic that chronicles the pre-Islamic history and myths of Iran and Central Asia. Full of battles and romances taking place across real geographical sites in the region, the stories and scenes are not merely illustrations of a text but have political significance when the context and period of their production are analysed. Their importance has carried over to the present day, and has been harnessed by Tajiks as a means to articulate their nascent national identity.

Ms. Comstock-Skipp’s Fulbright research investigates Tajik cultural and artistic history and heritage with regards to manuscript and wall paintings that portray subject matter from the Persian Shahnama epic. This Book of Kings chronicles the pre-Islamic history of Iran and Central Asia, comparable to Greek legends and Arthurian lore in the West in terms of its cultural significance. Its circulation in the manuscript arts has been well documented and researched with regards to Iran, but its significance to Tajik ideas of nationhood and identity in the context of a greater pan-Persianism that transcends modern borders has not. 

About the speaker
Ms. Jaimee Comstock-Skipp holds a BA from the University of California, Berkeley in Near Eastern studies with a specialty in Islamic civilisations. She also holds an MA from the Williams College graduate programme in the History of Art (2012), and a second MA from the Courtauld Institute of Art in London (2015), where she studied Mongol through Safavid Persian book arts. She studied Farsi and Tajiki as part of the Critical Languages Scholarship and the Critical Languages Institute programmes in Tajikistan, and was the resident director of the National Security Language Initiative for the Youth Tajiki programme in 2013 and 2014.

Molecular biology techniques have several applications, ranging from discovery of biological processes to informing disease diagnosis, prognosis and customized treatment. The series will serve as an introduction for participants to establish a basis in molecular biology techniques that can be developed further through additional reading and research.

The first workshop of the series aims to:

  • provide an hands-on experience by enabling the participants to perform and visualize nucleic acid extraction

  • Discuss the theoretical underpinning of extraction, quantification, visualization of proteins, and perform and visualize protein extraction.
  • Discuss the theoretical underpinning of polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and perform PCR.
  • Discuss the theoretical underpinning of cloning, observe the steps involved in cloning and visualize cloned products.
  • Discuss the theoretical underpinning of immunohistochemistry, observe the steps involved in immunohistochemistry, and visualize protein expression using immunohistochemistry technique.
