EventDetail:
Depression is a principal cause of needless suffering in the world, according to evidence amassed over decades. However, depression is seldom recognised or understood, especially by people in communities, governments, and the health sector, as a distinct problem from other issues that people endure. There is less done to prevent and relieve the suffering and difficulties associated with depression, and few governments recognise the impediment that depression poses on economic and social growth. In fact, mental disorders are frequently misdiagnosed and underreported, particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa.

Depression is a prevalent condition that affects an estimated 3.8% of the global population, including 5.0% of adults and 5.7% of those over the age of 60 years. Depression affects around 280 million individuals worldwide. Every year, over 700,000 people commit suicide due to depression. Despite the fact that there are proven, effective treatments for mental diseases, more than 75% of people in low- and middle-income countries are neglected.

More significantly, depression is an obstacle to sustainable development in all regions, preventing individuals from realising their full potential, undermining human capital, and being linked to early death through suicide and other disorders. 
The Lancet - World Psychiatric Association (WPA) Commission on Depression synthesised evidence from multiple contexts and developed action-oriented recommendations for a plethora of stakeholders, including communities and individuals afflicted by depression and their families; clinicians and public health practitioners; researchers who strive to comprehend as well as manage depression; as well as policymakers and health-care financiers.

During the African launch of The Lancet-WPA Commission, where the Commissioners including Dr Dixon Chibanda will convey the key messages, while invited speakers from these stakeholders will discuss and deliberate on the significance and implementation of these recommendations.

Prof Zul Merali - Founding Director, Brain & Mind Institute

  1. Prof. Lukoye Atwoli - Dean, Medical College, Aga Khan University, East Africa and Associate Director, Brain & Mind Institute

Participant Bios

Moderator 

Prof Zul Merali
Prof Zul Merali is the Founding Director of the Brain and Mind Institute at the Aga Khan University. He is a neuroscientist and pharmacologist by training (McGill University, University of Ottawa and Wharton), with over 40 years of academic engagement. Has published over 250 peer-reviewed scientific publications. He has used his proven academic and entrepreneurial ability to add value to forward thinking organizations to help address the mental health problem, locally, nationally and globally. His objectives have been to build and/or re-engineer organizations to deliver outstanding results and motivating and encouraging others towards positive change.

Perspectives

Dr Miriam Sabin, Executive Editor, The Lancet
Has been based in New York City since March, 2020 and is The Lancet Group’s Preprints Editor. Prior to that, she worked as the Accountability Manager at the Partnership for Maternal, Newborn & Child Health, hosted by the World Health Organization in Geneva. She has also held positions in the WHO HIV Department, UNAIDS, and the Global Fund and served as an editorial board member for the Bulletin of the World Health Organization. Prior to her time in Geneva, she was a “Disease Detective” in the US CDC Epidemic Intelligence Service (EIS) and was a Senior Research Scientist Officer in the Division of Viral Hepatitis and in the Division of Global HIV/AIDS. 

She has worked in Tunisia, Bangladesh, Denmark, and Brazil and holds a PhD from the University of Georgia (USA) where she specialized in the epidemiology of refugee mental health and posttraumatic stress disorder. She has an MSc in Social Work with a minor in Research from Columbia University (USA) and a BA in English from the University of Wisconsin-Madison (USA).

Dr Afzal Javed, President, The World Psychiatric Association
Dr. Afzal Javed is a president, The World Psychiatric Association. He also holds the honorary position of Chairman Pakistan Psychiatric Research Centre, Fountain House, Lahore (Pakistan).
He graduated from King Edward Medical College Lahore, Pakistan and received higher specialised training in Psychiatry from Pakistan and UK (from Royal Edinburgh Hospital, University of Edinburgh, and Institute of Psychiatry & Maudsley Hospital London).
He has served the UK Royal College of Psychiatrists as Deputy / Associate Registrar, member Board of International Affairs of the College, Chairman of West Midlands Division of the College & one of the lead College office bearers for SAS doctors & Patients & Carers groups. He was also elected as executive committee member of the College Faculty of Rehabilitation and Social Psychiatry & represents the faculty at Education and Training Committee of the College.
His role in international psychiatry is highlighted by his involvement with several professional organisations. 

Panel Members

Dr Dixon Chibanda
Dr Chibanda started the Friendship Bench in one of Harare’s townships called Mbare in 2007 and conceptualized the first Friendship Bench intervention that has now been refined and adapted considerably.
He has been involved in mental health research for many years. Dixon is a key player in bringing the various stakeholders from local health authorities, health professionals, national and international researchers and donors together to form successful collaborations. In his role as PI, he has led the Friendship Bench team through the rigorous exercise of the randomized control trial (RCT) which was able to deliver evidence for the intervention’s effectiveness. He is currently leading the team as they scale-up the Friendship Bench to over 60 primary health care clinics in the country.
Dixon Chibanda is also Director of the African Mental Health Research Initiative (AMARI). 

Prof Lukoye Atwoli 
Prof Atwoli is the Dean of the Medical College, East Africa and a Professor in Psychiatry with extensive leadership, teaching, and academic research experience. He is the former Dean of the Moi University School of Medicine, where he excelled at building collaborations and partnerships between the School of Medicine and academic medical centres in Africa, Europe, and the US, transforming it into a regionally leading research and graduate medical school. 
Prof Atwoli has a Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery from Moi University.  His residency (Master of Medicine) in Psychiatry was undertaken at the University of Nairobi.  Prof Atwoli has a PhD from the Department of Psychiatry and Mental Health at the University of Cape Town in South Africa.  He is a Visiting Scientist at the Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health and an Honorary Associate Professor at the Department of Psychiatry and Mental Health, University of Cape Town.  He is an international Faculty member at the Global Health Institute, Duke University and an external examiner for multiple universities.

Vivian Gaiko – Founder, Empower Mama Foundation Perinatal Mental Health Support 
Vivian Gaiko, a Hermes Olympus International Youth Awardee and Zuri Awards nominee is a laboratory medicine professional and is a passionate advocate for the mental and emotional wellness of pregnant and new parents. She has trained as a perinatal mental health support by Postpartum Support International and is also a trained perinatal bereavement counselor.
Vivian uses this information and her lived experience to empower young mothers to take care of their mental health and equips the grieving parents with tools to navigate the grief journey healthily and to also advocate for themselves as pregnancy and child losses are highly stigmatized.
A grieving parent who is unsupported in their grief may fall in between the cracks of reduced productivity or even prolonged grief disorders, depression or suicide. Through Empower Mama, Vivian offers grief support groups and workshops for various community groups like workplaces, churches and women groups. More than 600 families have been directly reached and thousands others empowered with information on how to be safe and caring communities for the grieving parents.
Some parents who went through work loss after child loss have been able to start businesses in honor of their children to raise awareness and advocate for others and also as a way of putting food on the table and contributing to the country's economy. Some are in the beauty and fashion industry, others in the bakery sector and others in the fashion arena. 
Ms. Gaiko featured as a lead role a short film titled 'Utapata Mwingine' translating as 'You Will Get Another One' which has screened in several Film Festivals in Kenya, Turkey, Tanzania, Nigeria, UK, USA, Rwanda. Notably is the Women's Voices Now and the Global Voices Film Festival supported by UNWomen in September 2021 and Africa Film Festival 
Vivian was a member of the core-team that planned the first Climb Out of The Darkness® (COTD) event in Africa, in her country Kenya in 2018. COTD is a worldwide event organized by Postpartum Support International to raise awareness on perinatal mental health and support the mental health of new families. Ms. Gaiko led the 2nd climb out event in 2019 which brought together healthcare workers (gynaecologists, paediatricians, psychologists), pregnant and new mothers and their support persons to highlight this issue.
Later in 2019, Vivian and her partner introduced Parent's Light Initiative, at a public health facility in Nairobi to help integrate maternal mental health services into their existing maternal and child health services. Vivian has stood before more than 4,500 pregnant and new parents from July 2019 to March 2020 to empower them on what maternal mental illnesses are, the red flags to look out for and where and when to seek for help. 
Vivian has demonstrated that impacting one life positively especially with regards to their health, can lead to a ripple effect of empowerment. The greatest asset is health and there's no health without mental health.

EventDetail:
Between 1990 and 2013, substantial progress has been made towards realising the vision to end all preventable maternal, newborn, and child deaths. Millions of lives have been saved:  child mortality fell by 49% and maternal mortality by 45%. Nevertheless, each day more than 800 women and 7700 newborns die from complications during pregnancy and childbirth, and 7300 women experience a stillbirth.

Key factors behind the reduction of maternal and child mortality include women agency, equity and empowerment, as well as improved access to essential interventions and services. Family planning, prevention of unsafe abortion, quality antenatal and delivery care,  and skilled birth attendance have all increased over the past two decades. However, huge inequities in coverage and quality continue, and furthermore stronger effort is needed to remove barriers to access, which continue to impede success.

With a concerted effort we can eliminate wide disparities in preventable mortality and morbidity. Investment in antenatal care and childbirth can quadruple returns in terms of women’s and newborn’s lives saved and stillbirths and disabilities reduced.  In particular, by improving access to essential health interventions and building resilient health systems, we can achieve the grand convergence within a generation and create a world in which no woman, child, or adolescent faces a greater risk of preventable death just because of where they live.

In light of that, this session will focus on a candid discussion around the same by six distinguished speakers from Aga Khan University's Centre of Excellence in Women and Child Health and partners.

EventDetail:
If you have a term paper, project report, PhD / graduate dissertation due, or you're currently at different stages of your academic journey and want to publish your work; this workshop is particularly for you. This workshop will familiarise you with writing the different sections of a scientific manuscript.

Please note: interested participants are required to submit a 250 word abstract outlining the manuscript that they wish to develop during the workshop.

Topics and Highlights:
The workshop follows a scientific approach, facilitated through lectures, structured around presentations, discussions, hands-on practice, and assignments.
  • Epidemiological study designs and their implications for writing
  • Effective literature search and critical appraisal of the literature
  • Succinct writing of different sections of a manuscript
  • Good ethics and publication guidelines
  • Manuscript submission and review process
  • Expert feedback on the manuscript

Access the complete event programme here.


At the end of the session, participants will be empowered with:
  • preparing an effective title that accurately represents the content
  • constructing an abstract- ensuring that its content and structure are appropriate
  • organising material into the appropriate sections (e.g. introduction, methods, results, discussion)
  • ensuring that the text follows a correct grammatical style including correct tense (e.g. writing about established facts in the present tense and about research findings in the past)

EventDetail:
Hidden hunger is a form of undernutrition that occurs when intake and absorption of vitamins and minerals (such as zinc, iodine, and iron) are too low to sustain good health and development. It is a global health crisis, driven in large part by poverty. More than 3 billion people around the world—mostly in Africa, Asia, and Latin America—simply can’t afford a diet of nourishing, diverse foods that provide enough essential vitamins and minerals (micronutrients). According to World Health Organization (WHO), the estimated annual loss in GDP from the impacts of hidden hunger amounts to USD 3 billion in Pakistan, USD 145 million in Uganda, and USD 289 million in Tanzania. 

Sustainably embedding fortified crops in food systems requires a comprehensive approach, from the crop research and development stage to reaching the consumers of these crops. This webinar will not only explore the impacts of hidden hunger in low- and middle-income countries, but also sustainable solutions to mitigating this challenge. The programme will be enriched by some of the global leading researchers in the field.

Host and Moderator
Dr Zulfiqar A Bhutta, Distinguished University Professor & Founding Director, Institute for Global Health and Development

Welcome Remarks
'Impacts of hidden hunger in LMICs: What does the future hold?' by Dr Kauser Abdulla Malik, HEC Distinguished Professor & Dean of Postgraduate Studies, Forman Christian College

1) 'Cost-effective methods for nutritional value addition' by Dr Erick Boy, Chief Nutritionist, HarvestPlus
2) 'Exploring sustainable solutions to global malnutrition' by Dr Nicola M Lowe, Professor & Director, Research Centre for Global Development, University of Central Lancashire

Dr Shabina Raza, Country Director, Nutrition International

EventDetail:
In this inaugural lecture for the Tejpar Professorship, Philip Wood sets out his plan for his new research project on Group Formation in the Abbasid Caliphate. His earlier work has engaged with how Christian groups in the Middle East have enforced boundaries with other populations, both other Christians and with pagans, Jews and Muslims. In particular, he has examined the way that history writing has functioned as an identitarian discourse, which legitimated social boundaries in the present by referring to an idealised representation of the past.

The Group Formation project seeks to understand how ethnic and religious communities have maintained their distinctiveness over time, or failed to do so. It aims to compare Jewish, Christian and Muslim populations across Iraq and the Levant to isolate the factors that allowed some groups to survive and flourish while others did not. Previous literature on this subject has tended to approach these issues through the rate of conversion to Islam. While this is an important viewpoint, this project focusses instead on the factors that allowed a group to retain coherence in a multicultural society, on how its leaders could maintain separation from outsiders while still gaining trust and acceptance from the Abbasid state.

Speaker

Philip Wood is the inaugural Tejpar Professor of Inter-Religious Studies at the Aga Khan University's Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations (AKU-ISMC), London, and a historian of Christians in the medieval Middle East, c.500-1000. He is also interested in issues of contemporary social integration and religious education. He is the author of Imam of the Christians: The World of Dionysius of Tel-mahre, 750-850 (Princeton 2021) and co-editor with Leif Stenberg of What is Islamic Studies? European and North American Approaches to a Contested Field (Edinburgh, 2022).

* This discussion will be followed by a reception.

EventDetail:
Introduction
There has been a steep rise in the incidence of twin pregnancies in the past two decades. Maternal and perinatal complications are higher in twins than in singleton pregnancies. A significant proportion of perinatal mortality and morbidity among twins is due to the high incidence of preterm delivery and the added complication of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS) in monochorionic twins.  

Early diagnosis of twins and their chronicity, close fetal surveillance, particularly of monochorionic twins, and prompt therapeutic intervention in TTS are necessary to reduce perinatal mortality.

Course Objectives
  • Understand the basic pathophysiology of  complicated twin pregnancies
  • Appreciate the rationale for managing selective fetal growth restriction in DCDA and MCDA twins
  • Critically analyze the evidence-based management of twins with discordant anomalies

Dr. Ayesha Malik, Department of OBGYN, Aga Khan University Hospital, Karachi

Speakers

  • Dr. Zaheena Islam, Department of OBGYN, Aga Khan University Hospital, Karachi
  • Dr. Dur e Shahwar, Department of OBGYN, Aga Khan University Hospital, Karachi

Who should attend
  • OBGYN Consultants and Trainees
  • Pediatric Consultant and Trainees

Topics 
  • Discordant anomalies in Twin pregnancies
  • Twin-Twin Transfusion Syndrome
  • Understanding Basics of Twin pregnancies
  • Selective Fetal Growth restriction and TRAP Syndrome in MCDA twins

Highlight
  • Pre and post workshop reading material will be provided

EventDetail:
We are delighted to invite you to the book launch of Islam and Modernism by Rasheed Araeen on Tuesday 6 December 2022 at the Aga Khan Centre in London.

A﻿bout the Book

Can art from the Muslim world be authentically modern and also express the spirit of Islam? The answer to this is yes. But this answer has little significance unless it is underpinned theoretically and legitimised institutionally; and the Muslim world does not yet have the ability to do this. The prevailing theories of modern art are Eurocentric within which there is no place of Islam. And although there is now tremendous creativity in the Muslim world, with its art festivals and biennales, and the success of its artist worldwide, it does not have its own art institutions, with the ability to recognise, theoretically and historically, what its artists do. All this is still dependent on the West. The task for the Muslim world now is therefore to establish its own institutions, according to its own view of things and values, to develop and promote scholarship, involving theories of art based on its own understanding of history, which would not only liberate it from its subservience to the West but also enable its modern artists to think and create freely and independently. This work of Rasheed Araeen is an attempt towards achieving these objectives.

Speakers

Rasheed Araeen is an artist, writer and the Founding Editor of Third Text. He is also the designer of Rhapsody in Four Colours sculpture at the heart of the Aga Khan Centre. As an artist, he began his journey in Pakistan in 1953, whilst also studying civil engineering. After doing some important works in Karachi, seminal to his subsequent pursuits, he came to the UK in 1964 and since then lives in London. In the 1960's and 1970's, he became active in various groups supporting liberation struggles, democracy and human rights, which in fact led him to writing 'Black Manifesto' (1975-76); and then to numerous publications: Black Phoenix (1978-79), Third Text (1987-2011), and Third Text Asia (2008-09). His present concern is with the Muslim world, for the promotion of its past achievements and what it can now do to be part of the modern world according to its own view of things, values and vision.

Jonas Otterbeck is Professor of Islamic Studies and holder of the Rasul-Walker Endowed Chair in Popular Culture in Islam at the Aga Khan University's Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations (AKU-ISMC). Professor Otterbeck is engaged in research about contemporary Islam. His most recent research is on Islamic art and popular culture. He also has an interest in research on music censorship and an engagement for artists’ right to expression.

Rebecca Heald is an independent curator and researcher specialising in the relationship between art and architecture and unwritten art histories. She has worked with leading organisations including Southbank Centre, Aga Khan Development Network, Tate, British Council, Art on the Underground, Argent, High Speed 2 and Oxford University Development.

*Refreshments will be available following the discussion.

Introduction 
Adolescents across the world face considerable challenges to their sexual and reproductive health and rights. These include: sexual coercion and intimate partner violence; lack of education and information; high rates of early and unwanted pregnancy; lack of access to health services, especially for contraception and safe abortion; gender inequalities and harmful traditional practices, such as female genital mutilation (FGM) and child, early and forced marriage; and risk of STIs (including HIV).
 

Course Objectives
-Understand the rights of adolescents and youth regarding access to sexual and reproductive health  (SRHR) knowledge and services 
-Build skills to respond to resistance in conservative context for provision of Sexual and Reproductive Health Education among adolescents 
-Understand the importance of Comprehensive Sexuality Education (CSE) for adolescents
-Understand and address barriers to access and use of contraception by adolescents (Adolescent-Friendly Services)

EventDetail:
As leaders, educators, parents and those responsible for grooming and nurturing children we need to work from a place of empathy. However, no matter what role we play in the life of a child, working from a place of empathy is not possible when we are disconnected from ourselves. 

This workshop is an opportunity to begin your journey towards a place of empathy through self awareness and inner transformation by reconnecting to your inner child.

You will:
  • Acquire a basic understanding of childhood trauma, abuse and its impact
  • Reconnect with your inner child to cultivate a sense of self-awareness
  • Learn to navigate daily routines and decisions from a place of empathy
  • Develop a greater sense of purpose by viewing adversities as opportunities
  • Understand the role of a caring adult in reversing the cycle of abuse
The workshop includes teaching, ice-breakers, experiential learning, interactive group sessions, roleplays, case-studies (lived experiences of trauma stories shared by the facilitator), videos and discussions, instructor-led activities, meditation and more.

Who should attend 
  • Teachers, parents, caregivers who work with children/youth and find it challenging to connect with or support them
  • Others who are interested in self awareness and inner transformation

Fee
PKR 14,500 per participant (inclusive of 5% Sindh Sales Tax) 

Facilitator
Ms Sabina Khatri, Sitara-e-Imtiaz; Founder and Chairperson, Kiran Foundation; and Honorary Senior Teaching Fellow, AKU-IED

Timings
9:30 am-5:30 pm

About the facilitator and workshop series
This workshop series was developed by Ms Sabina Khatri, the founder of the first and only Trauma-Informed, Mother-Child School System in Pakistan. It is rooted in the learnings from her 20 years of direct experience in working with children who have had a difficult childhood and a history of adverse childhood experiences. Though this workshop draws from trauma-informed knowledge and educational theories, the purpose of this workshop is not to intellectualize but rather to humanize the experience of understanding ourselves and others.

After immersing herself in community, Ms Khatri developed a rationale of her own, bringing together a deep understanding of our culture, values, and beliefs to trauma-informed education. This workshop will provide a microcosm of this framework. The aim is to discover and reconnect with the empath inside you through self-awareness and healing. Come on this journey with us!

EventDetail:
Following the inauguration of the Aga Khan University Hospital in 1986, the first postgraduate clinical training programs were launched to mark the beginning of Postgraduate Medical Education. Keeping in line with the educational mission of the University, in 1995, these programs were shifted to the purview of Aga Khan University (AKU) to enhance the educational and scholarly components of these programs.

The growing needs of the national healthcare system drove the expansion of the program from the initial 4 programs to 70+ programs currently being offered. The 700+ postgraduate trainee workforce imparts quality healthcare by acting as frontline healthcare workers at AKUH. 

The emphasis and scope of PGME’s education of training programs at AKUH encompass not only the acquisition of medical knowledge but also inculcating attributes such as communication skills, biomedical ethics, teaching skills, research methodology, and critical thinking while making its impact on national health systems. 

Of the 2000+ graduating residents and fellows, many are now serving as faculty and staff of teaching national and international institutions, whereas few of them are in leadership positions. Around one-third of the University’s clinical faculty at AKUH are PGME graduates. 

Some of the AKU’s PGME programs have been internationalized and established in East Africa as well as in Afghanistan. Last year PGME celebrated its 25 years and organized a series of events that mark the silver jubilee. 

Who should attend: Graduating Residents, Fellows and their families.

Infections are one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality around the globe. General practitioners, family physicians and internists are the frontline care providers for patients with infections, however, there is a significant lack of formal training in Infectious Diseases in our country. To address this gap, the Infectious Diseases Review Course has been designed to make physicians aware of the common infectious diseases that they come across in their day-to-day practice to improve patient outcomes. To identify the clinical presentation and management of common infectious diseases.

Following a keynote speech from Dr Kumanan Rasanathan, we will have Dr Karl Blanchet and Dr Zulfiqar Bhutt join a discussion between our Professors Shehla Zaidi and Jeff Tan, and chaired by D﻿r Sevgi Adak and moderated by Dr Natasha Palmer.

The panel will explore how various political, economic, and social factors shape the health outcomes of populations in Pakistan, and the challenges and opportunities in addressing health disparities. Panellists will share their insights on the impact of power dynamics, governance, policy making, and social structures on health outcomes and access to healthcare in Pakistan.

Attendees will have the opportunity to engage in a thought-provoking discussion, ask questions to the panellists, and learn from their expertise.

Drinks and canapes will be served.

Don't miss this opportunity to gain valuable insights into the complexities of global health and its social determinants in Pakistan. Register now to secure your spot at this informative and thought-provoking panel discussion!

  • Dr Karl Blanchet is the Director of the Geneva Centre of Humanitarian Studies and a Professor in Humanitarian Public Health at the Faculty of Medicine, University of Geneva.
  • Dr Shehla Zaidi is a Professor and joint faculty of Aga Khan University Pakistan and AKU (International) in the United Kingdom. She leads a portfolio of Health Policy & Systems Research with a focus on power and politics within policy, governance and financing. She has trained professionals serving in leadership capacity in Pakistan and Afghanistan, contributed to country policies and serves an expert in several international forums.
  • Dr Jeff Tan is Associate Professor of Political Economy at AKU-ISMC, has been a consultant to the UN Special Rapporteur on the Human Rights to Safe Drinking Water and Sanitation, and was principal investigator on a British Academy-funded project on community-based water management in Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan.
  • Dr Zulfiqar Bhutta is the Distinguished University Professor and Founding Director of the Institute for Global Health and Development and the Centre of Excellence in Women and Child Health, at the Aga Khan University. He also holds the Robert Harding Inaugural Chair in Global Child Health at the Hospital for Sick Children, Toronto, Co-Director of the SickKids Centre for Global Child Health a unique joint appointments.
  • Dr Kumanan Rasanathan is the Executive Director at Alliance for Health Policy & Systems Research and a public health physician with a strong background in health policy and systems research and extensive experience working at different levels of the World Health Organization and within the wider UN system. During his almost 25 years working in health systems, career highlights have included serving as Incident Manager for WHO for the COVID-19 response in Cambodia, helping to drive the development of the Sustainable Development Goal health agenda while at UNICEF, contributing to the work of the WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health, co-writing the 2008 WHO World Health Report on primary health care, and running meningococcal vaccine trials that enabled vaccine licensure and roll-out in New Zealand.
  • D﻿r Sevgi Adak is Associate Professor in Gender and Middle East Studies and Head of Research at AKU-ISMC. She completed her PhD in Middle Eastern Studies at Leiden University, the Netherlands. She holds MA and MPhil degrees in political science, from York University (Toronto) and Central European University (Budapest), respectively, and a second MA in history from Sabanci University (Istanbul). Prior to joining AKU-ISMC in January 2016, she was a research fellow at the International Institute for Social History, Amsterdam, and taught at Istanbul Bahçeşehir University. She is one of the editors of the Contemporary Turkey book series of IB Tauris and the British Institute at Ankara, and co-editor of the In Translation: Contemporary Thought in Muslim Contexts book series of the Edinburg University Press, published in association with the AKU-ISMC.
  • Dr Natasha Palmer is a Senior Research Fellow at the Institute for Global Health and Development at Queen Margaret University, Edinburgh. She has a PhD in Health Economics from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine and over 25 years experience working in health systems and health financing research and consulting. She has particular interest in health systems evaluation, health financing, non state actors in health and the role of Global Health Initiatives in health systems.

EventDetail:
• Introduction:

Stem cells are undifferentiated or partially differentiated cells capable of self-renewal that can differentiate into other cell types and tissues. Stem cell research in recent years has produced considerable implications for improving quality of life by providing new therapies for a number of conditions, including bone marrow transplantation, metabolic and autoimmune diseases, as well as certain cancers. The spectacular progress of basic stem cell and regenerative medicine research has led to a number of clinical trials across the world, leading to new prospects within all surgical specialties. 

At the 2020 global convocation of Aga Khan University (AKU), the Chancellor, His Highness the Aga Khan highlighted the role of AKU in building its capacity for cutting-edge research applicable to the distinctive health risks for populations in Asia and Africa. To this aim, the Chancellor had said “It [AKU] will seek to harness the enormous potential of advances in artificial intelligence, genomic medicine and stem cell science to address tomorrow’s challenges as well as today’s". 

With the redefined role of the Centre for Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research (CRM) under AKU Medical College (MC), this conference will provide a platform for the CRM faculty and researchers to build collaborations with AKU’s broader intellectual network, MC multidisciplinary teams and importantly with the surgeons at the department of surgery. This will positively enhance prospects of translating stem cell research from bench to bedside to fulfil the Chancellor’s vision as its goal.

  • Objectives:
To develop and support a highly collaborative environment for the stem cell research, clinical translation and education;
cultivate a broad range of interdisciplinary stem cell research (i.e., basic and translational research); and
encourage rapid translation of discoveries into innovative and practical clinical applications that will enhance the understanding, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of multiple human diseases.

• Moderator/s OR Course Directors OR Session Leadership
  1. Chair, Surgery: Prof. Saleem Islam
  2. Chair, Conference: Dr. Fazlur Rahman
  3. Chair Scientific Committee: Prof. Syed Ather Enam, SI
  4. Chair, Basic Sciences: Dr. Azhar Hussain
  5. Chair, Workshop Committee: Dr. Nadeem Siddiqui
  6. Chair, Publication Committee: Dr. Sana Zeeshan

• Who should attend:

Attendees include surgeons, surgical trainees, medical students, nurses, researchers, young scientists, academicians, educationists and allied specialties. 

• Topics: 
  1. The sub-themes will cover, but are not limited to the following:
  2. Safety and efficacy of stem cell therapy in various surgical subspecialties
  3. Sources/origin of stem cell and harvesting techniques 
  4. Stem cell manipulation and expansion
  5. Stem cell isolation, cryopreservation, and storage
  6. The implication and outcomes of stem cell therapy in oncology
  7. Diagnostic role of stem cells
  8. Utility of stem cells in regenerative and reconstructive therapies
  9. Stem cell therapies - ethics and legislation in LMICs context

EventDetail:
The Aga Khan University Graduate School of Media and Communications (GSMC) with support from the German Development Bank (KfW) is seeking to promote quality health reporting in East Africa through an impact-driven fellowship. This fellowship titled Excellence in Journalism will see 30 successful applicants undergo an 8-week programme which will support them with funding to do and publish quality stories. The programme will also provide training to build their capacity, and mentorship from journalism and environmental experts to guide them on the journey. 

 

GSMC is inviting journalists to submit proposals for cohort four of the programme. Applications will involve identification of a unique, emerging, or prevalent climate change issue which may be under reported along with a detailed execution plan. Successful candidates will be expected to conduct research and interviews, develop multimedia stories and have their stories published in a media outlet within the EAC region.

 

Stories should demonstrate clear understanding of the climate change issue being reported, have depth, be original and authentic, meet journalistic standards and provide pointers to possible solutions.

 

Applications are welcome from across the East Africa Community member states including Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Democratic Republic of Congo and Burundi. 

 

Successful applicants may receive up to $700 in financial support to complete their story.

 

Application Overview

  • Personal contact information 
  • Story idea and proposal: Provide a brief of the story you intend to report about and explain how you intend to execute it (maximum 200 words)
  • Indicate the media outlet where you intend to have it published
  • Commitment from the editor that the story will be published 
  • Two references
  • An updated copy of your CV/Resume. 

Click this link to complete the online application: bit.ly/3K3ynUu

About the presenter:

Dr Muhammad Jameel, Post-doctoral Fellow

Dr Muhammad Jameel has a profound interest in the fields of laboratory genetics and genomics, molecular genetic pathology and cytogenetics. 

He completed his PhD in Biotechnology, focusing on human molecular genetics from the National Institute for Biotechnology and Genetic Engineering (NIBGE), Faisalabad, in 2016. As part of his PhD research, he worked on advanced next-generation sequencing techniques at the Institute for Genetics and Pathology, and Biomedical Centrum, Uppsala University, Sweden. 

After his PhD, Dr Jameel joined the Human Molecular Genetics lab, at the Health Biotechnology Division, NIBGE as a senior researcher. He also served as an assistant professor at the Centre for Human Genetics, Hazara University, Mansehra. Before joining AKU-CRM, he was working as a post-doctoral researcher at the Human Molecular Genetics lab, Health Biotechnology Division, NIBGE, Faisalabad. Dr Jameel has 17 publications in well-reputed journals.

EventDetail:
The HD4 Pakistan Conference has been organised by AKU's Health Data Science Centre as a three-day event to showcase the studies done, and methods adopted in health care research utilising data science. The conference is divided into three themes; each theme will have a keynote address followed by talks on the methodological and implementation aspect of data science within that theme.

Day 1: 3rd March
  • Inaugural event: 5:00 pm - 7:35 pm
  • Networking dinner: 7:35 pm onwards
 
Day 2: 4th March
  • Session 1: Non-communicable diseases – 09:00 am - 11:10 am
  • Session 2: Maternal, neonatal, and child health – 11:10 am - 12:35 pm
  • Session 3: Infectious Diseases -– 2:00 pm - 3:25 pm
  • Health Data Science Pitches: 3:25 pm - 4:20 pm

THEME 1: NON-COMMUNICABLE DISEASES
The principal goals of this theme are to provide a broad overview of how health data is being used in the diagnosis and treatment of NCDs, and how the knowledge and skills needed to plan research on NCDs while utilizing heath data can be developed, as well as how epidemiological studies can be conducted by employing health data.

THEME 2: INFECTIOUS DISEASES
This section of the conference aims to ignite new research on data science approaches for infectious disease surveillance, modelling and control. It has become evident that big data and data science approaches are indispensable for the effective control of infectious diseases. There was always a gap between conventional public health and data science researchers. We hope that we can bridge this gap by featuring contributions from experts in both fields.

THEME 3: MATERNAL & CHILD HEALTH
Health data holds the answers to helping healthcare professionals guide wellness, inform the delivery of care, and lower the cost of care delivered. In LMICs, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning have greater potential to improve maternal and child health outcomes. The aim of this section of the conference is to explore the new opportunities of research that health data offers for improving health services and reducing cost of care.

At this conference, we will be joined by leading health care researchers from around the world for talks and panel discussions. The event also includes two workshops on 1) Improving Health using AI-based Techniques and Tools: Mental Health as a Case Study, 2) Text Analytics in Healthcare, conducted by experienced and renowned data science professionals. 

WORKSHOPS
Workshop 1 (2nd March 2023): Improving Health using AI-based Techniques and Tools: Mental Health as a Case Study
  • To provide a broad overview of AI applications in healthcare
  • To introduce AI-based techniques & tools in health
  • To introduce the impact of AI in mental health
Workshop 2 (3rd March 2023): Text Analytics in Healthcare
  • To develop an understanding of text analytics in the healthcare sector.
  • To introduce use cases and applications of AI on textual health data.
  • To demonstrate NLP tools on health data sets

Project Pitches
This conference is providing a platform for brilliant minds from various distinguished universities within Pakistan to sell their ideas and present thorough analyses that demonstrate their knowledge about modern health data science solution in the three distinct thematic areas of this event.

Organised By
The Health Data Science Center in collaboration with the Department of Medicine and the Department of Continuing Professional Education, Aga Khan University.

EventDetail:
This six-day course aims to give an overview of some important moments in medieval and modern Islamic history and in different theoretical approaches to the study of Islam and Muslims, such as the works of Edward Said and Talal Asad. It focuses on the Middle East and South Asia.

It does not aspire to give a complete chronological or geographical coverage, but it does aim to introduce key concepts and events that will be of relevance for anyone studying or teaching Islam. The course takes a social scientific perspective and does not assume any prior knowledge.

Aims of the course
  • Understand different theories for the formation of the Qur’an.
  • Situate Islamic theological developments into their political context
  • Evaluate the use of the terminology of ‘religion’ in the study of Islam
C﻿ourse Leader

Professor Philip Wood is a historian of the Middle East at AKU-ISMC. He is the current holder of the endowed Tejpar Chair in  Interreligious Studies. He has written widely on the histories of religious minorities in the caliphate and on the experience of Muslims as minorities in Britain. Together with Professor Leif Stenberg, he recently published What is Islamic Studies? He is also editing a second volume on Muslim and non-Muslim religious minorities in the Abbasid caliphate. His third monograph, on the Abbasid-era intellectual Dionysius of Tel-Mahre, was released with Princeton University Press in 2021.

EventDetail:
The course attempts to introduce participants to understanding ways in which Muslims use the Qur’an in practice in both religious and social contexts. After initially situating the Qur’an as a religious text within the context of Muslim beliefs and perceptions, the remaining sessions will explore the use of the Qur’an in calligraphy, in healing rituals, and in Sufi practices.

Aims of the course
  • Understand Muslim beliefs and perceptions about the Qur’an
  • Explore the recitation and writing of the Qur’an, including the skill and art of calligraphy
  • Consider activities that draw on the Qur’an as a source of comfort, healing and protection
  • Explore Sufi beliefs and practices as derived from the Qur’an
Course Leaders

Dr Walid Ghali is an Associate Professor at AKU-ISMC. He received his PhD from the Faculty of Arts, Cairo University, in 2012. Dr Ghali is Head Librarian at the Aga Khan Centre, where his current research focuses on the Islamic manuscript traditions, including Qur’anic manuscripts. He also teaches various subjects for MA students including Introduction to Sufism, Arabic Literature, and Muslim Thinkers in the 19th Century.

Professor Farouk Topan is a Professor Emeritus at AKU-ISMC. He has  published widely on his research interests which cover Islam in East Africa, Swahili  literature, language, and culture. His published works include Polemics and Language in Swahili Translations of the Qur’an: Mubarak Ahmad (2001), Abdullah Saleh al-Farsy (1982) and Ali Muhsin al-Barwani (2006), The Qur’an and Its Readers Worldwide: Contemporary Commentaries and Translations (2015), Approaches to the Qur’an in Sub-Saharan Africa (2019).

EventDetail:
AKU-ISMC’s new Centre for the Languages of the Muslim World is delighted to offer this short course as part of its Professional Development series. The course is aimed at professionals, scholars and students who work with Arabic text and would like to acquire knowledge of transliteration systems and gain or improve their practical transliteration skills under the guidance of experienced tutors. The course is a 5-hour practical workshop-style course taught in two highly interactive sessions. Both sessions incorporate tailored feedback from the tutors; prior to session II, participants are required to submit a short sample transliteration for discussion during the session. The course is equally well suited to native and non-native speakers of Arabic. 

Aims of the course
  • Develop an understanding of transliteration and transcription, linguistic issues, contextual needs, and specific problems of Arabic-to-roman rendering
  • Familiarisation with the various conventions and scholarly traditions
  • Practise contextually appropriate practical transliteration, with tailored feedback from the tutors
Course Leader

Dr Alex Bellem is a Linguist and Arabist, and Assistant Professor at AKU-ISMC, where she leads on developing the Institute’s new Centre for the Languages of the Muslim World. She specialises in comparative–theoretical phonology (& phonetics) and Arabic dialectology, with expertise in the languages & linguistics of the Middle East and contiguous regions. She collaborates with Rex Smith in a project on the language of texts composed in Literary Mixed (“Middle”) Arabic and has previously collaborated on projects on the Modern South Arabian languages Mehri and Sheret (Jibbali). She has broader research interests in folk literature, and in cultural heritage, and has also published on Iraqi folk poetry. She has held academic posts at Durham University, Salford University and the CBRL British Institute (Amman & Damascus), and at these institutions as well as SOAS she has extensive experience teaching linguistics, Arabic translation, and Arabic language she holds a PhD in Arabic Linguistics from SOAS, an MA from UCL (Linguistics), and a BA from Manchester University (Turkish & Arabic).

Course Co-Facilitator 

Professor G. Rex Smith is Visiting Professor in the School of Languages, Cultures and Societies, University of Leeds, and Professor Emeritus of the University of Manchester. He has taught and researched Arabic language and culture in a career spanning many years, and held academic posts at the Universities of Cambridge, Durham, Manchester and Leeds. He has published widely on (classical and “Middle”) Arabic, Yemeni history and culture, and Middle Eastern travel literature (both Arabic and French). Much of that research has involved translations from Arabic; perhaps most significantly his 2008 annotated translation of the 13th-century journey of Ibn al-Mujāwir, A Traveller in Thirteenth-Century Arabia. Among many other publications, Professor Smith co-authored a book on the Arabic scripts, A Brief Introduction to the Arabic Alphabet (with John F. Healey, Saqi Books, 2009). His two current projects are translations of the travel writing of the French littérateur Pierre Loti (Gerlach Press, 2021, 2022), and collaborative work with Alex Bellem on a comparative study of linguistic features of Literary Mixed (“Middle”) Arabic. He has a BA from SOAS in Classical Arabic, and an MA and PhD from the University of Cambridge.

EventDetail:
It’s not only about who tells the story. It’s also about how the story is told

 

As the world climbs out of the corona crisis, we face the threefold threat of climate change, deepening polarisation and media companies’ bleeding economies. The impacts of the climate crisis are already being felt, not least in sub-Saharan Africa. Authoritarian regimes are growing bolder as major democracies are being torn apart from within. Countless media went down during the pandemic and many of those remaining fight for their existence. However, journalists rose to the challenge of reporting on a global pandemic and met their societies’ needs, resulting in increased trust in reputable news brands and rising audiences. 

 

Now reporting must adapt to the current realities. Because, while much journalism is on track, some of today’s journalism seems to boost polarisation, news fatigue and news avoidance, not least among younger generations. We need to rethink and examine how journalism can be sustainable in itself, and at the same time better contribute to democratic, resilient and sustainable societies. This is equally true in East Africa, the Nordic countries, as in any part of the world.

 

The Aga Khan University Graduate School of Media and Communications (GSMC) together with Fojo Media Institute and Wits Centre for Journalism invite you to the Sustainable Journalism in Practice Conference that will bring together stakeholders to discuss new ways of doing journalism, that is constructive, sustainable and grounded in an African context and based on the core values of independent, public interest journalism.

 

Conference Leads

 

  • Lars Tallert - President of the Sustainable Journalism Partnership, Senior advisor at Fojo/Linnaeus University and Sweden’s representative to UNESCO’s IPDC Intergovernmental Council.
  • Prof. Nancy Booker - Interim Dean, GSMC
Title: Sustainable Journalism in Practice Conference
Venue: The Aga Khan University Graduate School of Media and Communications in Nairobi, Kenya

The Department for Educational Development (DED), Faculty of Health Sciences (FHS) at the Aga Khan University (AKU) aspires to emerge as a Centre of excellence in Health Professions Education (HPE) in the region. To celebrate AKU-ISMC’s publication of Muslim Cultures of the Indian Ocean: Diversity and Pluralism, Past and Present, please join Professors Stéphane Pradines and Farouk Topan and their guests Dr Farah Faizal, High Commissioner of the Republic of the Maldives, and Dr Annabel Teh Gallop, Head of Southeast Asia at the British Library, for a discussion of this rich crossroads of Muslim cultures.

A﻿bout the Book

Scholars are increasingly recognising the centrality of the Indian Ocean in the study of Muslim cultures. This volume, edited by AKU-ISMC's Professors Stéphane Pradines and Farouk Topan, explores the expanding and changing roles of these Muslim communities across the Indian Ocean world, from the seventh century to the medieval period to the present day. The book goes beyond the usual focus on geographical sub-regions to highlight different aspects of interconnectivity in relation to Islam. By analysing textual and material evidence, the fifteen papers in this volume examine identities and diasporas, manuscripts and literature, as well as vernacular and religious architecture. It explores the networks and movements of peoples, ideas and ideologies, as well as art, culture, religion and heritage.

Speakers

Stéphane Pradines is an archaeologist and Professor of Islamic Art and Architecture and the lead of the Indian Ocean programme at the Aga Khan University's Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations (AKU-ISMC) in London. Pradines is also a UNESCO, WMF and Google Arts expert for the Indian Ocean region. He is associate researcher to the CNRS Lab in Paris: UMR 8167 Orient & Méditerranée, Atlas of Medieval ports programme. He was the director of the excavations of the walls of Cairo (Egypt) and at excavations in the Indian Ocean (Maldives) and East Africa (Gedi in Kenya, Kilwa and Mafia in Tanzania, Mayotte in Comoros). He is now in charge of the excavations of the Lahore Fort, Pakistan (AKTC-SP). His latest book is Historic Mosques in Sub-Saharan Africa: From Timbuktu to Zanzibar (2022) and he is the Editor-in-Chief of the Journal of Material Cultures in the Muslim World. 

Farouk Topan is Professor Emeritus at the Aga Khan University's Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations (AKU-ISMC). He has also taught at the Universities of Dar es Salaam, Nairobi, Riyad and the School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London. His research interests and publications are in the fields of Swahili language, literature and identity; Islam in East Africa; spirit possession. He is also a writer of Swahili fiction and has published several short stories and two of his plays have been part of the school curriculum in Tanzania.

Dr Farah Faizal is the High Commissioner of the Republic of the Maldives in the United Kingdom. She has a PhD from the University of Keele, where her thesis was on Security Problems of Small Island Developing States (SIDS) with particular reference to the SIDS of the Indian Ocean. She is the co-author of A Clearing in the Thicket: Women, Security, South Asia (2005), which explores women's perspectives on security and related policy, focusing on women in South Asia who are battling society, insecurity and violence.

Dr Annabel Teh Gallop is Head of Southeast Asia at the British Library, with a specialism in Maritime Southeast Asia. Working with Malay and Indonesian manuscripts, she has a particular interest in letters, documents and seals, and in the illumination of the Qur’an and other Islamic manuscripts from Southeast Asia. She was co-director of the British Academy-funded research project Islam, Trade and Politics across the Indian Ocean (2009-2012), investigating Ottoman links with Southeast Asia.

EventDetail:
Join us for the 1st lecture of the AKU-ISMC Guest Professor Programme in which Professor Aaron Hughes will address a pressing issue facing modern liberal democracies, imagined as particularly acute in the aftermath of 9/11: when and how to accommodate religious minorities. The latter are often subsumed under the rather problematic and open-ended rubric “Muslims.” This has resulted in numerous political and legal attempts to confront, categorise, and ultimately control internal Muslim communities, just as it has been used to keep external ones at bay. This Muslim Question, however, is often less about actual Muslims than it is about idealised and reified ones, what Professor Hughes calls “the ubiquitous Muslim,” someone who is imagined to threaten so-called Western values from within. In this lecture, Professor Hughes will address how this “ubiquitous Muslim” — everywhere yet nowhere, named but nameless, both unsettled and unsettling—subsequently aids in the recalibration of now politicised commitments to perceived founding ideals, such as liberty and equality.

Speaker

Aaron Hughes is the Dean's Professor of the Humanities and Philip S. Bernstein Professor of Religion at the University of Rochester, USA. He is also Visiting Guest Professor at the Aga Khan University’s Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations (AKU-ISMC). Professor Hughes is the author of of numerous books on Islam and religion, including , most recently, An Anxious Inheritance Religious Others and the Shaping of Sunni Orthodoxy (Oxford University Press, 2022), From Seminary to University: An Institutional History of the Study of Religion in Canada (University of Toronto Press, 2020), Muslim and Jew: Origins, Growth, Resentment (Routledge, 2019), and Shared Identities: Medieval and Modern Imaginings of Judeo-Islam (Oxford University Press, 2017). For the 2022/23 academic year, he holds the Fulbright Distinguished Chair in North American Studies at Carleton University in Ottawa, Canada.

EventDetail:
Self-harm, a complex and often misunderstood behavior, is prevalent among many individuals, particularly adolescents and young adults, and is closely associated with mental ill-health such as depression and anxiety. However, due to the stigma attached to it, self-harm is often subject to misconceptions and judgmental attitudes, which further exacerbate the problem.

To observe Self-Injury Awareness Day, BMI will host a workshop with individuals who have experienced the devastating impact of suicide, suicide-lived experiences, or incidents of self-harm. We believe that lived experience insights can be informative in shaping effective suicide prevention strategies, treatment, policy and after care support. The event will also include policymakers, researchers, and providers of service who specialize in supporting individuals affected by suicide loss and self-harm.

In the same breath, we will have a round table discussion to explore the topic of self-harm and societal attitudes towards it. We will discuss the reasons behind self-harm, the warning signs, and its impact on individuals, their families, and society. We will also examine the stigma associated with self-harm and how it can hinder individuals from seeking help.

The discussion will aim to promote empathy towards those who self-harm by helping participants understand the underlying issues that lead to this behaviour.

The goal is to break down the stigma associated with self-harm and promote a culture of empathy and understanding. By the end of the discussion, we hope to have a deeper understanding and be better equipped to support those who engage in self-harm.
EventSubTitle: Understanding self-harm: Is our society empathetic or judgmental

EventDetail:
The Brain Awareness Week is observed worldwide, to help increase awareness about the importance of brain health and brain research.  At the Brain and Mind Institute (BMI), we celebrate the importance of brain research, promote brain health, and highlight the advancements and benefits of scientific discovery in matters of the brain and mind.

Brain science is particularly vital to the global south (including East Africa and South and Central Asia), where there is a significant burden of neurological and mental health disorders. The Brain and Mind Institute is contributing to brain research through various initiatives, including partnering with organizations such as the Davos Alzheimer's Collaborative. Together, we are establishing a Dementia Hub to advance Alzheimer's research, improve culturally sensitive care, and expand access to innovative treatments across the global south. Our data aims to contribute to a better global understanding of Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia, with a focus on vulnerable and underserved populations, accelerating the development of novel treatments based on a precision medicine approach.

The Brain Awareness Week provides a valuable opportunity to celebrate the complexity and importance of the brain, increase awareness about brain health, and highlight the advancements made in brain research. Furthermore, brain science can have a significant impact on addressing the burden of neurological and mental health disorders, especially in the regions served by AKU. Through continued research and partnerships, we also hope to reduce stigma surrounding mental illness, and develop innovative treatments to help those suffering in silence. So, during the Brain Awareness Week let us reflect on the organ that you often don’t think about – but is responsible for your thoughts, feelings, actions, memories and your personality; an organ that defines who you really are. The BMI’s vison is “Healthy Brain, Healthy World”.

EventDetail:
Organized by the Data Innovation Office, this webinar will focus on understanding exceptional cases encountered during the application of the Kenya Data Protection laws. 

The Kenya Data Protection Act of 2019 provides a comprehensive legal framework for the protection of personal data in Kenya. However, the Act also contains several exceptions that allow for the processing of personal data without consent or other safeguards in certain circumstances. These exceptions include national security, public interest, journalistic purposes, historical or scientific research, and others. Understanding these exceptions and their application is crucial for data controllers and processors who operate in Kenya or deal with Kenyan data subjects.  

In this webinar, we will explore the scope and rationale of these exceptions and discuss case studies, as well as the challenges and risks they pose for data protection compliance. We will also discuss some best practices and recommendations for navigating these exceptions in a responsible and ethical manner. The webinar will be led by an expert in Kenyan data protection law and will feature a Q&A session at the end.  

Whether you are a researcher, a journalist, or a data enthusiast, this webinar will help you gain a deeper understanding of the exceptions in the Kenya Data Protection Act and how they affect your data processing activities. 

The event will be held virtually.  

Entry is free upon registration.

EventDetail:
The Aga Khan University Graduate School of Media and Communications (GSMC) together with Fojo Media Institute and Wits Centre for Journalism invite you to the Sustainable Journalism in Practice Conference that will bring together stakeholders to discuss new ways of doing journalism, that is constructive, sustainable and grounded in an African context and based on the core values of independent, public interest journalism.

 

As the world climbs out of the corona crisis, we face the threefold threat of climate change, deepening polarisation and media companies’ bleeding economies. The impacts of the climate crisis are already being felt, not least in sub-Saharan Africa. Authoritarian regimes are growing bolder as major democracies are being torn apart from within. Countless media went down during the pandemic and many of those remaining fight for their existence. However, journalists rose to the challenge of reporting on a global pandemic and met their societies’ needs, resulting in increased trust in reputable news brands and rising audiences. 

 

Now reporting must adapt to the current realities. Because, while much journalism is on track, some of today’s journalism seems to boost polarisation, news fatigue and news avoidance, not least among younger generations. We need to rethink and examine how journalism can be sustainable in itself, and at the same time better contribute to democratic, resilient and sustainable societies. This is equally true in East Africa, the Nordic countries, as in any part of the world.

EventDetail:
This annual exploratory and informal workshop offers the opportunity to reflect on methodologies, research agendas, and case studies for investigating history writing in Arabic in the Middle East, North Africa, and beyond in any period from the seventh century to the present. 

We are interested in papers that consider the practical and conceptual challenges of working on history writing in Arabic. Papers might elucidate the following sorts of questions: 

  • How did adherents of different confessional or juristic traditions, men and women, and members of different social classes within societies that became “Islamic” imagine the shape and meaning of their specific societies’ own pasts, and their relation to the universal history of the Islamic community? Which ways of writing, remembering, or commemorating did they develop? 
  • How can we broaden our scope beyond just textual historiography? 
  • How can marginalised communities and varieties of Arabic be given due attention? 
  • How can works of fiction contribute to our understanding of the past?
  • How can we explore the past algorithmically? Can digital methods enhance our understanding of the past? Can they also limit or even alter it? Which new digital tools are being developed? What seem to be particularly promising approaches? What is lacking? 
  • In what ways do educational institutions, museums, media organisations and proponents of heritage use history writing to shape loyalties and senses of belonging in society? 
  • How is the past used in creative arts, re-enactment, games, and augmented reality?
Contributions are invited from scholars at all career levels, addressing any period and any part of the Middle East and North Africa, broadly defined. This year we anticipate running the workshop from the Aga Khan Centre in London, with the possibility to have an online component featuring participants who are unable to travel to the UK. As in past years, there is a small budget to provide some travel assistance for scholars outside of London.

Arabic Pasts is co-organized by Hugh Kennedy (SOAS), James McDougall (Oxford), Lorenz Nigst (AKU-ISMC), and Sarah Bowen Savant (AKU-ISMC).

Please submit an abstract of 300 words or less in word document by Friday, 12 May 2023 to ArabicPastsConf@aku.edu.

Curriculum mapping is an effective tool for educators to align instruction with desired goals and outcomes. It allows teachers and school administrators to explore what is taught, how it is taught, and the alignment of learning standards with teaching. By using this mapping technique, educators can ensure that their students are receiving the best instruction possible by focusing on specific learning objectives. Entity: Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations
EventDetail:
Join us for the screening of A Ramadan in Lisbon, a film by a collective of anthropologists and artists documenting Muslim experiences in Portugal. The film reveals a multicultural Lisbon as it follows the daily experiences of a group of Muslims in the city’s diverse religious landscape during the holy month of Ramadan. A Ramadan in Lisbon has been shown at numerous festivals, conferences, and workshops, including the Indie Lisboa International Independent Film Festival (2019) and Distribue 2020 Toronto, the biennial conference of the Society for Cultural Anthropology and the Society for Visual Anthropology.   

The screening will be followed by a conversation with one of the directors of the film, Raquel Carvalheira, about the making of the film, their humanist approach to cinema and what it means to be a Muslim observing Ramadan in a context where fasting is not a common and majority practice. 

The film is in Portuguese, with English subtitles.

Film Credit:

A Ramadan in Lisbon · Um Ramadão em Lisboa

Directors: Amaya Sumpsi, Carlos Lima, Catarina Alves Costa, Joana Lucas, Raquel Carvalheira, & Teresa Costa

68 (min) | Portugal | Portuguese, English, Arabic, Creole & Bengali · English subtitles 

Speaker:

Raquel Carvalheira is an Invited Assistant Professor of Anthropology at NOVA University, Lisbon, and Guest Scholar at Aga Khan University’s Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations. She holds a PhD in Anthropology from the Institute of Social Sciences, University of Lisbon, with a dissertation focusing on the transformations of family organization in Morocco and the impact of social and legal changes on young women’s expectations on conjugality. Since July 2017, Raquel Carvalheira is a post-doctoral research fellow at the Centre for Research in Anthropology (CRIA) in Lisbon, working on a project about gender, family and charity among Muslims in Portugal. She is one of the directors of the film, A Ramadan in Lisbon.

*The discussion will be followed by a reception.

EventDetail:
Introduction

 

The Network of Quality, Teaching and Learning (QTL_net) is pleased to announce its annual call for grant applications in the area of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL). 

 

Aim

 

The SoTL Grants are designed to fund teaching innovation research projects with an aim to:

 

  • Recognize and reward faculty who aim to improve teaching and learning in their classrooms.
  • Ensure self-reflection on teaching practice within or across disciplines; and,
  • Disseminate the research to benefit teaching practice within AKU and beyond.

 

SoTL grants aligns with A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, K1, K2, K3, K4, K5, K6, V3, V4 of the UKPSF

 

Funding Available

 

This grant is funded and administered by the QTL_net. Up to a maximum of $5000 (USD) will be granted per approved project dependent on the scope and need of the proposed project. Ethical approval as per AKU policies, respective of the country in which the research is taking place, will be required prior to the release of funding to successful applicants.

 

Eligibility


  • Full time faculty members who have held at least three years of continuous service at AKU.
  • Multidisciplinary /Interdisciplinary collaborative projects within and across entities or with other faculty members and graduate students are highly encouraged.
  • Projects focused on teaching post Covid-19 pandemic are highly encouraged.
  • Applicants should not be recipients of 2021 or 2022 SoTL Grants Awards by QTL_net. 


Application process

Application submissions must include the online application form and CVs of all participating investigators. Completed applications must be received through an online form no later than 20:00 hrs. (PKT) | 18:00 hrs. (EAT) |16:00 hrs. (BST) on Monday, 31st July 2023.

 

Webinar

 

For more information on SoTL grants requirements and guidelines for writing a proposal, sign up for a webinar session scheduled for Thursday, 04th May 2023, 14:00- 15:30 hrs. (PKT) | 12:00-13:30 hrs. (EAT) | 10:00-11:30 hrs. (BST)

The Teaching and Learning Enhancement Workshop (TLEW) is a compulsory workshop offered by the Network of Quality, Teaching and Learning for AKU's faculty and academic support staff members. It aims to enhance the faculty's competence and confidence as facilitators of learning and engage them in reflecting on their teaching. TLEW is a pre-requisite to gaining the UK Higher Education Academy TEACH CPD Fellowship .This workshop aligns to: A1, A2, A3, A4, A5; K1, K2, K3, K5, K6 and V1, V2, V4 of the UK Professional Standards Framework (UKPSF).

EventDetail:
Gulbenkian Museum Academy and the Aga Khan University's Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations (AKU-ISMC) in collaboration offers a two-day workshop on Introduction to Islamic Manuscripts and Digital Codicology. 

Abstract

Exploring the esteemed manuscript collection of the Calouste Gulbenkian Museum, this 2-day short course is an introduction to codicology, manuscript studies, and digital humanities.

The course will be both theoretical and practical. This will include a demonstration of handling Islamic manuscripts, and hands-on-training in automatically transcribing manuscripts using the latest Text Recognition software for manuscripts, through the platform eScriptorium.

This course is an introductory course, so it is applicable to anyone with an interest in manuscripts, libraries, archives, codicology, museums, digital humanities, and the fields of Islamic Art and Middle Eastern studies. 

Convenor bios

This course will be organised and taught by Jessica Hallett from the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation, and Dr. Walid Ghali and Dr. Mathew Barber from Aga Khan University's Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations (AKU-ISMC). 

Dr. Jessica Hallett is Senior Curator of the Middle East and China, and Head of Research at Calouste Gulbenkian Museum.

Associate Professor Walid Ghali is Head Librarian of the Aga Khan Library in London and Associate Professor of Islamic and Arabic studies.

Assistant Professor Mathew Barber is from the Centre for Digital Humanities  of AKU-ISMC  and is a Historian who uses a combination of digital and traditional methods, using computational text reuse detection to identify so-called “lost” texts.

Participant requirements

Attendees would be expected to bring a laptop for the eScriptorium session.

This event is in English without simultaneous interpretation. While this course will involve textual analysis of manuscripts in Arabic and other languages, no prior language knowledge (other than English) is required for this introductory course. 

Attendees would also need to pick a digitised manuscript that they could use to practice with during the workshop. Help with this can be provided by the organisers. The digitised manuscript should preferably be in a language that the attendee understands, as they will be practicing transcription during the session. Attendees should contact organisers if their manuscript is in a language other than Arabic, Persian, Urdu or Ottoman Turkish. 

Programme Fees

£ 89/- for professionals.
£39/- for students

We offer up to three fee-waivers for people unable to pay the registration fee. For more information, please send an email to the following address: shortcourse.ismc@aku.edu. 

P﻿rogramme Schedule:

Day 1 – Thursday 26th October 2023

09:30 – 10:00. Arrivals and refreshments
10:00 – 10:30. Introduction to the course and the Gulbenkian Museum

Welcome, Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation and AKU.

Introduction by Walid Ghali concerning the overall academic approach of the course.

Overview by Jessica Hallett of the Gulbenkian Manuscript Collection, its history, and the types of works we will explore during the course. 

10:30 – 11:30. Session 1 What is Codicology? 
This session aims to provide an overview of the field of codicology. Particularly, it explores the role it plays in manuscript studies and in identifying the critical features of Islamic manuscripts and collections. By the end of the session, participants should be able to answer the following questions: What is codicology? Why is it important? What are the basic terminologies in the field? What are the main features of the Islamic manuscripts? (Titles, colophons, dates etc.)

This session will also be devoted to studying the writing materials of Islamic manuscripts to address textual and historical questions such as dating, localisation, and socio-cultural and economic considerations. This presentation will focus on the writing supports (papyrus, parchment, and paper), page-preparation techniques, inks (black and coloured inks) and bindings.

11:30 – 11:45. Break
11:45 – 13:00. Exploring Arts of the Book from the Gulbenkian Collection 
13:00 – 14:00. Lunch and break.
14:00 – 15:00. Session 2. ParaTextual Analysis/Text Transmission 

This session will concentrate on the waqfiyyas of books. Apart from the legal issues of the waqf, from formulas, and textual structures, it will explore the spiritual and social reward of the waqf, and the rich documentary value of the waqfiyyas. Additionally, this session will highlight several other types of notes that provide data on the history of a manuscript and its transmission. These include: corrections, comments, and other marginal notes related to the text of the manuscript book- Collation, Certificates, Seal impressions and so on.

15:00 – 16:00. Exploring Manuscripts from the Gulbenkian Collection
16:00 – 16:15. Break
16:15 – 17:30. Session 2 Continued. 

Day 2 – Friday 27th October 2023

09:30 – 11:00. Session 1. Digital Codicology, encoding and transcribing manuscripts through eScriptorium

This practical session will provide a detailed introduction and tutorial for the Open-Source transcription tool eScriptorium. EScriptorium uses the latest machine-learning technology to annotate and transcribe manuscripts, and it has been designed for use with low-resource languages (such as Arabic, Persian, and Urdu). The session will be broken into three parts. This first part will briefly introduce the concepts of machine learning, and Optical Character Recognition, the principles behind training segmentation and transcription models, and introduce the tool eScriptorium. 

11:00 – 11:15. Break
11:15 – 12:30. Session 1 Continued. 

The is the first session providing hands-on training of using eScriptorium. Attendees will use the tool to annotate regions and lines in a manuscript and will learn how to digitally encode some of the codicological features discussed in other sessions.

12:30-13:00. Visit to the Islamic Gallery of the Calouste Gulbenkian Museum
13:00 – 14:00. Lunch and break. 
14:00 – 16:00. Session 1 Continued.

The is the second session providing hands-on training of using eScriptorium. In this session they will use eScriptorium to create manual and automatic transcriptions of their manuscripts. They will then learn how to user eScriptorium to train models to detect and annotate features in a manuscript and to improve transcription accuracy. 

16:00 – 16:15. Break.
16:15 – 17:30. Conclusion, and Q&A
