EventDetail:
Introduction

The Network of Quality, Teaching and Learning (QTL_net), supported by Haile T. Debas Teacher's Academy (HTDTA), is pleased to announce its annual call for grant applications in the area of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL). 

 

Aim

The SoTL Grants are designed to fund teaching innovation research projects with an aim to:

  • Recognize and reward faculty who aim to improve teaching and learning in their classrooms.
  • Provide opportunities for reflective educators to transform their teaching practices into research; and,
  • Disseminate the research to benefit teaching practice within AKU and beyond.

SoTL grants aligns with A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, K1, K2, K3, K4, K5, K6, V3, V4 of the UKPSF

 

Funding Available

This grant is funded and administered by the QTL_net. Up to a maximum of $5000 (USD) will be granted per approved project dependent on the scope and need of the proposed project. Ethical approval as per AKU policies, respective of the country in which the research is taking place, will be required prior to the release of funding to successful applicants.

 

Eligibility

  • Full time faculty members who have held at least three years of continuous service at AKU.
  • Multidisciplinary /Interdisciplinary collaborative projects within and across entities or with other faculty members and graduate students are highly encouraged.
  • Applicants should not be recipients of 2022 or 2023 SoTL Grants Awards by QTL_net. 


Application process

Application submissions must include the online application form and CVs of all participating investigators. Completed applications must be received through an online form no later than 20:00 hrs. (PKT) | 18:00 hrs. (EAT) |16:00 hrs. (BST) on Wednesday, 31st July 2024.

 

Webinar

EventDetail:
It is no exaggeration to say that Albert Einstein revolutionised our understanding of nature. While Einstein receives due credit for his contributions to the theory of relativity, his impact on quantum theory may be underrated. 

About the talk
After providing an overview of Einstein’s scientific work, this talk will delve into other important aspects of his life and career that are often overlooked in academia. The focal points of the discussion will include Einstein's views on education, imagination, philosophy, scientific methodology, pacifism, nationalism, militarism, nuclear disarmament, social justice, and the social responsibility of scientists.

About the Speaker
Muhammad Hamza Waseem is pursuing a DPhil in Physics at the University of Oxford. His studies are funded by the Rhodes Trust and Magdalen College, Oxford. His current research revolves around quantum foundations, quantum structures, applied category theory, mathematical linguistics, and magnonics. He also co-authored a book 'Quantum Mechanics in the Single Photon Laboratory' published by the Institute of Physics, UK. Hamza teaches mathematics and physics at Mathematical Institute and Department of Computer Science at Oxford University.  He has also been a Lecturer in Physics at Magdalen College. He is a Research Scientist at Cambridge Quantum and a Research Fellow at Global Centre for Advanced Studies, Dublin. 

Moderator
Dr Farid Panjwani, Professor and Dean, AKU-IED

In today's digital age, effective management of library resources is crucial for providing efficient and accurate information retrieval services to users. The MARC - Machine-Readable Cataloging - format stands as a cornerstone in the organization and dissemination of bibliographic information in libraries worldwide. Understanding MARC is essential for library professionals to efficiently catalogue, classify, and retrieve resources. This workshop aims to provide library professionals with a comprehensive understanding of MARC, its principles, and practical applications in library settings.

Learning Outcomes
  • Get familiar with MARC structure, fields, and subfields
  • Understand the significance of MARC in library cataloging
  • Get hands-on experience in creating and editing MARC records
  • Explore advanced MARC techniques and best practices for efficient cataloging
  • Discuss the integration of MARC with modern library management systems

Entity: Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations
EventDetail:
AKU-ISMC is organising a two-day in-person workshop to discuss Muhammad Abduh as one of the most influential figures in the modern history of Muslim societies and the reform movement.

 

Although his demise was at an early age (53 years) over a century ago, his thoughts and ideas are still discussed in different spheres. In the chaotic political, social and religious circumstances we find ourselves in post-Arab Spring, thinkers and scholars increasingly turn to the work of some great reformers who appeared in the late 19th century.

 

Muhammad ‘Abduh (1849-1905) is an Egyptian philosopher, sociologist, and reformer ranked one of the most remarkable ﬁgures in the contemporary Muslim world. At his death in 1323/1905, he left numerous disciples and works of genuine interest and inestimable value. He was, and still is, commonly given the superb title “al-Ustādh al-Imām” (The Master and Guide); this title alone shows his inﬂuence upon his contemporaries.

 

Muhammad Abduh was one of those reformers who tried to explain the reasons for the decline of Muslims and their cultures. Muhammad ‘Abduh was born in Egypt, an autonomous province of the ancient Ottoman Empire. He was instrumental in developing one of the first political parties in Egypt (The National Party); he participated in a failed attempt at revolution ‘Urabi, 1881), went into exile, and died in Egypt under British occupation. He had many occupations: journalist, teacher, writer, politician, and the Grand Muftī of Egypt. Politically, he lived through extraordinary eventful times, and politics occupied him throughout his life.

 

"How Far Has It Gone? Exploring Muhammad ‘Abduh (d. 1905) and His Program of Islamic Reform," is scheduled for April 29th-30th, 2024. Join us for an enriching exploration of Muhammad ‘Abduh's impactful vision for Islamic reform.

Virtual open days are indeed a valuable way to explore educational study options at AKU-ISMC (Aga Khan University's Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations) and discover the various opportunities we have to offer. Here are some key points about the benefits of virtual open days:

1. Information and Insights: Virtual open days provide prospective students with a wealth of information about the institution, its programs, faculty, and campus facilities. It's an excellent opportunity to gain insights into what makes AKU-ISMC unique.

2. Interact with Expert Academics: Attending a virtual open day allows you to hear from the institute's expert academics. They can provide valuable information about the courses, research opportunities, and the academic environment at AKU-ISMC.

3. Student Perspective: Hearing from student representatives provides a unique perspective on what it's like to study at AKU-ISMC. They can share their personal experiences, insights, and answer questions about student life.

4. Q&A and Support: Virtual open days typically include Q&A sessions where you can get answers to your specific questions. This is helpful for clarifying doubts about admission requirements, financial aid, or any other concerns you may have.

5. Convenience: Virtual open days offer the convenience of attending from the comfort of your own home, eliminating the need for travel and making it accessible to a broader audience.

6. Application Guidance: AKU-ISMC can provide guidance on the application process during the virtual open day. This can be immensely helpful in ensuring you submit a strong application.

Virtual open days are an effective and convenient way to explore educational opportunities at AKU-ISMC, and they offer valuable insights into what the institution has to offer. If you're considering studying at AKU-ISMC, participating in one of these events is a great first step in your journey.

​About Life Conversations
Life Conversations is a public lecture series by the Aga Khan University (AKU), East Africa, held once a quarter. This session will explore how colonial influences have shaped educational policies and practices and how these legacies continue to influence the political landscape of education today. Dr Asghar Ali Dashti has served the Department of International Relations, Federal Urdu University, Karachi, since 2008. About the Session:

This EdTech Lounge is dedicated to exploring the role of student-teacher partnerships in higher education. The collaborative relationship between students and educators is important to create an environment that is conducive to learning and growth. Through students' active engagement in co-creating curriculum and learning processes, teachers can gain valuable insights into the diverse needs and preferences of their students, while empowering learners to take ownership of their educational journey. However, student-teacher partnership is not without its challenges. Power dynamics, skill differentials, communication barriers, time constraints, and socio-cultural factors can influence these relationships.

 

In this conversation, we have the privilege of hearing from esteemed experts representing the University of Queensland, Aga Khan University, and the University of Central Asia. Join us as they share their experiences and perspectives on the intricacies of student-teacher partnerships.

 

Speaker: 

Professor Kelly Matthews

Professor Matthews researches student voice and student partnership in higher education. Scholars in 44 countries and across 21 discipline areas have cited Kelly's influential and far-reaching research. In the past five years, she has completed a National Teaching Fellowship and secured new funding from universities, the Australian Department of Education, the U21 Global Enhancement Fund and AdvanceHE with keynote invitations from institutions in Australia, China, Germany, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Norway, and the UK. Recognised as an Australian Learning and Teaching Fellow (2015) and a Principal Fellow of the Higher Education Academy (2023), Kelly has received numerous awards for her collaborative leadership, embodying her dedication to advancing educational excellence in partnership with students and teachers. Entity: Centre for Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research
EventDetail:
Hematopoietic/blood stem cells (HSCs) are immature cells capable of differentiating into various types of blood cells such as white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. These cells are present in both peripheral blood and bone marrow. They are scarce, typically constituting only 0.01 to 0.05% of cells in the bone marrow. CD34 is widely recognized as a surface marker commonly associated with HSCs.

Pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) originate from the inner cell mass of preimplantation embryos. They possess the capacity for indefinite self-renewal and can differentiate into cells from all three germ layers, potentially giving rise to any cell type in the body. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), generated artificially in laboratory settings from somatic cells such as skin biopsies, display similar functionalities to PSCs. The application of iPSCs holds great promise in regenerative medicine. These cells represent a valuable reservoir of stem cells capable of differentiating into various cell types.

CRISPR-Cas9, often referred to as molecular scissors, is a groundbreaking gene-editing tool with two main components: a guide RNA responsible for locating the target gene and Cas9, an endonuclease that induces a double-stranded DNA break, facilitating genome modifications. It facilitates the rapid, cost-effective, and simple correction of genetic errors, along with the ability to regulate gene activity within cells. With its revolutionary potential, CRISPR-Cas9 finds diverse applications, including the rapid development of cellular and animal models, functional genomic screenings, live imaging of the cellular genome, and the development of gene-editing therapies for genetic disorders.

During this 3-day workshop, participants will receive training in isolating and characterizing hematopoietic stem cells using magnetic associated cell sorting (MACS) technology and cytogenetic techniques. Additionally, the particpants will explore methods for optimizing somatic cell reprogramming to reliably generate iPSCs in the laboratory, suitable for a wide range of applications. 

This workshop is designed for researchers who are interested in generating induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from both healthy and patient samples. Participants will acquire comprehensive knowledge on HSCs and iPSC derivation, with a focus on differentiating iPSCs into various lineages.

The participants will have the opportunity to learn sgRNAs-designing using software, synthesis of sgRNA, preparing CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) and Neon transfection of the target cells with CRSIPR-Cas9. They will also learn how to evaluate the double strand break in the transfected cells. 

Exosomes are nanosized membrane vesicles secreted by all types of cells including stem cells. In the workshop, exosomes will be engineered to efficiently target the HSCs and deliver CRISPR-Cas9 for gene editing in-vivo. Likewise, we will also offer hands on practice for exosomes isolation and liposomes fabrication, characterization and CRISPR-Cas9 loading on these nano-vehicles for efficient gene editing. A short session will also be arranged for retro/lenti viral transduction used in gene therapy.

Registration Criteria: 

PhD students/ MPhil Student/ Research Staff/ Research Associate/ Faculty

Submission Requirements:

1. Applicants are required to submit their current curriculum vitae (CV) 

2. Applicants must submit a concise one-page motivation letter outlining their reasons for applying to the workshop, their interest in the subject matter, their goals and expectations for participating, and any relevant experiences or skills that make them a suitable candidate.

Selection Criteria:

Applicants will be evaluated based on the relevance and depth of their academic and professional background to the workshop topic.

Notification and Confirmation:

Successful applicants will be notified of their acceptance into the workshop via email.

Accepted participants will be required to confirm their attendance within a specified timeframe and complete any additional administrative requirements, if applicable.

Diversity and Inclusion:

The selection process will aim to promote diversity and inclusion by considering factors such as gender, ethnicity, geographical location, and academic/professional background.

A limited number of bursaries are available to support candidates residing outside Karachi.

Liver diseases during pregnancy can pose significant risks to both the mother and the fetus. The importance of these conditions lies in their potential to lead to complications that can jeopardize the health of both the mother and the baby. They require careful management and monitoring to minimize risks and optimize outcomes. Early detection, timely intervention, and close collaboration between obstetricians and hepatologists are essential in managing these complex cases.

• Describe the underlying principles for managing a pregnant patient with acute liver failure.
• Understand the safety profile of various medications for treating chronic hepatitis in pregnancy.

This 10-day course featured intensive lectures by distinguished international faculty and participant-led poster sessions, offering a balanced approach to deepen students' insights and expertise in neuropsychopharmacology. The school addressed the basics of nervous system physiology, focusing on drug targets, neurotransmitters, receptors, and drug mechanisms of action.

The course also covered various aspects of neuropsychopharmacology, including the fundamentals of drug development such as preclinical testing, clinical trials, and regulatory approvals. It delved into the neurobiology of mental disorders, exploring brain circuits, genetics, and environmental factors.

The use of neuroimaging techniques to study brain structure and activity were discussed. The importance of collaborative teams involving psychiatrists, psychologists, and neuroscientists in research and clinical applications were emphasised. Ethical considerations, including informed consent, patient autonomy, and reporting of serious adverse events (SAEs), were also addressed.

Participants also had the opportunity to participate in the Neuroscience Symposium that took place in Nairobi on 10 - 11 June, 2024.

About the talk
This lecture problematizes the widely accepted classification of English-medium private schools in Pakistan which reproduces academic literature along the binaries of elite/non-elite and rich/poor. It seeks to expand this classification to recognize the existence of middle-tier English-medium private schools which are neither elite nor low-fee. 

Unlike elite schools, the families that send their kids to middle-tier schools predominantly speak Urdu or a regional language at home. Additionally, middle-tier school parents have tertiary degrees and occupy middle management positions professionally which make them distinct from low-fee school parents who tend to be mostly uneducated and work as manual workers or laborers. 

The presentation will further situate these schools in the global educational discourse on immersion and submersion in order to examine whether Pakistani students’ language learning experiences in middle-tier schools are additive and/or subtractive. 

The speaker will draw from personal encounters as an educator and parent as well as share empirical findings from a case study carried out at a middle-tier school in Karachi to shed light on the changed educational landscape and highlight the need for researchers to step beyond binaries and explore how bilingualism/multilingualism affects a cross-section of Pakistan’s student population, not just the lower socioeconomic groups.

About the Speaker
Saulat Pervez is a Researcher at the International Institute of Islamic Thought (IIIT) based in Virginia, United States. She has extensive experience in the field of education in the private schooling sector in Karachi, Pakistan, which is the subject and site of her research in the context of postcolonial cultures influencing social class, language disparities, and reading attitudes. She is particularly interested in examining bi/multilingual contexts and how the prevalence of a dominant, colonial language (English) not only marginalizes the native language (Urdu) but also creates obstacles in the formation of reading and writing cultures in both languages.

In the complex landscape of humanitarian crises, mental health often remains sidelined despite its critical importance. The Institute for Global Health and Development at Aga Khan University is proud to present a groundbreaking webinar titled "Mental Health in Humanitarian Settings," aimed at illuminating this vital yet often overlooked aspect of humanitarian aid.

 

Amidst the turmoil of humanitarian crises, individuals endure immense challenges such as displacement, conflict, and profound loss. These adversities deeply impact mental well-being, yet mental health support frequently receives inadequate attention in humanitarian responses. This webinar seeks to spotlight the daunting challenges confronting individuals in humanitarian settings while exploring effective strategies for addressing their mental health needs.

EventDetail:
Introduction:

Fever is a common yet multifaceted condition in pediatric patients, often causing significant concern for parents and healthcare providers alike. Proper understanding and management of febrile illnesses are crucial in ensuring the well-being of children.

This webinar "Exploring Fever Management in Children" aims to address the complexities surrounding pediatric fevers. Participants will gain valuable insights from Dr. Ali Faisal, an expert in Paediatrics & Child Health. Dr. Faisal will share his extensive knowledge and experience to help attendees navigate the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges of managing fever in children.


Course Objectives:

  • Understanding the causes and origins of Febrile Illness in children. 
  • Learn about the various pathogens and underlying conditions that can cause fever in children, and how these conditions present clinically. 
  • Management, Discharge, and Follow-Up Plans for Febrile Children.
  • Discover effective management strategies, including criteria for safe discharge and robust follow-up plans to ensure ongoing recovery and well-being.

Topics/Highlights:

EventDetail:
About the talk
The speaker will explore the crucial role of data-driven policy advocacy in enhancing social accountability within Bangladesh's education sector. Despite high enrollment rates, the Bangladeshi education system faces significant challenges related to quality and equality (Jashim, 2019). The shift from community-sponsored schools to a centralized system has resulted in deficiencies in adequacy, accountability, and robust community monitoring (M. Rahman et al., 2010).

In this challenging context, Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) and Community-Based Organizations (CBOs) play a pivotal role in strengthening social accountability. This process starts with robust data collection and evidence generation. Validating this data through community dialogues aids in understanding and addressing contextual factors, fostering accountability among service providers, receivers, and policymakers. These efforts enhance community engagement and ensure that local insights inform national policy decisions.

The discussion will also highlight how Institute of Informatics and Development (IID), a policy research institute in Bangladesh, leverages data-driven policy advocacy to strengthen social accountability through local and national partnerships. Through its 3i (Inquire, Inform, Involve) approach, the Institute collects grassroots data and conducts local townhall meetings, partnering with CBOs to engage various stakeholders in reflecting on and understanding the data.

Additionally, the Institute focuses on building the capacity of CSOs and CBOs, empowering them to advocate for educational needs. It also works with youth, enhancing their policy advocacy skills through Policy Camps and Hackathons. Insights from grassroots data, local dialogues, and youth demands are shared with national policymakers through Policy Conclaves. Partnership with the Parliamentary Caucus is crucial in sensitizing policymakers, leading to stronger social accountability in education at all levels. 

About the Speaker
Syeed Ahamed is a distinguished public policy analyst and the founding CEO, IID in Dhaka. Since 2013, he has been leading IID’s mission to promote an informed, inclusive, and democratic society. Prior to his role at IID, he served as a Research Fellow at the University of Melbourne, Australia. Syeed also coordinates the CSO Alliance Secretariat and leads the GPE-EOL funded e!quality education project in Bangladesh. He holds significant roles in international networks, including Steering Group Member of NEQMAP at UNESCO Bangkok and Country Focal of the Nairobi-based PAL Network.

EventDetail:
AKU-ISMC’s new Centre for the Languages of the Muslim World is delighted to offer this new short course as part of its Professional Development series. Introduction to Arabic Translation is a 10-hour online course designed to introduce participants to key issues inherent in translation from Arabic to English and to provide a foundation for further study and professional practice in Arabic > English translation.

This stimulating course is taught in 2-hour sessions across 5 weeks and is highly interactive. The course is taught mostly via English, with extensive use made of Arabic, and is open to non-native speakers of either/ both languages with advanced proficiency.

Introduction to Arabic Translation is open to participants from a wide range of educational and professional backgrounds. The course will function primarily to support potential translators considering a career move into Arabic/ English translation, via the exploration of key issues in Arabic-to-English translation, and an introduction to the underpinnings of translation methodology. The course tutor is a trained linguist and Arabist, with extensive experience of teaching and examining Arabic > English translation to postgraduate and undergraduate university students of varying backgrounds within highly rated and accredited university programmes in the UK.

Aims of the course

  • Study a selected range of Arabic texts in order to comparatively analyse competing translations of each, via exercises in contrastive stylistics
  • Identify and discuss typical rhetorical features of Arabic and English
  • Facilitate an understanding of key issues in Arabic-to-English translation
  • Introduce the underpinnings of translation methodology

Course Leader

Dr Alex Bellem is a Linguist and Arabist, and Assistant Professor at AKU-ISMC, where she leads on developing the Institute’s new Centre for the Languages of the Muslim World. She specialises in comparative–theoretical phonology (& phonetics) and Arabic dialectology, with expertise in the languages & linguistics of the Middle East and contiguous regions. She collaborates with Rex Smith in a project on the language of texts composed in Literary Mixed (“Middle”) Arabic and has previously collaborated on projects on the Modern South Arabian languages Mehri and Sheret (Jibbali). She has broader research interests in folk literature, and in cultural heritage, and has also published on Iraqi folk poetry. She has held academic posts at Durham University, Salford University and the CBRL British Institute (Amman & Damascus), and at these institutions as well as SOAS she has gained extensive experience teaching linguistics, Arabic translation, and Arabic language. She holds a PhD in Arabic Linguistics from SOAS, an MA from UCL (Linguistics), and a BA from Manchester University (Turkish & Arabic).

Date and time

31 October, 7, 14, 21, 28 November | 14:00 – 16:00 (London time)

Eligibility Criteria

The course assumes full reading ability of the Arabic script, and at least some basic knowledge of, or working familiarity with, the Arabic language. The course is equally well suited to both native and non-native speakers of Arabic.

Note

The course will be delivered via Zoom. Readings and further details will be provided later upon registration.

This course will not be recorded.

AKU-ISMC’s new Centre for the Languages of the Muslim World is delighted to offer this short course as part of its Professional Development series. Arabic Transliteration for Academics, Publishers and Librarians is aimed at professionals, scholars and students who work with Arabic text and would like to acquire knowledge of transliteration systems and gain or improve their practical transliteration skills under the guidance of experienced tutors.

The course is a 5-hour practical workshop-style course taught in two highly interactive sessions. Both sessions incorporate tailored feedback from the tutors.

In session I, participants will learn about transliteration and transcription, the various conventions and scholarly traditions, linguistic issues, contextual needs, and specific problems of Arabic-to-roman rendering; participants will learn and practise contextually appropriate practical transliteration, with tailored feedback from the tutors. Session II will comprise a “problem clinic” workshop focused on short, sample texts chosen by each participant and submitted in advance. During the course, consideration will also be given to issues of bias and ideology.

The course is equally well suited to native and non-native speakers of Arabic.

Aims of the course

  • Develop an understanding of transliteration and transcription, linguistic issues, contextual needs, and specific problems of Arabic-to-roman rendering
  • Familiarisation with the various conventions and scholarly traditions
  • Practise contextually appropriate practical transliteration, with tailored feedback from the tutors

Course Leader

Dr Alex Bellem is a Linguist and Arabist, and Assistant Professor at AKU-ISMC, where she leads on developing the Institute’s new Centre for the Languages of the Muslim World. She specialises in comparative–theoretical phonology (& phonetics) and Arabic dialectology, with expertise in the languages & linguistics of the Middle East and contiguous regions. She collaborates with Rex Smith in a project on the language of texts composed in Literary Mixed (“Middle”) Arabic and has previously collaborated on projects on the Modern South Arabian languages Mehri and Sheret (Jibbali). She has broader research interests in folk literature, and in cultural heritage, and has also published on Iraqi folk poetry. She has held academic posts at Durham University, Salford University and the CBRL British Institute (Amman & Damascus), and at these institutions as well as SOAS she has gained extensive experience teaching linguistics, Arabic translation, and Arabic language. She holds a PhD in Arabic Linguistics from SOAS, an MA from UCL (Linguistics), and a BA from Manchester University (Turkish & Arabic).

Course Co-facilitator

Professor G. Rex Smith is Professor Emeritus of the University of Manchester, and was most recently Visiting Professor in the School of Languages, Cultures and Societies, University of Leeds (2014 – 2020). He has taught and researched Arabic language and culture in a career spanning many years, and held academic posts at the Universities of Cambridge, Durham, Manchester and Leeds. He has published widely on (classical and “Middle”) Arabic, Yemeni history and culture, and Middle Eastern travel literature (both Arabic and French). Much of that research has involved translations from Arabic; perhaps most significantly his 2008 annotated translation of the 13th-century journey of Ibn al-Mujāwir, A Traveller in Thirteenth-Century Arabia. Among many other publications, Professor Smith co-authored a book on the Arabic scripts, A Brief Introduction to the Arabic Alphabet (with John F. Healey, Saqi Books, 2009). His two current projects are translations of the travel writing of the French littérateur Pierre Loti (Gerlach Press, 2021, 2022), and collaborative work with Alex Bellem on a comparative study of linguistic features of Literary Mixed (“Middle”) Arabic. He has a BA from SOAS in Classical Arabic, and an MA and PhD from the University of Cambridge.

EventDetail:
The second annual IIS/AKU-ISMC Graduate Conference: Challenges in Muslim Societies is a collaboration between The Aga Khan University- Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations and the Institute of Ismaili Studies to showcase student-led research at both institutions. 

The conference features a wide range of speakers from the IIS and AKU-ISMC programmes presenting on various topics in Islamic studies. The presentations are divided into four thematic panels: 

  • Identity and Making Space 
  • Media and Representation 
  • Oppression and Strife 
  • Ismaili Intellectual History 

The presentations will be followed by a live concert, exclusive to attendees of the conference.

The IIS/AKU-ISMC Graduate Conference will be streamed to the Global Jamat and other constituents of the IIS and AKU-ISMC around the world via Zoom. 

Please note filming and photography may take place during the event, and be used across our website, newsletters and social media accounts. These could include broad shots of the audience and lecture theatre, speakers during the talk, and of audience members participating in Q&A.  

Views expressed in this lecture are those of the presenting scholars, not necessarily of IIS, the Ismaili community or leadership. Promotion of this lecture is not an explicit endorsement of the ideas presented.

EventDetail:
Join us for an engaging discussion on the essential role of moral education in shaping responsible and conscientious future generations!

About the talk
Despite the global emphasis on developing moral values and prosocial behaviors through education, many schools, including those in Pakistan, often neglect the crucial aspect of moral education. While the primary focus remains on academic knowledge, the nurturing of students' moral and ethical development frequently takes a back seat. This oversight is exacerbated in Pakistan by disparities among various educational institutions—public schools, private schools, and religious seminaries—each presenting distinct standards and approaches to teaching moral values, often resulting in inconsistent moral guidance for students.

The session will highlight the pivotal role of teachers in moral education, and explore how teachers' moral beliefs and practices impact students’ ethical development, addressing challenges such as the influence of untrained educators and the need for effective teacher training.

Attendees will gain insights into the challenges faced by the Pakistani education system in nurturing moral values and the disparities among different types of schools. The seminar aims to foster a deeper understanding of how educational institutions can better fulfill their responsibility in developing students' moral and ethical dimensions.

About the Speaker
Dr Rabia Nauman's research interests focus on moral education, and she has conducted multiple small-scale and large-scale studies in this area. Her work emphasizes the importance of integrating moral values into educational practices and the pivotal role of teachers in fostering ethical development among students.
EventSummary: Kazim Bacchus Research Seminar

EventDetail:
Introduction

The field of laboratory medicine is continually evolving, with newer advanced technologies and changing practices reshaping the diagnostic landscape. There is a need to keep our local pathologists abreast of these disruptive changes and to showcase the work done by our local pathologists within the Pakistani context. With the theme "Future of Pathology - Adapting to a Changing Landscape," this event aims to identify current gaps, emerging trends, and technological advancements necessary for progress. EventDetail:
Maznah Mohamad

 

In Malaysia, as in many other Muslim-majority nations today, it is Bureaucratic Islam, rather than violent, militant demands that is driving religion as a state agenda. In her study of Malaysia, Maznah Mohamad characterises the inordinate power of this bureaucracy as taking on elements of a ‘Divine Bureaucracy’, to denote its ability to straddle two compelling spaces – on the one hand, the ‘non-rational’ sacred realm, and on the other hand, the ‘rational’ designs of organised life. She argues that this Divine Bureaucracy seeks to define the ground rules and sanctions towards what it sees to be the perfection of Muslim life. This includes establishing elaborately correct rituals around worship, to ideal family formation, to the inculcation of spiritualism in the national education curriculum, and to the purification of money, accumulation and wealth.

 

In this lecture, Professor Mohamad will focus on discussing how the Syariah has been reformulated to embody a new Malay-Muslim masculinity and femininity. In doing so it has also re-defined Muslim-non-Muslim intimate and social relations in a plural society. Despite all these, Malaysia has several paradoxes. It has seen few openly violent racial-based conflicts, and gender inequality has not been its worst failings. But there are other egregious costs. Could this be due to the consolidation of a Divine Bureaucracy which is the definitive Islam of the present period, and how so? The lecture will address these questions and expand on Professor Mohamad’s analysis of Bureaucratic Islam in Malaysia.

About the speaker

Maznah Mohamad – Biodata

Maznah Mohamad, formerly Associate Professor of Malay Studies (till June 2024), is 2024 AKU-ISMC Guest Scholar. She also currently holds the position of Honorary Fellow at the Department of Malay Studies of the National University of Singapore (NUS). Before joining NUS, she held the position of Visiting Chair in ASEAN and International Studies at the Munk Centre for International Studies, University of Toronto, Canada, from January to December 2001. At NUS, she was first appointed as a Visiting Senior Research Fellow with the Asia Research Institute (ARI) in 2006. Her single authored books include The Malay Handloom Weavers: A Study of the Rise and Decline of Traditional Manufacture (ISEAS, 1996), Feminism and the Women’s Movement in Malaysia (Routledge, 2006), and The Divine Bureaucracy and Disenchantment of Social Life: A Study of Bureaucratic Islam in Malaysia (Palgrave Macmillan, 2020). She served as Head of the Department of Malay Studies from June 2019 till December 2023. While serving as Head of Department she continued to be active in research by leading several research projects, which resulted in two forthcoming co-authored books: Visual Representation of Femininities of the Malay World: Camera, Chimera, Colonisation (Amsterdam University Press) and Sexuality and Islamic Spirituality in Early Malay Writings: A Textual History of Sex and Gender (I.B Tauris/Bloomsbury Press), both expected to be published by 2025.

This event will be followed by a drinks reception.

About the Talk
Educational technology (EdTech) investors have become increasingly influential in shaping education, yet their role remains underexplored. This seminar seeks to bridge this gap by introducing the grammar and landscape of EdTech investment into education research. The speakers will empirically examine venture capital EdTech investors, arguing that they act as both economic and political actors. By directing investments and promoting specific visions, these investors play a crucial role in constructing the EdTech industry. They legitimize their influence in education through narratives of expertise and claims of social impact, while also consolidating the industry by building social networks that drive forward-looking agendas. This analysis offers fresh insights into the power dynamics of EdTech investment and proposes a research agenda to explore the evolving relationships between the education, technology, and finance sectors. The presentation will also delve into the role of EdTech companies and their impact on the higher education sector.

About the Speakers
Dr Janja Komljenovic is a Senior Lecturer in Education Futures, University of Edinburgh. Her research focuses on the political economy of higher education and its digital transformation. She is especially interested in digital markets, EdTech, and datafication in higher education. Her interdisciplinary approach intersects economic sociology, science and technology studies, and higher education research.

Dr Ben Williamson is a Senior Lecturer and Co-Director, Centre for Research in Digital Education, University of Edinburgh. His research focuses on data, platforms and digital infrastructures in education, and their implications for policy and knowledge production. He is an editor of Learning, Media and Technology, and the author of Big Data in Education: The digital future of learning, policy and practice.

We announced and launched the Brain Resilience Kenya Study, a pioneering research project by the Brain & Mind Institute supported by Wellcome Leap and Temasek Trust, focused on understanding the factors that contribute to resilient aging among Kenyan adults aged 35 and above.

What We Aim to Discover

  • The social, psychological, and physical determinants of resilient aging.
  • Why some individuals thrive despite adversity, while others face accelerated aging.
  • Unique cultural factors that promote healthy brain aging and reduce risks like frailty and dementia.

Why It Matters

As major health challenges like cancer and dementia increasingly affect Kenyans, this study is set to make a lasting impact. Our findings will pave the way for:

  • Culturally relevant insights to support aging populations.
  • Innovative findings on how stressors—such as illness, poverty, and climate change—affect well-being.
  • A blueprint for stronger healthier communities not only in Kenya but in Africa as a whole.

Transforming our understanding of Aging in Kenya

This study represents a bold step toward unlocking the secrets of resilient aging. By shedding light on how our minds and bodies can thrive amidst adversity, we are poised to contribute to a brighter, healthier future for generations to come

About the Author

Dr Anjum Halai
Professor and Vice-Provost, AKU

Dr Halai has a long-standing and international experience in education in low-income and lower-middle-income countries like Pakistan and those in East Africa. She obtained her doctoral degree from Oxford University UK. She was an adjunct professor at the University of Alberta Canada (2011–2016) and a research fellow at the Centre for International Education, School of Education & Social Work, University of Sussex UK. 

Her research interests are in social justice issues in education. She has published widely in the area of mathematics teacher education, and on issues related to language and gender in education. She led the task force set up at the Aga Khan University (AKU) to develop a policy on awareness and prevention of gender-based harassment. She is also a member of the Advisory Committee on Women’s Leadership Academy at AKU. 

Dr Halai plays an active role on several international forums to enable equitable participation in education of youth, especially young women from disadvantaged contexts. These forums include the International Commission of Mathematical Instruction-Berlin, the Commission of Developing Countries, and the World Academy of Art and Science. She led the development of AKU’s Faculty of Arts and Sciences. Currently, she is serving as Professor of Education and Vice Provost at AKU in Pakistan.

Featured Book
Teaching and Teacher Education in Pakistan: Historical and Contemporary Perspectives
This book explores teaching and teacher education along the continuum of teachers’ careers within the context of Pakistan. It makes a significant contribution by consolidating historical and contemporary perspectives on teaching and teacher education into one concise volume, grounded in the social, cultural, political, and fiscal landscape of Pakistan—a lower middle-income country. The aim is to provide actionable recommendations for addressing issues within this field in the contemporary, fast-changing world. It argues that to adequately prepare children and youth for a dynamic world, teaching and teacher education must undergo transformation. Teacher education provision needs to be nimble and responsive to new teaching methods and emerging needs for skills development. Teaching must also accommodate the diversity in classrooms resulting from significant demographic shifts, increasing socio-economic divides, persistent gender inequities, conflicts, and disruptive digital technologies, among other factors. Divided into two interconnected sections, the first situates the evolution of teacher education within the global context before shifting focus to Pakistan's historical post-colonial policy landscape as a lower-middle-income country. Finally, it addresses the current context amidst the digital revolution, neo-liberal policies, and privatization. The second section draws upon highly relevant classroom-based research from Pakistan to provide insights into key issues in teaching and their implications for teacher education. Overall, the book offers profound insights applicable to teaching and teacher education in other similar post-colonial lower-middle-income countries.

About the talk
Premodern literature presents unique challenges for scholars due to its often unreliable nature, particularly as historical evidence from periods where other forms of documentation are scarce. Classical and medieval texts frequently blur the lines between literature and history, prompting some to question their use as reliable sources. However, as historian Hayden White suggests, the fluidity between history and literature allows us to gauge reliability by "contrasting" or "likening it to the imaginable."

This seminar delves into the complexities of interpreting classical and medieval texts—works that may contain supernatural elements, exaggerations, or biases, yet still offer valuable insights. Focusing on Arabic and Persian sources such as Ibn Munqibḥ’s biography, Qazwīnī’s Kitāb ʻAjāʼib, al-Nadīm’s Kitâb al-Fihrist, and the Šāh-nāma, the talk will also touch on select European texts. The discussion will explore how medieval conceptions of history and narrative differ from modern views and what can be reasonably deduced when approached with a critical eye.

About the Speaker
Dr Anum Tariq Dada is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Social Sciences and Liberal Arts, IBA. Her research centers on the textual and cultural interactions between Muslims and Christians during the High and Late Middle Ages, with a focus on gender, race, the marvellous in medieval literature, and the medical humanities.

Join us for an opportunity to intellectually engage with visionary scholars!

About the Talk
Staged Sufism is a phenomenon seen both locally and globally, particularly when it is marketed through poetry, performances, and music in line with the logic of contemporary consumer societies. Drawing from ongoing research by Professors Walid Ghali (on Egyptian contemporary Sufi music groups) and Jonas Otterbeck (on pop-nashid and Sufi-inspired rock), this event presents key findings and observations. The discussions will explore performance personas, the transformation and preservation of Sufi poetry, the didactics of performance, and the pedagogical value of contemporary music.

About the Presenters
Professor Jonas Otterbeck is the Rasul-Walker Chair in Popular Culture in Islam, AKU-ISMC, London. He researches contemporary expression of religion among Muslims in Europe. His latest research revolves around creative expressions making references to Islam for example among London’s Muslim artists (music, photography, dance). His book Awakening of Islamic Pop Music (EUP, 2021) is published open access. 

Dr Walid Ghali is a Professor of Arabic and Islamic studies at AKU-ISMC and a specialist in Arabic manuscripts studies. He also leads the Aga Khan Library in the United Kingdom. He teaches courses on Sufism, Islamic manuscripts, and Muslim reform. He is the Chair of the Islamic Manuscript Association and a member of the Editorial Board of Abdou-Filali Ansari's Occasional Papers published by AKU-ISMC. Dr Ghali has published in different research areas. His latest publication is a book on the leading Egyptian figure and Muslim reformer, Muhammad ‘Abduh (d.1905).

EventDetail:
Dementia, a condition that impairs memory and cognitive function, is becoming more prevalent in sub-Saharan Africa, including East Africa. Despite this growing concern, there remains limited information about the condition, particularly in Kenya, where culturally appropriate diagnostic tools are lacking. 
In response to this gap, an ethnographic study led by Dr. Edna Bosire from BMI, with support from the Davos Alzheimer’s Collaborative, sought to better understand dementia care in Kenya. The findings of the study will be launched this and will highlight the optimism of patients and caregivers regarding treatment, but it also uncovers significant challenges. Many families struggle with the high costs of care and the lack of skills needed to manage dementia at home. 
Additionally, the study reveals that public awareness of dementia remains low, with mixed attitudes towards clinical research participation and bio-sample collection. As the country faces these challenges, the upcoming October release of the study's findings is expected to inform future strategies for improving dementia diagnosis and care in Kenya.

EventDetail:
Join us for the second lecture of the AKU-ISMC Guest Scholar Programme 2024 in which Professor Ilkka Lindstedt will shed light on the history of pre-Islamic Arabia. Was the rise of Islam a black swan event? That is, was it something completely unexpected and something that totally transformed Arabia? This has recently been suggested by Michael Cook (following Nassim Taleb). In this lecture, Professor Lindstedt will explain what the material evidence (in particular, inscriptions) from pre-Islamic times tells us about the religious map of Arabia. The pre-Islamic inscriptions display a multicultural Arabia, where many languages were spoken and written, where various ethno-tribal identities existed, and where monotheist faiths were spreading.  He will argue that, far from being a black swan event, the rise of Islam should be understood as a continuation of the slow but steady spread of forms of monotheism in Arabia. 

 

About the Speaker

Ilkka Lindstedt (Ph.D., University of Helsinki) is 2024 AKU-ISMC Guest Scholar, and Lecturer in Islamic theology at the University of Helsinki, Finland. He has published scholarly articles on pre-Islamic Arabia, early Islam, Arabic epigraphy, and Arabic historiography. He is particularly interested in changes in religious groups and ideas in late antique Arabia. His monograph Muhammad and His Followers in Context: The Religious Map of Late Antique Arabia was published by Brill in 2023.

 

The discussion will be followed by a reception.

To celebrate AKU Author’s Day 2024, join us for an evening of conversation between Sanaa Alimia, Bloomsbury Pakistan Book Prize winner and author of Refugee Cities: How Afghans Changed Urban Pakistan, Asim Qureshi, co-author of When only God Can See: The Faith of Muslim Political Prisoners and Fatima Rajina, author of British Bangladeshi Muslims in the East End: The Changing Landscape of Dress and Language.

The journalist and presenter Malia Bouattia will discuss with the three authors how their books are woven together through the writing of people's histories and rendering visible racialised, purposefully marginalised and often dehumanised subjects.

 

Malia Bouattia is a senior editor for The New Arab and heads up the Opinion desk.

 

Dr. Sanaa Alimia is an Associate Professor of Political Science at the Aga Khan University, Institute of the Study of Muslim Civilisations. Alimia is the author of the Bloomsbury Pakitstan Book Award winning Refugee Cities: How Afghans Changed Urban Pakistan (2022 and 2024). She is a co-editor of Red Pepper, a quarterly print magazine.
 
Dr. Asim Qureshi is the Research Director at CAGE International. Qureshi has authored Rules of the Game: Detention, Deportation, Disappearance (2009), A Virtue of Disobedience (2018) and most recently, with Walaa Quisay, When only God Can See: The Faith of Muslim Political Prisoners (2024). He was also the editor of Refuse to Condemn: Resisting Racism in Times of National Security (2019).
 
Dr. Fatima Rajina is a Senior Legacy in Action Research Fellow at the Stephen Lawrence Research Centre at De Montfort University. Rajina is the author of British Bangladesh Muslims in the East End: The Changing Landscape of Dress and Language (2024).

EventDetail:
Join us for the third lecture of the AKU-ISMC Guest Scholar Programme 2024 in which Professor Jakob Skovgaard-Petersen will delve into the history of state muftis in the Muslim world. From the late 19th century, emerging Muslim states have established a position as the Mufti of the State, thus transforming a venerable academic specialist into a functionary in the modern state. Outlining the typical intentions in the creation of such a position and the difficulties with it, the lecture will zoom into the Egyptian state mufti office, the Dar al-Ifta, and the men who held office in it. Professor Skovgaard-Petersen will outline the significant changes that this institution has undergone in the 21st century. The lecture will conclude by discussing the merits of such an institutional approach, and what a study of the Muftis and their fatwas can tell us.


About the Speaker

Jakob Skovgaard-Petersen (Dr.Phil) is 2024 AKU-ISMC Guest Scholar, and Professor of Arabic and Islamic Studies at the University of Copenhagen. He specializes in contemporary Islam in the Arab World, more specifically in the role of the Sunni ulama in Arab states, the establishment of a modern public sphere and the role Islam on Arab television, and modern Arab historiography and the interpretation of Islamic history. Professor Skovgaard-Petersen is the author and co-editor of several volumes, including The Global Mufti. The Phenomenon of Yusuf al-Qaradawi (co-edited with Bettina Gräf, Columbia University Press, 2009), Defining Islam for the Egyptian State: Muftis and Fatwas of the Dar al-Ifra (Brill, 1997), and Law and the Islamic world. Past and Present (co-edited with Christopher Toll, The Royal Danish Academy of Sciences and Letters, 1994).

 

The lecture will be followed by a drinks reception.

EventDetail:
The Aga Khan Award for Architecture (AKAA) and the Aga Khan University, Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations (AKU-ISMC) invites you to join us for a discussion on the creation of the Palestinian Museum in Birzeit (West Bank), including the significance of its 2016 opening, winning the AKAA in 2019, its existence in the current moment, and the possibilities the Museum represents for the future. 

Speakers: Tomà Berlanda, Adrian Lahoud, Hanan Toukan, Róisín Heneghan. 

Moderators: Shahzad Bashir

 

Tomà Berlanda

Tomà Berlanda is Professor of Architectural Technology at the Politecnico di Torino, Honorary Research Associate at the University of Cape Town and co-founder of astudio.space architecture & urbanism. He holds a Diploma in Architecture from the Accademia di Architettura in Mendrisio and a PhD in Architecture from the Politecnico di Torino. His teaching and research focus on notions of environment, construction, ground, and land across geographies of the South. With his collaborative practices he has produced internationally recognised design work in Eastern and Southern Africa. He is the author of Architectural Topographies (2014), Interpreting Kigali: Architectural Inquiries and Prospects for a Developing African City (together with K. H. Smith, 2018), and editor of Architecture of Commonality. Grounds for Hope (2024).

Róisín Heneghan 

Róisín Heneghan is an architect and co-founder of heneghan peng architects. She received a Bachelor of Architecture from University College Dublin and a master’s in Architecture from Harvard University’s Graduate School of Design. Significant projects include the Palestinian Museum in Birzeit which was awarded the Aga Khan Award in Architecture in 2019, The Grand Egyptian Museum, Giant’ Causeway Visitors’ Centre, Stock well street building for Greenwich University and Welcome and Arrival at Storm King Art.


Hanan Toukan

Hanan Toukan is Associate Professor of Politics and Middle East Studies at Bard College Berlin on leave). She is currently based at the American University of Beirut -Mediterraneo in Cyprus and teaching in the Philosophy, Politics and Economics Program. Her research and writing sits at the intersection of Middle Eastern studies, international politics, critical theory, colonial/postcolonial studies, and visual culture. She has published in the Journal of Visual Culture, Radical Philosophy, Perspectives on Politics, Cultural Politics, Jerusalem Quarterly and the Journal for Palestine Studies, amongst others. Her book “The Politics of Art: Dissent and Cultural Diplomacy in Palestine, Lebanon and Jordan” is published with Stanford University Press (2021) and is based on her PhD which she completed at SOAS and which won the Middle East Studies Association of North American Malcolm H. Kerr Award for best PhD in the Social Sciences for 2012.

 

Adrian Lahoud

Adrian Lahoud is Dean of the School of Architecture at the Royal College of Art and Professor of Architecture and Urbanism. Prior to his current role, he was director of the MA programme at the Centre for Research Architecture, Goldsmiths. In 2019, he curated the inaugural Sharjah Architecture Triennial on the theme ‘Rights of Future Generations.’ His research work focuses on the global south and the impact of climate change.

This seminar presents a report by the University of Cambridge's Faculty of Education and the Centre for Lebanese Studies, in partnership with the UNRWA, examining the impact of the Gaza war on education since October 2023. The discussion will highlight the war’s toll on students, teachers, and counselors, sharing firsthand accounts from frontline staff and aid workers. It includes estimates of learning loss and calls for urgent action to restore education in Gaza, emphasizing the need for safe learning spaces and protection for young people. The seminar will urge the international community to take concrete steps toward rebuilding education in Palestine for a just peace.

His extensive background includes roles as UNESCO Senior Policy Analyst, UK Department for International Development Team Leader for Education, and Director of the Centre for International Teacher Education in South Africa. His research focuses on international education policy, with an emphasis on equity, social justice, and teacher development. Currently, Yusuf is leading large-scale studies on global education policy and teacher professionalism.

EventDetail: This talk examines the troubled history of law and prostitution in colonial India from the late nineteenth to the mid-twentieth century across contexts of statewide regulatory laws, cantonment codes, municipal rules, and border regimes. It explores how legislation on prostitution was translated from letter into practice and how this process was appropriated by subaltern Indian women wconfronted, stymied, and evaded the legal policing of prostitution on the scattered ground of empire. By emphasizing themes of trouble and disruption, this talk presents a new reading of colonial interventions into gender as they unfolded on the ground.

EventDetail:
Zulfikar Ali Bhutto Jr., an environmentalist deeply connected to the landscapes of Karachi and Larkana, grew up surrounded by the natural beauty of the Arabian Sea and the Indus River. This unique proximity to water, shaped his perspective on Pakistan, encouraging him to see the country not just as a political or geographical entity but as a living, breathing ecosystem unified by the rivers of the Indus drainage basin. This vision inspired him to recognize the vital connection between people and nature, seeing the rivers as lifelines that sustain the environment, communities, and biodiversity across Pakistan.

In his upcoming talk, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto Jr. will share his remarkable journey of transformation. Starting as a textile artist, he found creative expression through fabrics and patterns, drawing inspiration from Pakistan's cultural and natural heritage. Over time, his artistic work evolved into a deeper commitment to protecting the environment, as he realized the urgent need for conservation efforts in a rapidly changing world.

This shift led him to establish Bulhan Bachao, a community-driven initiative focused on conservation and sustainability. Through Bulhan Bachao, Zulfikar works with local communities to protect natural resources, raise awareness about environmental challenges, and promote actions that ensure a healthier future for both people and the planet. His story is one of creativity, passion, and determination, offering valuable insights into how individuals can combine art and advocacy to drive meaningful change.

EventDetail:
This workshop is designed to equip physicians with essential knowledge and skills for management of common endocrine emergencies in children. Using a flipped approach, participants will engage in self-directed learning through course content provided before the live workshop. During the workshop there will be focused talks for the whole group of participants.
Later the participant will be divided into small groups in breakout rooms on zoom platform for interactive, case-based discussions. This flipped format encourages active learning, collaboration, and real-time problem-solving, ensuring the participants are equipped to respond quickly and effectively for Paediatric Endocrine Emergencies.
The following critical conditions requiring immediate intervention are included in the workshop:
• #DiabeticKetoacidosis (DKA)
• #Hypoglycemia in Neonates and Children
• Sodium and Fluid Balance Disorders
• Hypo and #Hypercalcemic Situations
• #Adrenal Insufficiency
The focus will be on recognizing, assessing, and managing these emergencies in a structured, evidence-based manner.
Study material and clinical cases will be provided to participants prior to the workshop through email and they will be expected to have done prior reading before joining the workshop.
By the end of this program, the participants will be able to:
• Identify and recognise signs of paediatric endocrine emergencies, such as DKA, adrenal insufficiency, calcium, fluid & sodium imbalances, and hypoglycaemia.
• Plan what investigations need to be sent in these emergencies and interpret relevant lab results.
• Develop and Implement Treatment Plans by creating effective, evidence-based management strategies for each endocrine emergency, focusing on rapid stabilization and ongoing monitoring.
• Apply safe, guideline-based approaches to fluid and electrolyte replacement for optimal patient outcomes.
• Anticipate, recognize and address Complications and intervene effectively to prevent escalation.
Instructional Strategies:
• Flipped learning strategy with provision of course material before hand.
• Faculty-led presentations and discussion
• Interactive case-based learning in small groups
• Who can Attend:
• Paediatric Residents
• Paeds/Adult Endocrinology Fellows
• Family Physicians, Paediatricians

Rapidly identifying and managing life-threatening conditions with focused ultrasound is vital in emergency and critical care. This hands-on, full-day workshop equips you with the skills to master Point-of-Care Ultrasound (PoCUS) and make life-saving decisions. 

Through a combination of interactive presentations, hands-on sessions, and case-based discussions, this workshop provides a unique and practical approach to skill development.

Who Should Attend?

Adult and pediatric physicians, working in Emergency, ICU, and Acute Medicine

Workshop Modules

  • Basic orientation of ultrasound machine (Knobology and Image interpretation)
  • Approach to a patient with undifferentiated shock (inferior vena cava assessment, abdominal aortic aneurysm, intraabdominal free fluid, cardiac tamponade, left ventricular dysfunction, & massive pulmonary embolism)
  • Approach to a patient with shortness of breath (tension pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, pleural effusion, & pneumonia)
  • Role of PoCUS in cardiac arrest (cardiac standstill, pseudo PEA, & PoCUS pulse check)

Learning Outcomes

  • Understand the basic knobology and ultrasound image interpretation
  • Apply PoCUS to rapidly assess patients with undifferentiated shock (cardiogenic shock, septic shock, hypovolemic and obstructive shock)
  • Acquire the skills to use PoCUS in the assessment of patients with undifferentiated shortness of breath (Pneumothorax, Pleural effusion, Pulmonary edema, & Pneumonia)
  • Gain confidence in utilizing PoCUS as a valuable diagnostic tool in cardiac arrest (H's and T's and PoCUS Pulse Check)

Art is something that makes you breathe with a different kind of happiness." - Anni Albers 

Tribal Truck Art is an organization that is committed to the preservation of this unique form of folk art, which has originated in Pakistan only. Anjum Rana represents the new Pakistani woman, entrepreneurial, accomplished and creative. An interior designer, who restores and reproduces antique furniture.

Anjum Rana has made it her goal to bring this art into the mainstream, into our homes, and give it the recognition it so richly deserves. She has worked in close association with the master craftsmen -the truck painters for the past seven years. She directs them in painting their richly textured motifs on everyday objects that are usually connected in some way with the everyday life of the truckers. Lamps, lanterns, mugs, kettles, trays, boxes, watering cans, buckets etc become collectable home accessories. The painters have a new source of income, their art - a new legitimacy.

In collaboration with Tribal Truck Art, an organization dedicated to the preservation of this distinctive kind of folk art, FAS arranged a truck art workshop for its students. Anjum Rana, embodies the modern Pakistani lady and is determined to mainstream this art. Students learned and practiced truck art designs in this session to gain knowledge of the methods used in this popular art form that is widely used in Pakistan and South Asia. Together, the workshop enables students to continue thinking critically about the development of elite and popular cultures, as well as the hierarchical distinctions between "fine art" and "craft". We kept the designs and decorated our Dean's Conference room. The pieces are designed by our talented students.

EventSummary: Explore Pakistan's vibrant truck art heritage with dazzling colors, intricate designs, and cultural stories that celebrate tradition and creativity

EventDetail: Gianluca Parolin, a comparative lawyer specializing in constitutional design, State-Islam relations, citizenship, and the semiotics and imagery of law, explores the role of Community-Based Water Management (CBWM). CBWM remains a key model for implementing and sustaining rural water supply services in low- and middle-income countries, including Pakistan, and has recently been expanded to urban centers. However, its sustainability depends on policy and institutional support within the context of a fragmented state with limited capacity. Dr. Jeff Tan, Professor of Political Economy at the Aga Khan University’s Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations (AKU-ISMC) in London, examines the limitations of CBWM and its continued promotion despite evidence of unsustainability. Adding to the discussion, Pawan Sachdeva, Non-Executive Director at Water Management International Pte Ltd in Singapore, highlights the successful implementation of a large-scale CBWM program in Gilgit-Baltistan and evaluates its potential scalability to other regions of the country.
EventSubTitle: Sustainability of Community-Based Water Management: Challenges and Prospects
EventSummary: CBWM is key for water supply in Pakistan but needs policy support. This talk explores its challenges, successes in Gilgit-Baltistan, and scalability nationwide.
Title: Water Governance Talk

EventDetail: Join us for an insightful and engaging seminar that explores the fascinating intersection of law and audio-visual media. Titled "Visual Imaginaries of Law: Ramadan Television Drama (and Beyond)," this session is designed to encourage deep reflection on how our perceptions of the law are influenced and shaped by the narratives presented in audio-visual media. By examining the portrayal of legal themes in popular Ramadan television dramas, we aim to spark critical discussions about the broader implications of media on public understanding of justice and legal principles. This seminar is a unique opportunity for participants to broaden their perspectives and actively contribute to a meaningful dialogue. Importantly, we emphasize the need to include Pakistan in these discussions, as the local media landscape plays a vital role in shaping societal views on law and justice. Don’t miss this chance to engage with experts and peers on this crucial topic!
EventSubTitle: Exploring the Impact of Ramadan Dramas on Law: A Discussion on Media & Justice
EventSummary: Join the seminar "Visual Imaginaries of Law" to explore how Ramadan dramas shape our understanding of law, with a focus on including Pakistan in the discussion.

EventDetail: FAS students of City Learning: A Research Exploration of Karachi set out to explore the city’s old quarters an early wintery morning. Starting at the Indo-Gothic Structure Empress Market, Karachi’s oldest bazaar, they roamed its narrow passages, passing heaps of spices, produce and the odd cat begging for meat from a sympathetic vendor. From there, it was a short walk across Saddar’s busy streets to Bohri Bazaar, a sheltered market with cobbled streets and still-shuttered shops in the early morning. Next stop was TDF Ghar, a pre-partition home-turned museum for hot chai, before heading over to Frere Hall to admire Sadequain’s mural. They then visited the Khalikdina Hall, a community centre built in 1906 and site of the Trial of Maulana Mohammad Ali Johar and Shaukhat Ali for their support of the Khilafat movement. The building and old library has been recently restored by Numaish Karachi. They ended the trip with a lunch of nihari and gulab jamuns at Karachi’s famed Burns Road Food Street.
EventSummary: Students of the City Learning course explored old Karachi and the surrounding vicinity, including Empress Market, Bohri Bazaar and Frere Hall

EventDetail:
Spoken Stage, an artist collective focused on helping young people unlock their creative voice, delivered a multidisciplinary workshop as part of FAS’ City Learning Workshop. They drew from the city in text and context and the emergence of the modern city in literary and cultural imaginations, with particular attention to multi-sensory experiences of the city. Activities included finding your creative voice, line poetry, spoken word performance, improv and drawing.

Students then went on to write their own poetry and scripts to share in class.

Spoken Stage
Established in 2014, Spoken Stage strives to promote freedom of expression through art, performance, and writing in Pakistan. They regularly host poetry slams and open-mics, and facilitate creativity workshops as public space pop-ups, at schools and at cultural institutions, including the British Council. Spoken Stage represented Pakistan in 2016 at India’s inaugural National Poetry Slam in Bangalore, and has performed at the Women of the World Festival 2019, Karachi Literature Festival, at cultural centres like Khalidina Hall and more. 

Mariam Riaz Paracha | founder | Spoken Stage

Mariam is an artist, performer and poet. She holds an MFA in Theatre Education from Emerson College, USA, and works with people from underrepresented communities to develop their creative voice. She recently served as a mentor on Urban Word’s Youth’s National Youth Poet Laureate programme, where her mentee was named Pakistan’s first Youth Poet Laureate. Mariam is also Art Director and Assistant Director at Mano Animation Studios, Pakistan’s first hand-drawn animation studio and the team behind The Glassworker (2024).

Shameneh Majid | Communications Manager | Spoken Stage
Shameneh is a performer, writer and professor. She represented Pakistan in 2016 at India’s first National Poetry Slam in Bangalore, and multiple KLF panels and performances. Her poetry explores the idea of the body, the self, womanhood, families, and relationships. She also teaches writing and research at several higher education institutions in Karachi.

EventDetail:
The workshop served as an innovative platform that brought students into the dynamic and evolving dialogue at the crossroads of art and ecology. Designed to foster creativity and critical thinking, the event highlighted the critical role that artistic expression can play in addressing ecological challenges. Participants were introduced to contemporary practices and ideas that merge the artistic and environmental spheres, emphasizing how creativity can inspire action in the face of global crises like climate change.

Through a variety of engaging activities, the workshop offered students the chance to immerse themselves in experiential learning. This approach allowed participants to step beyond theoretical discussions and actively engage in imaginative problem-solving. Guided by experts in the fields of art and environmental science, students were encouraged to think outside traditional boundaries, exploring innovative ways to visualize and communicate complex ecological issues.

One of the core focuses of the workshop was to inspire participants to develop solutions that blend aesthetics with sustainability. Activities ranged from creating art pieces using recycled materials to brainstorming projects that incorporate both artistic and ecological principles. These exercises aimed not only to showcase the power of art as a medium for advocacy but also to equip students with the tools and confidence to propose actionable solutions to pressing environmental challenges.

By the end of the workshop, students had gained a deeper understanding of the synergies between art and ecology. They left with a renewed sense of purpose, armed with fresh ideas and a broader perspective on how interdisciplinary approaches can lead to impactful change. This hands-on experience not only enriched their academic journey but also empowered them to become active contributors to the global effort against climate change.
EventSubTitle: Exploring Creative Solutions at the Intersection of Art and Ecology
EventSummary: The workshop explored the fusion of art and ecology, offering hands-on learning to inspire imaginative approaches to tackling climate change challenges.

It is our great pleasure to invite you to attend 23rd Annual Meeting of the Asian Oceanian Myology Centre to be held online, hosted by Aga Khan University, Karachi, Pakistan, from 6th to 8th of November 2025. This is a premier conference dedicated to advancing knowledge and collaboration in the field of muscle and nerve disorders. This conference brings together leading experts, researchers, and clinicians from across the region and beyond to share the latest developments, innovative research, and clinical advancements in myology.

With a diverse programme featuring keynote presentations, interactive sessions and clinicopathological sessions we aim to foster meaningful dialogue, inspire new ideas, and strengthen partnerships that will drive progress in the diagnosis, treatment, and care of neuromuscular disorders.

About AOMC:

Established in January 2001, AOMC emerged from the collective endeavors of founding members hailing from 11 countries and regions. Since its inception, AOMC has been steadfast in its mission to elevate the standards of neuromuscular care. It is dedicated to promoting research, education, and clinical excellence in the field of neuromuscular medicine.  From promoting cutting-edge research to offering educational opportunities for emerging investigators and clinicians, AOMC has stood as a beacon of progress and collaboration. AOMC welcomes all professionals working in the neuromuscular field, fostering a multidisciplinary approach that enriches the study of neuromuscular disorders and the care of those affected.

We invite you to engage, learn, and contribute your research, as we work together to improve the lives of individuals affected by these neuromuscular disorders. Thank you for joining us, and we look forward to an enriching and memorable conference experience!

Objectives:   

  • To discuss basic principles of clinical evaluation of neuromuscular disorders.
  • Review of findings of muscle pathology in different neuromuscular disorders.
  • Updates on treatment and management of specific neuromuscular disorders.
  • Updates on ongoing research in the field of neuromuscular diseases. 

Who should attend?

Neurologists, Neuropathologists, Clinicians, Students and Trainees

Dr. Sara Khan

Speaker's profile
Dr Shamsh Kassim-Lakha is the Founding President of the Aga Khan University (AKU), the first private university chartered in South Asia. Over nearly three decades, he led its development, establishing its globally recognised programmes in Pakistan, East Africa and the UK. 

Since 1996, he has been instrumental in leading conceptualization of the University of Central Asia (UCA) and negotiating the International Treaty with Tajikistan, Kyrgyz Republic, Kazakhstan, and His Highness the Aga Khan which founded the University in 2000.  Since 2014, Dr Kassim-Lakha serves as Chairman of the Board of UCA. Concurrently, he served as the Diplomatic Representative of the Aga Khan Development Network to the Kyrgyz Republic from 2014–2022.

During the initial two decades of his career, he served as Managing Director of Industrial Promotion Services of Pakistan under the Aga Khan Fund for Economic Development and established a major manufacturing and venture capital conglomerate. 

Dr Kassim-Lakha’s public service has been equally illustrious. From 2007-2008, he served as the Federal Minister of Education and Minister of Science and Technology. As Minister of State, he co-chaired the Taskforce for Reform of Higher Education, whose recommendations resulted in the establishment of the Higher Education Commission (HEC). Following his retirement from AKU, he continued contributing to higher education as a member of the Higher Education Commission (2007–2011 and 2018–2022). 

He led the conceptualisation of the Pakistan Centre for Philanthropy and chaired its Board of Directors for 15 years. He also led the Committee which wrote Pakistan's National Environment Protection Act (1997). His works have been published in renowned journals, including The Lancet and Nature.

Dr Kassim-Lakha has received honorary degrees from McMaster University, Canada and the Aga Khan University. In recognition of his public service, he was awarded Pakistan’s Sitara-e-Imtiaz, Hilal-e-Imtiaz, France’s Officer of the National Order of Merit and Medal of Honour from Kyrgyztan.
