Introduction

The National Symposium on Primary Health Care aims to enhance strategies, identify synergies and align organizational efforts and goals towards the achievement of Universal Health Coverage. As such, the Symposium will serve as a platform to gather stakeholders, pool technical resources and expertise to address the defined challenges in Primary Health Care, influence policies through evidence-informed advocacy, encourage data sharing, and promote collective action.

The Symposium is organized as part of the PHC Learning Agenda (PLA) Pakistan, a two-year joint initiative of the Aga Khan University (AKU) and Gates Foundation (BMGF). The rationale of this initiative is to help share information and exchange good practices on different aspects of PHC in the country.

Event Objectives
  • Reinforcement of the importance of primary health care in advancing towards UHC
  • Sharing positive experiences and lessons learnt about PHC among provinces
  • Furnish evidence and propose way forward in unexplored areas of PHC in Pakistan
  • Enhanced networking among Consortium members in support of PHC

Topics/Highlights
  • Primary Health Care: Global Perspective from World Health Organization, Geneva
  • High-level Ministerial Panel Discussion on the Future of Primary Health care in Pakistan
  • Innovative Financing for PHC in L&MICs
  • Financing for PHC in Pakistan
  • Health Insurance for PHC
  • Primary Health care in the post-covid era
  • Person centered Primary Health care
  • State and readiness of primary health care in Pakistan
  • Health Information Systems in PHC
  • Electronic Medical Records: Experience from Punjab
  • Global Burden of Disease 2023 - Trends in Pakistan
  • Monitoring Quality of PHC in L&MICs
  • The role of digital health
  • Exploring uncharted areas of research in Primary Health Care in Pakistan. These will include:
  •   o Urban primary health care
  •   o Quality of primary health care
  •   o Primary health care and family planning
  •   o Gender dynamics in primary health care
  •   o Primary health care responsiveness and patient experience
  • Building Capacity for Research in PHC
  • Special sessions on Innovations in Primary Health care: Experience from Pakistan
Speakers
Speakers will participate in-person. Confirmed speakers include:
  • Enis Baris, Professor of Health Metrics Sciences and Director of Global Health Policy Partnerships at Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME), University of Washington and Adjunct Professor at the McGill University, Montreal, Quebec, Canada
  • Kara Hanson, Professor of Health Economics and Dean, Faculty of Public Health & Policy, London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LHSTM)
  • Margaret Kruk, Distinguished Endowed Professor of Health Systems & Medicine, University Wide QuEST Center Director, Washington University in St. Louis 
  • Katherine Rouleau, Professor, Department of Family and Community Medicine, University of Toronto 
  • Eduardo Banzon, Director-Health at the Asian Development Bank
  • Ali Mokdad, Professor Health Metrics Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME); Chief Strategy Officer of Population Health at University of Washington
  • Raza Zaidi, E4H Technical Director, UK’s Evidence for Health Programme, Ministry of National Health Services, Regulations & Coordination
  • Sameen Siddiqi, Professor, Department of Community Health Sciences (CHS) Aga Khan University 
  • Zahid Memon, Associate Professor, Department of Community Health Sciences (CHS), Aga Khan University
  • Unab Khan, Professor, Chairperson, Department of Family Medicine, Aga Khan University
  • Hammad Yunus, Consultant Health Financial Analyst

This awareness session explores innovative classroom practices from systems like the International Baccalaureate (IB), Nordic schools, and project-based learning. Learn how to implement integrated, outcome-based approaches and inclusive strategies for students with special needs. Dive into concepts like Approaches to Learning (ATL) and Approaches to Teaching (ATT) to foster self-regulated, lifelong learners through skills like critical thinking, inquiry, and collaboration. Discover practical tools like mindfulness, mind mapping, play-based, and experiential learning to make education more meaningful and relevant.

  • Analyze best practices from globally recognized classroom initiatives, such as IB and Nordic education systems, to identify strategies suitable for local classroom dynamics. 
  • Apply techniques such as mindfulness and mind mapping by integrating globally practiced exercises like observation and listening into lesson plans. 
  • Develop strategies to foster inquiry-based learning and critical thinking using methodologies practiced in IB's Approaches to Learning and Approaches to Teaching. 
  • Evaluate inclusive education strategies used in IB and other systems to identify and accommodate students with special needs in classroom activities.
  • Create formative assessments inspired by Nordic and IB systems, incorporating methods that extend beyond traditional written formats and emphasize experiential learning for primary years.
  • Design strategies to adapt local curriculum from traditional lecture-based methods to play-based and experiential learning models that align with project-based learning principles.

EventDetail:
The course aims to develop knowledge and skills to understand, critique and improve policy processes and the politics that surround educational policy decisions. The course tries to develop participants understanding pertaining to theories, ideologies and positional ties of actors who have influence on determining and achieving policy objectives. Various levels of policy (global, national, local) will be considered for understanding policy production and implementation within re-configured state structures. The implications of policy decisions for educational processes and outcomes at system level will also be explored. The course is primarily concerned with public policy, however, lessons for institutional level policy can be drawn. We hope that the participants who graduate from this course, would be able to actively participate at different stages of policy happenings at institutional, provincial, national or global levels.

Duration
16 Weeks starting Tuesday, February 11, 2025
  
Learning Outcomes
  • Gain theoretical insights into the field of policy studies 
  • Critique various theoretical positioning in education policy and locate the flow of power and politics in education policy 
  • Develop an understanding of changing global and national context of education and its implications for education policy and governance 
  • Examine the ‘policy trajectory’ from problem identification to policy formulation, implementation and evaluation 
  • Distinguish between ‘analysis of policy’ and ‘analysis for policy’ and to see their implications for policy decisions and practice 
  • Conduct Policy analysis and design policy research to promote evidence-informed policy 
  • Understand the issues surrounding the implementation of policy and be able to suggest their ramification 
  • Appreciate particular issues of education policy implementation in developing countries 
  • Understand policy advocacy and importance of communicating policy messages to various stakeholders in an accessible form 
  • Recognize institutions as part of broader education system and be able to develop and implement policy at that level in light of broader public policy 

Facilitator
Dr Sajid Ali, Professor, AKU-IED 
 
Participant profile
Policy makers, management level individuals from NGOs, academics, education experts, school heads and teacher educators

About the talk
The proposed template for spiritual education is founded upon particular accounts of spirituality and the purpose of schooling. Following Michael Hand, spirituality is activity which practitioners believe connects them with the transcendent. Following Michael Young, schools should enable the understanding and utilisation of knowledge not usually accessed outside of school. The template is unlikely to be of use in schools which reject these accounts. However, whilst the speaker argues for a non-confessional spiritual education, the template could be utilised in a range of contexts, including the confessional. The template asks, “so what?” in relation to contexts and people, and their interrelationships.

About the Speaker
Dr Jo Fraser-Pearce is the Faculty Tutor for Postgraduate Taught Provision at the Institute of Education (IOE). With a decade of experience teaching Religious Education in secondary schools across London, she brings both practical expertise and deep theoretical insights into the field. Her doctoral research focused on spiritual education in Steiner Waldorf schools, and her academic interests extend to the complex relationship between religion and education more broadly. Through her work, she continues to explore how schools engage with religious and spiritual learning in diverse educational settings.

Discover how algebraic reasoning is woven across different strands of the math curriculum and how it progresses in various educational systems. This course equips educators with creative strategies—like function machines, storytelling, and pattern recognition—to make algebra more engaging. Participants will explore hands-on and digital tools, develop effective lesson plans, and cultivate problem-solving skills in students. Perfect for teachers looking to enhance their instructional approach and build deeper mathematical understanding in the classroom!

  • Compare the progression of algebraic concepts in different mathematics curriculums (NC, AKU-EB, Cambridge, and IBEC) 
  • Build mathematical habits of mind by fostering patience and persistence through reasoning, problem-solving, and mathematical modeling 
  • Solve algebraic expressions and equations using innovative approaches –such as function machines, storytelling, doing-undoing strategies, and pattern seeking, using both virtual and concrete material 
  • Design lesson plans and select appropriate teaching/learning materials/resources (digital and concrete) to develop students’ knowledge, skills and attitudes essential for developing algebraic thinking

EventDetail:
The Aga Khan University (International) - Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations (AKU-ISMC), in collaboration with the Academy of Sciences (Portugal), is pleased to announce an advanced training course entitled Manuscripts for Research: An Advanced Course in Arabic Manuscript Studies, which will be held at the prestigious Library of the Academy of Sciences of Lisbon (founded on 24 December 1779). The course will take place from 22-25 July 2025.

During this workshop, participants will delve into the vibrant manuscript collection at the Academy of Sciences of Lisbon. This remarkable collection encompasses a diverse array of subjects and regions. The course will include interactive lectures on philology, as well as hands-on sessions centred around a selection of manuscripts from this invaluable collection.

Course Pre-requisite 

This intensive four-day training course is designed for researchers, librarians, curators, and anyone engaged with Islamic manuscripts. As an advanced course, it primarily targets those who have experience with manuscripts or archival documents. All participants should possess a solid reading knowledge of Arabic and/or Persian.

Please note that the hands-on sessions are limited to 15 persons (to be divided into two groups) for conservation and pedagogical reasons. All instructions will be in English.

Learning outcomes

  • Understanding the history of Arabic manuscripts.
  • Understanding the different methods of composition and authorship traditions.
  • Understanding of the text layout and paratextual elements.
  • Learning the main steps to start editing a manuscript.
Course Faculty

Professor Walid Ghali has designed the course. He is a Professor of Arabic and Islamic studies at AKU-ISMC and a specialist in Arabic manuscripts studies. He also leads the Aga Khan Library in the United Kingdom. He received his PhD in 2012 from Cairo University, Faculty of Arts in Arabic manuscripts traditions. He completed coursework for a master’s in Islamic studies. He is currently Chairing the Board of the Islamic Manuscript Association. He also teaches various subjects for MA students, including Introduction to Sufism, Arabic Literature, and Muslim Thinkers in the 19th Century.

Dr Éléonore Cellard holds a PhD in Arabic Language and Literature from INALCO (2015). Her doctoral thesis, entitled “La Transmission manuscrite du Coran: Étude d’un corpus de manuscrits datables du 2e H./8e siècle J.-C.,” was supervised by Georgine Ayoub (INALCO) and François Déroche (EPHE). After completing her PhD, she served as a research and teaching assistant at the Collège de France for the ‘History of the Qur’an’ chair (2015-2018), later working as a post-doctoral researcher leading a project on a significant Qur’anic manuscript attributed to the Caliph Uthman (forthcoming monograph, 2024). She has engaged in several international research projects (Coranica and Paleocoran), led training courses in manuscript studies, and published a monograph (Codex Amrensis 1, 2018) along with several reference articles.

Dr Juan Acevedo is a co-convenor, a graduate in Classics from the Universidad de Los Andes (Mérida, Venezuela) with a PhD in History of Philosophy from the Warburg Institute (London). After years of working as an editor on Islamic Studies and Comparative Religion, he is currently a Research Fellow at the Inter-University Centre for the History of Science and Technology (CIUHCT), University of Lisbon, studying early modern technoscience across Eurasia, in particular Arabic manuscripts on Indian Ocean navigation. His main research interest is in conceptual and cultural history, especially at the foundations, where cultures come together, and metaphysics and craftsmanship overlap through shared cosmological principles.

Educational psychology is a branch of psychology that specializes in understanding teaching and learning in educational settings. In this branch, teachers are encouraged to understand individual differences, socioeconomic differences, neurodivergent learners, and assessment all while help students comprehend, reflect, and respond through writing. In addition, teachers will teach students how to compose using their writing tools, writing grids and rubrics. Teachers will help students narrate their inner voice.

    -Identify the attitudes and skills of an effective teacher. 
    -Discuss how social context of families, peers and schools are linked to teaching and learning. 
  • Module 2: Introduction to Neurodiversity and Neurodivergent Learners 
    -Define and describe neurodiversity and neurodivergent learners.   
    -Dissuss ways to improve teaching in an evolving classroom.
    -Identify neurodivergent learners, assess needs, and respond through accommodations.  
  • Module 3: Introduction to Classroom Management for Neurodivergent Learners
    -Describe ideas about classroom management. 
    -Identify key components of good classroom management through effective teaching.

    -Utilize the "I do, We do, You do" strategy along with provided writing tools to develop a structured personal narrative
    -Assess students’ work using a rubric that correlates with the writing worksheet

Entity: Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations
EventDetail:
The Aga Khan University (International) in the United Kingdom, in collaboration with the Ismaili Centre and the Aga Khan Museum, offers a face-to-face short course on Governing Diversity: Engaging with a Complex World.

This course examines how different kinds of states have treated diversity among their subjects. Looking at case studies ranging from the Romans and the Mughals to modern states in Europe and North America, it invites us to ask how far different kinds of subject expected to see themselves represented in the state and what kinds of ethnic or religious hierarchies the state endorsed. It also asks us to think about how different social groups functioned internally: how did their leaders manage the balancing act between the demands of the state and those of their community? How did they gather and spend revenues? And how did they secure the boundaries of their community against outsiders? The course will also include a study session at the Aga Khan Museum and a reflection on the course from the perspective of the local Ismaili community: does history offer lessons or models that can be used in the present day?

Learning outcomes:

  • Evaluate the utility of different kinds of technical vocabulary to analyse group behaviour
  • Compare the experience of minorities in different contexts
  • Analyse the interaction of legal policy, demography and political systems in the experience of minorities
  • Combine art historical evidence with written evidence to develop a holistic model of cultural interaction

Programme Agenda: Click [here] to view the programme agenda. Please note that the agenda is subject to change, and the final version will be emailed to all registered participants before the event.

Course Faculty:

Professor Philip Wood

Prof. Philip Wood is a course lead for this short course. Dr. Wood studies West Asia before and after the Arab conquests (roughly 400-900CE). He is particularly interested in the history of Christian communities in Syria and Iraq, and in the formation and preservation of group identities more broadly. His books have analysed Syriac speaking Christian groups in the later Roman Empire, the Sasanian Empire and the Abbasid Caliphate. He has recently published *The Imam of the Christians: The World of Dionysius of Tel-Mahre, 750-850* (Princeton, 2021), and, alongside Professor Leif Stenberg, *What is Islamic Studies? European and North American Approaches to a Contested Field* (Edinburgh, 2022).

Professor Shahzad Bashir

Prof. Shahzad Bashir is dean, Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations, Aga Khan University (International) in the United Kingdom. His most recent books are the Open Access multi-modal digital monograph A New Vision for Islamic Pasts and Futures (MIT Press 2022) and The Market in Poetry in the Persian World  (Cambridge 2021). He is currently working on the possibility of theorising history via photography and a cultural history of knowledge in India circa 1750–1850.

Dr. Ulrike Al-Khamis

Dr. Ulrike Al-Khamis is the Director and CEO of the Aga Khan Museum. She has over 20 years of experience as a curator and senior advisor for museum and cultural projects, collaborating with institutions such as the National Museums of Scotland and Glasgow. More recently, Dr. Al-Khamis served as Co-Director of the Sharjah Museum of Islamic Civilisation and Senior Strategic Advisor to the Sharjah Museums Department in the United Arab Emirates.

 

Ms Erfa Alani

Erfa Alani is the Inaugural Executive Director of Small Business Centres Ontario, where she leads a network of 54 centres supporting entrepreneurs across the province. A seasoned public sector strategist, she also helped found Invest Ontario, the province’s investment attraction agency, where she served as its first Chief of Staff.

Her career spans international development, trade negotiations, and institutional transformation—including work with the Aga Khan Development Network in Sub-Saharan Africa and as a Canadian representative in trade talks with the European Union, the United States, and Mexico.

A former refugee, trained lawyer, and widowed mother of two, Erfa brings a deeply personal understanding to questions of identity, pluralism, and governance. She has advised on inclusive economic policy, led cross-cultural negotiations, and championed ethical leadership across sectors. Her academic work explores the intersection of happiness, trust, and pluralism in sustainable development.

Erfa is a graduate of the International Waezeen Training Programme. Known for her systems-level thinking and disarming storytelling, Erfa closes this programme by offering an Ismaili perspective on governing diversity—inviting reflection on the inherited language of faith, the burden and beauty of difference, and what it means to live our history forward.

Faiza Damji-Karim

Faiza Karim is a skilled educator and researcher with extensive experience in adult education and curriculum development. Faiza holds a Bachelor of Arts in Anthropology and History, a Bachelor of Education, and a diploma as an Intervenor for Deaf-Blind Persons. She also earned a Master of Arts in Teaching from University College London's Faculty of Education and Society, as well as a Master of Arts in Education specialising in Muslim societies and civilizations. Faiza recently completed the Postgraduate Research Fellowship at the Institute of Ismaili Studies; her research explored "The Sense of Belonging Among Queer Ismaili Muslims in Canada: A Qualitative Study on Belonging and Community." Guided by a commitment to inclusion and empowerment, Faiza’s work bridges academic excellence and practical application.

EventDetail:
The Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences at Aga Khan University (AKU-FAS), Karachi, and the Psychology Department at the University of Exeter (UoE), UK, are co-hosting a special conference on psychoanalysis. This event will explore how psychoanalytic thinking can be applied in Pakistan and the challenges it faces. The conference is led by Prof. Duane Rousselle (AKU) and Dr. Marta Bolognani (UoE).

Why This Conference?

Psychoanalysis has often been seen as a Western concept, overlooking local knowledge and cultural perspectives. While this critique is acknowledged globally, Pakistan still has limited access to psychoanalytic training and clinical practice. This conference aims to bring together experts and enthusiasts to discuss its relevance in Pakistan and the possibilities for future development.

Event Highlights
  • Keynote Speaker: Dr. Shameel Khan (Psychiatrist, Psychotherapist, and Assistant Professor at IBA, Karachi)
  • Guest Speakers: Prof. Richard Mizen (University of Exeter, UK), Prof. Frank Rollier (Clinical Section of Nice, France), and Prof. Gary Winship (Nottingham University, UK & Director of the British Journal of Psychotherapy).
  • Conference Structure:
                 - Two days of presentations and discussions, open to both clinicians and non-clinicians.
                 - A third day dedicated to clinical supervision groups for clinicians (limited slots available)

Call for Papers

We invite clinicians and non-clinicians with an interest in psychoanalysis to submit their abstracts by December 31, 2024. Papers can be short (10–20 min) or long (up to 45 min) and should relate to topics such as:

  • Psychoanalysis in Literature and Philosophy
  • Clinical Case Discussions
  • Psychoanalytic Training
  • Identity and Violence

For the clinical supervision day (April 14, 2025), interested clinicians can apply to present cases in small discussion groups led by experienced supervisors. Registration required: Psychoanalysis, Pakistan

📅 Deadline for Abstract Submission: December 31, 2024
📧 Send your abstracts to duane.rousselle@aku.edu or m.bolognani@exeter.ac.uk

For general inquiries about psychoanalysis in Pakistan and the conference, feel free to reach out. We look forward to your participation!

Early teaching experiences are critical in shaping a teacher’s career (Bullough, 1997), with school administrators playing a pivotal role in their adjustment and professional growth (Brock & Grady, 2001). This KBRS presents findings from a qualitative case study examining the challenges novice teachers face during their initial years and the support provided by school administrators. The study offers valuable policy and practical insights to enhance teacher retention and development.

About the Speaker
Dr. Duishon Alievich Shamatov, an Associate Professor at Nazarbayev University’s Graduate School of Education, teaches Educational Leadership and Research Methods. He earned a Master’s in Teacher Education from AKU-IED and a PhD from the University of Toronto. His doctoral research focused on beginning teachers in post-Soviet Kyrgyzstan. With research experience across Central Asia and beyond, his interests include educational reforms, rural education, teacher training, and student assessment. A recipient of multiple NU Teaching Awards, he has been recognized for innovation, leadership, and teaching excellence.

EventDetail:
This talk explores the entanglement of bodies of water, landscapes, and infrastructure both historical and contemporary-while weaving together issues of land contestation, borders, and resource extraction. Through readings from fieldnotes that began in 2007 with a long-term investigation of Manora Island, a defense outpost facing the Arabian Sea, Naiza Khan examines the intricate relationships between the monsoon, empire, and migration across the Indian Ocean. This visual and textual journey brings together ideas of embodiment and ecology, considering the ocean as a heterogeneous assemblage of power, colonial history, and collective memory. 

About the Artist:

Naiza Khan is a multi-disciplinary artist whose practice combines critical research, documentation, and mapping-based exploration. She works with drawing, sculpture, archival materialc, and film to address themes of land, body, and memory. Trained at Oxford and Goldsmiths, Naiza Khan has exhted at the Venice, Gwangju, and Sharjah Biennales. A co-founder of the Vasl Artists' Collective, she has also shaped art education and curation in Pakistan.
EventSubTitle: Exploring Coastal Narratives and Artistic Reflections

EventDetail:
Questioning is more than just a technique—it is a powerful tool that fuels curiosity, deepens understanding, and nurtures independent thinking. When students learn to formulate their own questions, they shift from passive recipients to active participants in their learning journey. This process enhances student engagement, ownership, and critical thinking.
 
In this interactive workshop, participants will explore the Question Formulation Technique (QFT) a structured approach that empowers students to generate, refine, and prioritize their own questions. By integrating QFT into their teaching, educators can create environment where curiosity drives learning. 

Learning Outcomes  
  • Recognize the role of student-led questioning in fostering critical thinking, engagement, and deeper learning. 
  • Understand the QFT as a structured method for helping students generate, refine, and prioritize questions. 
  • Apply the QFT to support students in formulating meaningful questions that drive learning. 
  • Reflect on and adapt their teaching practices to encourage student curiosity and questioning 

Facilitator 
Rakshanda Ovais is a distinguished educationist with over 25 years of experience in educational leadership, teacher professional development, and school organization and management. She is committed to applying her extensive expertise to design and implement tailored professional development programs for both teachers and educational leaders. Her primary focus is on building leadership capacity, enhancing teacher development, and fostering organizational improvement. 

Who should attend
Teachers, Coordinators, School Leaders, and Educators from primary and secondary levels 

Investment 
PKR 4200

RTT is a four-day workshop (June 12-13 & 16-17) designed to support members in creating or redesigning their courses and aligning their teaching practices with student learning outcomes. Dementia remains a growing public health challenge worldwide, yet attitudes and perceptions toward the condition vary across cultures, often influencing care, diagnosis and policy responses. This webinar presented insights from a recent study conducted by AKU’s Brain and Mind Institute examining the attitudes and perceptions of dementia in Kenya and their impact on individuals, families and communities.
The discussion explored key findings from the study, including the role of cultural beliefs, systemic challenges and public awareness in shaping dementia care. The session also highlighted how research can inform better policy, advocacy and community engagement strategies to improve dementia support in Kenya.

  3. Jackline Thairu - Radiographer, MRI Technologist, Educator and Advocate
  4. Dr Vaibhav Narayan - Executive Vice President and Head of Strategy and Innovation, Davos Alzheimer’s Collaborative

EventDetail:
The Abdullah Shah Ghazi Shrine in Karachi stands as a significant spiritual and cultural landmark, attracting visitors from diverse backgrounds. Situated in the Clifton area, this shrine is dedicated to Abdullah Shah Ghazi, an 8th-century Sufi mystic revered for his teachings on love, tolerance, and spirituality. 

Architectural Features:

The shrine is perched atop a hill, featuring a prominent green-and-white striped dome. Its square chamber is adorned with traditional Sindhi tile work, flags, and buntings, creating a vibrant and welcoming atmosphere. Visitors ascend a series of steps to reach the main chamber, where devotees pay their respects.

Spiritual Significance:

As one of Karachi's oldest landmarks, the shrine attracts devotees who come to seek blessings and participate in communal prayers. The site embodies the inclusive spirit of Sufism, fostering unity among visitors. An enduring belief among locals is that the shrine's presence protects Karachi from natural disasters, particularly cyclones originating from the Arabian Sea. 

Community Services:

A notable aspect of the shrine is its langar, a free kitchen that serves meals to those in need, continuing a tradition initiated in the 1930s by Syed Nadir Ali Shah, the shrine's custodian at the time. This practice exemplifies the Sufi commitment to compassion and community service. 

Visiting Experience:

Visitors can expect a serene environment filled with the sounds of devotional music and the aroma of incense. The shrine is particularly lively during the annual Urs festival, commemorating Abdullah Shah Ghazi's death anniversary, featuring Qawwali performances and other cultural activities.

Practical Information:

  • Location: Clifton, Karachi, Pakistan.

  • Visiting Hours: Open daily; peak times include Thursdays and during religious festivals.

  • Dress Code: Modest attire is recommended out of respect for the sacred site.

A trip to the Abdullah Shah Ghazi Shrine offers a unique blend of spiritual enrichment, historical appreciation, and cultural immersion, making it a must-visit destination in Karachi.

EventDetail:
For many Kenyan families, dementia is a silent struggle; misunderstood, often ignored and wrapped in stigma. When a loved one starts forgetting names, getting lost in familiar places, or struggling to communicate, it is commonly dismissed as “just old age.” In some cases, cultural beliefs blame supernatural forces, delaying much-needed medical help. By the time families seek care, the disease has often progressed to an advanced stage.

Even then, the journey to diagnosis and support is riddled with obstacles. A shortage of trained healthcare professionals, high costs of care, and a lack of awareness leave many families feeling lost and overwhelmed.

A study by the Aga Khan University’s Brain and Mind Institute (BMI) in collaboration with the Davos Alzheimer’s Collaborative (DAC), sheds light on these challenges. Led by Dr Edna Bosire, the research explored perceptions of dementia among patients, caregivers, and health care providers at Aga Khan University Hospital, Nairobi, as well as within informal settlements.

“The findings reveal a troubling reality: stigma, lack of awareness and misinformation prevent early diagnosis, caregivers are left to shoulder the burden with little support, and participation in dementia research is hindered by cultural concerns and mistrust,” said Dr Bosire.​
EventSummary: Dementia in Kenya: How stigma and misconceptions shape care

EventDetail:
Dr Duane Rousselle, Associate Professor and Associate Dean – Research at FAS launched his book titled - Psychoanalytic Sociology: A New Theory of the Social Bond.

Singularities are isolated social bonds. They lack a common language with one another and express themselves with certainty. Strangeness is therefore no longer constitutive to the social bond. It has become elevated to the very principle of social order. Our social world has become strange.
Dr. Duane Rousselle explores this new theory of the social bond while accounting for recent developments in the cultural logic of capitalism. Each chapter offers a different and compelling perspective on broader phenomena and notions of estrangement within civilization through explorations of the evil empire, rogue states, the master-slave dialectic, and the new status of knowledge that is at stake in the era of singularities.
This book offers enriched and novel dialogues across Freudian and Lacanian psychoanalysis, Marxist and anarchist theory, and theoretical sociology with illustrative contemporary examples. Psychoanalytic Sociology argues that our current social crises are exemplified by the way social groups project their own inhumanity onto others. Written in Russia during the outbreak of the Ukrainian crisis, it prophesied new uncompromising and aggressive wars, the confluence of 'foreign agent' laws and 'cancel culture.' The war among singularities runs very deep and exists on every scale (e.g., interpersonal, institutional, and cultural). This book navigates this strange new social world and invents a language capable of articulating it.

Table of Contents

1. Foreigners and Singularities: What Does it Mean to be Strange?
2. Uncanny Doubles: What Do You See When You Look into Putin's Eyes?
3. From Estrangement to Being Strange in Public: The Mode of Production or the Mode of Prosumption?
4. Outsiders & Insiders: Sociology in Crisis
5. Perverts, Monsters, and Postmodern Wisdom: Social Origins of Doubt & Certainty
6. 'I Wanted to be His Slave!': Life & Death Strategies
7. A Physicist, Media Theorist, and Psychoanalyst Walk into a Classroom: Transcribed Presentations from [Three Experts]
8. Real Walls: An Uncompromising War
EventSummary: Dr. Duane Rousselle launched Psychoanalytic Sociology, exploring social bonds, estrangement, and cultural shifts through psychoanalysis, Marxism, and sociology
Title: Dr. Duane's Book Launch
Venue: D Lab at 10th Floor Alishah Abdul Rehman Kanji Building

EventDetail:
The annual Arabic Pasts workshop brings together scholars at all career stages to reflect on methodologies, research agendas, and case studies for investigating history writing in Arabic in the Middle East, North Africa, and beyond in any period from the seventh century to the present.


This year the Arabic Pasts workshop welcomes Queen Mary University of London as a partner. We will host the workshop in person at the Aga Khan Centre and welcome proposals that deal with the practical and conceptual challenges of working on history writing in Arabic. We encourage scholars working at all career stages to join us. 

By way of example, papers might elucidate the following sorts of questions - or others:

  • How do nations today tell their stories with respect to their pasts?  In what ways do educational institutions, museums, media organisations and proponents of heritage use history writing to shape loyalties and senses of belonging in society?
  • When and how did pre-modern and modern historians writing in Arabic conceptualize the history of Palestine as a distinct geographical and political unit?  What are the Arabic historiographical traditions regarding the city of Gaza and its hinterland, and how have they developed in the last two centuries?
  • How is the past used in creative arts, re-enactment, games, and augmented reality?
  • What do we consider works of fiction and how do they differ in authorial intent from historical chronicles? Does this authorial intent make a difference in how we treat these sources? What can we learn from combinations of fiction and non-fiction sources, if anything?
  • What is the relationship between Arabic and other languages and scripts in bi/multi-lingual and bi/multi-alphabetic texts (tarikh, documents, other genres) across time?
  • How can marginalised communities and their varieties of Arabic be given due attention?
  • How can all genders (including non-binary) be given due attention when our sources are often composed by male political, intellectual and religious elites? 
  • How can we explore the past algorithmically? Can digital methods enhance our understanding of the past? Can they also limit or even alter it? Which new digital tools are being developed? What seem to be particularly promising approaches? What is lacking?


Prior to the workshop, we will also run a hands-on workshop on digital methods for Arabic texts - no experience necessary. Please get in touch early if you are interested in joining as we will have to cap participation.

Arabic Pasts is co-convened by Anna Chrysostomides (Queen Mary), Yossi Rapoport (Queen Mary), Hugh Kennedy (SOAS), Lorenz Nigst (AKU-ISMC), and Sarah Bowen Savant (AKU-ISMC).


Please submit an abstract of 300 words or less in word document by Friday, 30 May 2025 to ArabicPastsConf@aku.edu. Also please be in touch if you would like to join the digital methods workshop.

EventDetail:
Rapidly identifying and managing life-threatening conditions with focused ultrasound is vital in emergency and critical care. This hands-on, full-day workshop equips you with the skills to master Point-of-Care Ultrasound (PoCUS) and make life-saving decisions. 

Through a combination of interactive presentations, hands-on sessions, and case-based discussions, this workshop provides a unique and practical approach to skill development.

Who Should Attend?

Adult and pediatric physicians, working in Emergency, ICU, and Acute Medicine. Students and interns are not eligible to attend.

Workshop Modules

  1. Basic orientation of ultrasound machine (Knobology and Image interpretation)
  2. Approach to a patient with undifferentiated shock (inferior vena cava assessment, abdominal aortic aneurysm, intraabdominal free fluid, cardiac tamponade, left ventricular dysfunction, & massive pulmonary embolism)
  3. Approach to a patient with shortness of breath (tension pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, pleural effusion, & pneumonia)
  4. Role of PoCUS in cardiac arrest (cardiac standstill, pseudo PEA, & PoCUS pulse check)
  5. PoCUS-guided central venous catheter (CVC) insertion
Learning Outcomes

  1. Understand the basic knobology and ultrasound image interpretation
  2. Apply PoCUS to rapidly assess patients with undifferentiated shock (cardiogenic shock, septic shock, hypovolemic and obstructive shock)
  3. Acquire the skills to use PoCUS in the assessment of patients with undifferentiated shortness of breath (Pneumothorax, Pleural effusion, Pulmonary edema, & Pneumonia)
  4. Gain confidence in utilizing PoCUS as a valuable diagnostic tool in cardiac arrest (H's and T's and PoCUS Pulse Check)
  5. Gain proficiency in using PoCUS for central venous catheter insertion
Workshop Director
Dr Noman Ali, Assistant Professor & Consultant, Department of Emergency Medicine, AKUH

EventDetail:
In the face of accelerating climate crisis, the need to align scientific research, policy making, and grassroots advocacy has never been more urgent. This talk explores how evidence-based science can inform inclusive policies and empower communities to act for environmental sustainability. Drawing on lived experiences from Gilgit-Baltistan to classrooms across Pakistan, Dr. Fozia Parveen will share her insights on creating contextual resources, conducting research, and translating that synergy into action through education, policy influence, and youth-led initiatives.

The session will highlight examples such as the Climate Action Fellowship to demonstrate Chow environmental scientists can serve as connectors between knowledge and impact. The taik aims to offer a hopeful yet action-oriented roadmap toward a more just, resilient, and sustainable future. The audience will be invited to reflect on these insights and engage in the conversation.

About Dr Fozia Parveen

Dr. Fozia Parveen is an environmental scientist and currently affiliated with the Aga Khan University's Faculty of Arts and Sciences (FAS) and Institute for Educational Development (IED), where she leads Initiatives to mainstream climate and environmental education. With a DPhil in Engineering Science from the University of Oxford and prior experience at LUMS, Dr. Fozia brings expertise in water and wastewater treatment, microplastic pollution, and sustainability-focused behaviour change. She teaches courses on Sustainable Development, Environmental Education, and Climate Change.

She is also on the Board of Governors in Pakistan as well as WWF International's Senior Advisory Group for Thriving Biodiversity. Dr. Parveen has also been shortlisted for the prestigious Young Global Leaders (YGL) class of 2025.
EventSummary: Dr. Fozia Parveen will share how science, policy, and advocacy can unite for climate action, drawing on youth-led efforts and local insights across Pakistan.

This talk looks at Iranian - Israeli relations from the Pahlavi era before the 1979 Revolution to the present day. It focuses on Iran's shifting role in the Middle East, from a pro-Western monarchy to an Islamic Republic with regional ambitions. The discussion will also briefly touch on current nuclear negotiations and their impact on Iran's international stance.

About Hadi Enayat

Hadi Enayat is an Assistant Professor at the Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilizations at Aga Khan University in London. He specialises in the political sociology of the Middle East with a particular focus on religion, law, political theology and intellectual history. He is the author of Law, State and Society in Modern Iran (Palgrave Macmillan 2013 winner of the Biennial Mossadegh Prize 2013), Islam and Secularism in Post-Colonial Thought: A Cartography of Asadian Genealogies (Palgrave Macmillan 2017), The Rule of Law in the Islamic Republic of Iran: Power, Institutions and the Limits of Reform (co-edited with Mirjam Kuenkler, Cambridge University Press 2025).

EventDetail:
The Aga Khan University (International) in the United Kingdom, in collaboration with His Highness’ National Council for the UK, and the Aga Khan Museum, offers a face-to-face short course on Governing Diversity: Engaging with a Complex World at Ismaili Centre, London. A distinguished presence in South Kensington since its inauguration in 1985, the Ismaili Centre, London, stands proudly amongst world-renowned museums in the city's vibrant Cultural Quarter. Discover the serene Roof Garden, often hailed as one of London's best-kept secrets, and the Zamana Space, a dynamic hub dedicated to cultural enrichment and learning, frequently partnering with fellow institutions of the prestigious Exhibition Road Cultural Group, a collective of 16 leading arts, culture, and educational bodies in South Kensington, counting the Ismaili Centre as an integral member.

This course examines how different kinds of states have treated diversity among their subjects. Looking at case studies ranging from the Romans and the Mughals to modern states in Europe and North America, it invites us to ask how far different kinds of subject expected to see themselves represented in the state and what kinds of ethnic or religious hierarchies the state endorsed. It also asks us to think about how different social groups functioned internally: how did their leaders manage the balancing act between the demands of the state and those of their community? How did they gather and spend revenues? And how did they secure the boundaries of their community against outsiders? The course will also include a study session at the Aga Khan Museum and a reflection on the course from the perspective of the local Ismaili community: does history offer lessons or models that can be used in the present day?

Learning outcomes:

  • Evaluate the utility of different kinds of technical vocabulary to analyse group behaviour
  • Compare the experience of minorities in different contexts
  • Analyse the interaction of legal policy, demography and political systems in the experience of minorities
  • Combine art historical evidence with written evidence to develop a holistic model of cultural interaction

Draft Agenda

Course faculty:

Professor Philip Wood

Prof. Philip Wood is a course lead for this short course. Dr. Wood studies West Asia before and after the Arab conquests (roughly 400-900CE). He is particularly interested in the history of Christian communities in Syria and Iraq, and in the formation and preservation of group identities more broadly. His books have analysed Syriac speaking Christian groups in the later Roman Empire, the Sasanian Empire and the Abbasid Caliphate. He has recently published *The Imam of the Christians: The World of Dionysius of Tel-Mahre, 750-850* (Princeton, 2021), and, alongside Professor Leif Stenberg, *What is Islamic Studies? European and North American Approaches to a Contested Field* (Edinburgh, 2022).

Dr Hadi Enayat

Dr. Hadi Enayat is an Assistant Professor at the Institute For the Study of Muslim Civilisations at Aga Khan University in London, and a Research Fellow at the Foreign Policy - Centre, UK. He specialises in the political sociology of the Middle East with a particular focus on Iran.

Dr Ulrike Al-Khamis

Dr. Ulrike Al-Khamis is the Director and CEO of the Aga Khan Museum. She has over 20 years of experience as a curator and senior advisor for museum and cultural projects, collaborating with institutions such as the National Museums of Scotland and Glasgow. More recently, Dr. Al-Khamis served as Co-Director of the Sharjah Museum of Islamic Civilisation and Senior Strategic Advisor to the Sharjah Museums Department in the United Arab Emirates.

EventDetail:
Increasingly across the Global South – including Gilgit-Baltistan in northern Pakistan – the failure of public services such as water has brought community-led development to the heart of development policy. But can communities replace government and manage their own water services? What is the evidence of successful community management of water and how sustainable is this?

Sustaining and Scaling Up Community Managed Water presents the results of a two-and-a-half year research project on the Water and Sanitation Extension Programme (WASEP) that has successfully delivered water to over 400,000 people in Gilgit-Baltistan. Edited by Jeff Tan, Stephen M. Lyon and Attaullah Shah, this book draws on a large-scale survey of over 3,300 households supplemented by in-depth interviews with community water management committees and focus group discussions with residents. The results highlight WASEP’s success in reaching communities previously without safe drinking water, but also point to the challenges communities face in sustaining water services, with implications for policy. 

Join lead editor Jeff Tan for a real-world discussion of the challenges faced by community water management. Dr Tan was Principle Investigator for this British Academy-funded research project and is Professor of Political Economy and Head of Education and Learning at AKU-ISMC.

Whether you work in development, sustainability, water management or community leadership, this event offers valuable lessons on scaling up impact without losing community ownership.

The event will be held at the Aga Khan Centre in London and will also be streamed live via Zoom.

Accidents don’t clock out—so neither should your preparedness. Our corporate First Responder Course is designed to empower your team to act confidently in any healthcare emergency.​​

 

Who is a First Responder? 

A first responder is a person trained to provide immediate assistance or aid, during an emergency or disaster, to those in need. First responders play a crucial role in ensuring the safety and well-being of their community, and people around them. Their quick response can make a significant difference in saving lives and reducing the severity of injuries.

About the Course

​Our full-day course on emergency aid will teach you how to respond immediately to medical emergencies in the workplace. Using our world-class simulation facilities, you will learn:

Office emergency readiness​

CPR training

Stroke, heart attack & choking response

Electric shock

Fainting, head trauma, bleeding

Allergic reactions and breathing difficulties

Scalds and burns

Through simulation and feedback you will learn situational awareness; the necessity for rapid effective communication in the first few moments of an emergency, and how to protect yourself and your colleagues from infection risks of uncontrolled bleeding and other medical crises. 

 

​Certification by AKU and the US-based Society for Simulation in Healthcare (SSH).

EventDetail:
Introduction:
The 6th Hybrid Annual Pakistan Paediatric Neuro-oncology Symposium (6thPNOS) focuses on the pivotal theme: "Global Standardization in the Management of Childhood Brain Tumors".

Childhood brain tumors remain one of the most complex and life-threatening paediatric cancers, requiring a comprehensive, multidisciplinary approach. The disparities in outcomes between high-income countries and low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) are stark — largely due to differences in early detection, access to specialized care, and the availability of standardized treatment protocols.

This symposium seeks to address these challenges by promoting alignment with internationally recognized standards of care. By focusing on regional adaptation of global best practices, this event will help pave the way for more unified, equitable, and effective care pathways in paediatric neuro-oncology, particularly in LMICs.

Objectives:
  • Establish Paediatric Neuro-Oncology as an essential sub-specialty of paediatric oncology in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), in alignment with global standards of care.
  • Recognize and support all allied specialties — including paediatric radiation oncology, paediatric neurosurgery, neuroradiology, pathology, palliative care, and nursing — as vital contributors to the standardized multidisciplinary management of childhood brain tumors.
  • Improve outcomes of paediatric brain tumors in LMICs by fostering international collaborations, twinning programs, and partnerships that promote the adoption of globally accepted protocols.
  • Provide evidence-based updates from diverse disciplines involved in the care of pediatric brain tumors to support the implementation of global best practices.

Who should attend?

Consultant and postgraduate trainees in pediatric oncology, neurosurgery, pediatric medicine, radiology, radiation oncology, palliative care, pathology and all physicians, medical students and allied healthcare staff taking care of children with brain tumors

Organised by: Department of Oncology in collaboration with Department of Continuing Professional Education

EventDetail:
About the talk
This talk presents a theoretical framework for Muslim science educators called Islamic Scientific Critical-Consciousness, and shares preliminary findings from a year long case study that makes use of participatory action research in an Islamic faith based school and in a Muslim majority public school in England. Usama will explore how Islamic scientific heritage can be meaningfully connected with modern science to promote a culturally grounded approach to science education. He will present how critical-consciousness can be developed in Muslim students’ by identifying secular-liberal ideologies often framed as “neutral” or “objective” in science textbooks and the wider literature. He will propose how this process can cultivate both agency and ethical orientation in pursuing scientific knowledge. Developed through participatory action research, the framework draws on Paulo Freire’s critical-consciousness and Muhammad Iqbal’s conception of Khudi.

About the speaker
Usama Javed Mirza is a science educator and social entrepreneur. He is currently pursuing his PhD at the Faculty of Education University of Cambridge on a Gates Cambridge scholarship. Previously as a Fulbright scholar he completed his Masters in Education at Teachers College Columbia University, is a New York State trained Emergency Medical Technician and also has a Bachelor's degree in Physics from the Lahore University of Management Sciences. He is the founder of Saving 9, a prehospital care social enterprise that creates communities of care around medical and psychological emergencies.
Title: Decolonizing Science Education

EventDetail:
Researchers and policy makers convene for Equitable Education in Sindh

Karachi, Pakistan – August 4, 2025:  The critical policy roundtable, convened at the Aga Khan University (AKU), underscored a unified commitment to embedding field-based research evidence directly into educational reforms.

Prominent educationists, researchers, and policymakers from Sindh emphasized the critical need to cultivate a culture of data utilization within the education sector, ensuring effective policymaking, particularly for enhancing the quality of learning for all children, with a special focus on marginalized communities.

Part of the Data and Research in Education – Research Consortium (DARE-RC), funded by the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO), the event focused on integrating rigorous research insights with the province’s education priorities.

The discussions across key themes, including Equitable Access and Inclusion, Strengthening Frontline Education Provision, Building Climate Resilient Education Systems, and Governance, Management, and Effective Data Use, will directly inform targeted policy development. This collaborative effort will also shape Sindh’s upcoming education sector plan, translating research findings into tangible policy actions. The DARE-RC consortium affirmed its ongoing engagement with Sindh’s education sector, ensuring that evidence continuously informs policy.

Dr Farid Panjwani, Dean of the AKU Institute for Educational Development in Pakistan (IED, PK), highlighted the need for informed steps based on field-based evidence for educational reforms. “Research based evidence is a necessary though not sufficient ingredient of policy making. The DARE- RC project is designed to strengthen sound evidence. The most important feature of the project is that all the research ideas are field based, rather than top down. The 18 studies in Sindh offer empirically validated pathways to improve learning outcomes, and we urge stakeholders to leverage these insights for systemic change.”

Dr Ehtesham Anwar, Team Lead DARE-RC, further emphasized the vital role of data use for effective policymaking, he commented "DARE-RC is honoured to be the largest, and first of its kind initiative, in Pakistan where research will inform the decision making in as important a sector as education - the lifeline of the country."

Richard Yates, Deputy Head of Mission, British Deputy High Commision, Karachi said: “Education Is vitally important for the development of individuals but also for countries and UK government is pleased to support education through this Programme.”

The event, jointly organised by IED, PK, Oxford Policy Management (OPM), and Sightsavers marks a significant step towards a more evidence-based and equitable education system in Sindh.
Title: DARE RC Sindh Policy Roundtable
Venue: AKU University Centre, Hall A, 11th Floor

What if a probe could guide your next clinical move? This hands-on POCUS workshop brings ultrasound to the frontline. Scan for shock. Scan for breathlessness. Learn to identify key pathologies in real-time and turn images into confident decisions. Because when time is tight, clarity matters.

  2. Approach to a patient with undifferentiated shock (inferior vena cava assessment, abdominal aortic aneurysm, intraabdominal free fluid, left ventricular dysfunction, and cardiac tamponade)

AI in education is a revolutionary opportunity to make lessons more engaging and innovative. As Gen-Z and Gen Alpha students grapple through the process and challenges of using AI effectively, in this workshop, we will focus on how young minds can use human intelligence to manage AI for learning. We will also shed light on the role teachers, subject leads, and management play in ethical incorporation of AI-assisted teaching to stimulate student learning.

The Counsellors' Connect event will run twice, on August 26th and 28th, 2025.

Who Should Attend?
Principals, counsellors, academic coordinators, teachers, educators

Facilitator: Jennifer Johnson

Bio: Jennifer Johnson has 15 years of industry experience and a decade long involvement with Education Technology. Former Head of Digital Learning at Karachi Grammar School, she has been the inaugural leader for the EdTech infrastructure and programmes at the school. She has pioneered the Teaching with Digital Technologies Diploma Professional Development Qualification at Cambridge University and was invited to speak at Cambridge Schools Conference in 2018 and 2020. With a double Bachelors in Literature and Business Administration from Pakistan and USA, and Certificate in Educational Leadership from Cambridge, she aims to make the era of AI intellectually relevant for educators.

Key Takeaways
 
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:
  • Understand the role of AI in education.
  • Explore classroom-ready AI tools for lesson planning, feedback, and student engagement.
  • Identify common AI challenges faced by students - and how to address them.
  • Examine ethical considerations when using AI in teaching and assessments.
  • Design learning environments that balance AI support with human-centered pedagogy.
  • Develop school-wide policies for responsible AI use, from classroom to leadership levels.

Join the Aga Khan University Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations (AKU-ISMC) for a Book Launch to celebrate the publication of The Beautiful Game on a Muslim Pitch: How Football and Religion are Shaping Identity and Society. The book's two editors, Aaron W. Hughes and Leif Stenberg will discuss how football and religion are becoming increasingly interlinked in Muslim contexts. And also what role they will play in the fast-changing global landscape.

 

The first part of the book tackles how, in Muslim contexts, football and religion interact in the creation of an individual’s identity – whether as a player or as a fan. The second half of the book examines how those same elements are used by both political and religious establishments in their attempts to disseminate or propagate their larger messages.

 

The Beautiful Game on a Muslim Pitch has been published jointly by Edinburgh University Press and AKU-ISMC in the Exploring Muslim Contexts series. The ebooks are available for free, Open Access.

Aaron W. Hughes is Dean’s Professor of the Humanities and the Philip S. Bernstein Professor of Religion at the University of Rochester. Leif Stenberg is Professor in Islamic Studies at AKU-ISMC and visiting professor at Karlsbad University.

Aim of the Course

This certificate course aims to equip teachers and practitioners working with young children to recognize, understand, and respond to the needs of neurodiverse learners in the early years. It promotes evidence-based inclusive classroom strategies, practical tools, and an inclusive mindset that embraces and celebrates the diverse ways children think and learn within mainstream classroom settings.

Learning Objectives of the Course

By the end of the course, participants should be able to:

 

  • Understand early brain development, developmental domains, and variations in children’s growth.
  • Define neurodiversity and explain its significance in early education.
  • Identify early signs of neurodivergence and collaborate with families/specialists for support.
  • Describe strengths and challenges of neurodivergent children (e.g., ADHD, autism, dyslexia).
  • Develop neurodiversity-informed classroom strategies for inclusive learning.
  • Apply trauma-informed practices to address stress, trauma, and discrimination in children.

Duration of the course: 24 weeks (100 hours)

Introduction:
Fetal Growth Restriction (FGR) remains one of the most challenging cases in maternal–fetal medicine, often determining the difference between survival, morbidity, and long-term outcomes. Despite the wealth of research, many clinicians struggle with applying complex Doppler physiology, differentiating early from late presentations, and making timely, individualized management decisions.
 
This half-day workshop, Management of Fetal Growth Restriction: Understanding Pathways, Patterns, and Practice, is designed to bridge that gap. With interactive lectures, real-world case discussions, and evidence-based insights, participants will gain the practical wisdom and confidence to navigate subtle diagnostic dilemmas and optimize outcomes for both mother and baby. Whether you are a trainee building your foundation or a seasoned consultant refining your expertise, this workshop offers indispensable knowledge that translates science directly into clinical care—making it a must-attend for anyone dedicated to advancing perinatal excellence.

Course Objectives
  • Interpret Umbilical Artery, Middle Cerebral Artery and Ductus venosus Doppler Indices
  • Differentiate between early-onset and late-onset FGR and formulate distinct management strategies for each
  • Identify diagnostic clues of late-onset FGR and Justify time and mode of delivery
  • Integrate evidence-based guidelines with real-world case discussions to formulate individualized management plans for FGR
Who should attend
Obstetrics and Gynaecology Consultants, Trainees, Students, Nurses

EventDetail:
Every time we go online—scrolling social media, shopping, or even just reading the news—we leave behind digital traces. These “footprints” are collected, analysed, and sold by powerful technology companies. Dr Nejra van Zalk explores how Big Tech turns our clicks, likes, and searches into profit, shaping not only the ads we see but also the opinions we form and the choices we make. Dr van Zalk will offer a nuanced look at the benefits of our digital lives: connection, convenience, creativity, while uncovering the hidden costs of data tracking and influence, and what it means for our mental health in a world where attention has become the ultimate commodity.

 

Dr Nejra van Zalk is an Associate Professor in Design Psychology at Imperial College London’s Dyson School of Design Engineering. Her research explores how technology and design shape behaviour, emotions, and decision-making, with a focus on mental health. She leads the Design Psychology Lab, investigating the psychological mechanisms through which products, services, and interventions can enhance individual and societal wellbeing.

 

The event will be held at the Aga Khan Centre in London and will also be streamed live via Zoom.

Dr Kamran Abbasi, Editor-in-Chief British Medical Journal (BMJ), will talk with Dr Shehla Zaidi about how professional and academic journals like the BMJ have had to evolve in the 21st century to continue to serve as forums for new research. 

 

Kamran Abbasi is a doctor, journalist, editor and broadcaster. Following five years in hospital medicine, working in various medical specialties such as psychiatry and cardiology, he moved into senior editorial roles at the BMJ from 1997 to 2005. He returned to The BMJ in his role as executive editor for content, leading the journal's strategic growth internationally, digitally and in print. Kamran was made Editor in chief, The BMJ in December 2021.

 

Shehla Zaidi is Visiting Professor of Health Policy and Systems Research at the Aga Khan University. Currently based at University College London, where she leads the Global Healthcare Management programme, one of UCL’s largest postgraduate programmes and an established thought leader on public private partnerships with research focus on the Middle East, South Asia and Pakistan. 

 

The event will be held at the Aga Khan Centre in London and will also be streamed live via Zoom.

EventDetail:
This seminar addresses the explosion of interest within Academia in alternative methods for both doing and publishing research. Using his own research project The Native and Refugee as a case study, Malek Rasamny will explore a whole host of non-paper associated media from blogs to websites to documentary film. In particular, he will look at how the medium of film can radically transform research output – from using different styles of filming (journalistic, agit-prop, experimental) to how it can be formatted (from clips and shorts to feature-length documentary films). He will also touch on different approaches to the writing, archiving, curation and pedagogy of your research when utilising these new media approaches. Also included will be a screening of his documentary ‘Spaces of Exception’.

 

Malek Rasamny is the co-founder and co-producer of The Native and the Refugee, a multimedia research project that juxtaposes Native reservations in the United States and Palestinian refugee camps in the Middle East. He is the co-director of the documentary film ‘Spaces of Exception’ and co-author of the book The Mohawk Warrior Society. He is currently a doctoral candidate at Paris Nanterre University where he is researching the relationship between reincarnation and memories of the Lebanese Civil War amongst the Druze community.

EventDetail:
From griefbots to therapy chatbots, AI is increasingly designed to comfort us. But what does it mean when an AI seems to care? Can a machine without feelings provide real care - or does it merely simulate empathy? This lecture examines how people experience emotions in relation to AI, and whether the simulations offered by systems like ChatGPT can become meaningful in therapeutic and intimate encounters. Drawing on affect theory, phenomenology, and ethnographic research with people who form relationships with chatbots, Cearns explores how these technologies reshape our understandings of self and other, intimacy and care. Ultimately, the question whether AI's "mask of empathy" reveals more about machines, or about the embodied, relational nature of human feeling itself. 

Jennifer Cearns is Lecturer in AI at the Department of Social Anthropology and Centre for Digital Trust and Security at the University of Manchester. Her research currently focuses on human-AI relations, affective computing and empathic AI, and how digital technologies affect personhood and identity. 

 

This event will be held at the Impact Hub - London Euston and will also be streamed live via Zoom.

Rapidly identifying and managing life-threatening conditions with focused ultrasound is vital in emergency and critical care. This hands-on, full-day workshop equips you with the skills to master Point-of-Care Ultrasound (PoCUS) and make life-saving decisions.

Through a combination of interactive presentations, hands-on sessions, and case-based discussions, this workshop provides a unique and practical approach to skill development.

Who Should Attend?
Adult and pediatric physicians, working in Emergency, ICU, and Acute Medicine. Students and interns are not eligible to attend.

Workshop Modules
  • Basic orientation of ultrasound machine (Knobology and Image interpretation)
  • Approach to a patient with undifferentiated shock (inferior vena cava assessment, abdominal aortic aneurysm, intraabdominal free fluid, cardiac tamponade, left ventricular dysfunction, & massive pulmonary embolism)
  • Approach to a patient with respiratory failure (tension pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, pleural effusion, & pneumonia)
  • Role of PoCUS in cardiac arrest (cardiac standstill, pseudo PEA, & PoCUS pulse check)
  • Learning to perform ultrasound-guided central venous catheter (CVC) insertion

Learning Outcomes
  • Understand the basic knobology and ultrasound image interpretation
  • Apply PoCUS to rapidly assess patients with undifferentiated shock (cardiogenic shock, septic shock, hypovolemic and obstructive shock)
  • Acquire the skills to use PoCUS in the assessment of patients with undifferentiated respiratory failure (Pneumothorax, Pleural effusion, Pulmonary edema, & Pneumonia)
  • Gain confidence in utilizing PoCUS as a valuable diagnostic tool in cardiac arrest (H's and T's and PoCUS Pulse Check)
  • Learn to perform ultrasound-guided Central Venous Catheter (CVC) insertion

Workshop Director
  • Dr Noman Ali, Assistant Professor & Consultant, Department of Emergency Medicine, AKUH

Consultants, Department of Emergency Medicine, AKU:

About the Conference

As climate change intensifies across Pakistan and other low-income settings, the built environment has become a critical frontline of resilience. To address this growing challenge, the Institute for Global Health & Development at Aga Khan University, in collaboration with the Sustainable Development Solutions Network Pakistan, is hosting the IGHD Annual Conference 2025: “Climate Change and the Built Environment: Promoting Resilience & Adaptation in Low-Income Settings.” The conference will take place at Aga Khan University, Karachi, on November 28–29, 2025.

This year’s conference brings together leading national and international experts in architecture, urban planning, climate science, public health, and sustainable development to examine how homes, settlements, health systems, and public infrastructure can be better designed and adapted to withstand intensifying climate impacts. Through keynote addresses, case studies, and thematic sessions, speakers will explore climate-resilient architectural practices, indigenous and rural solutions, innovative low-carbon design, and approaches for strengthening health systems against environmental stressors.

The programme will highlight evidence-based strategies from Pakistan and around the world—featuring expertise from universities, government ministries, global development partners, and civil society—to guide policy, research, and on-ground implementation. Participants will gain insights into IGHD, AKDN, and SDSN Pakistan’s collaborative efforts to advance climate-resilient development within vulnerable communities.

This is an excellent opportunity to engage with specialists, explore practical solutions, and connect with partners committed to building a safer, more resilient future.

EventDetail:
About the Conference

The Supporting Women in Science (SWIS) Conference 2025, hosted by the Institute for Global Health & Development (IGHD) at Aga Khan University in collaboration with the University of Oxford, marks the culmination of Phase III of the SWIS Initiative. Taking place on 26–27 November 2025 at AKU’s Main Auditorium in Karachi, the conference brings together women scientists, senior academics, global mentors, and institutional partners to celebrate research achievements from South-Central Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa.

This year’s programme showcases the scientific contributions of Cohort 1 and 2 fellows, whose work spans child development, chronic diseases, infectious disease research, adolescent health, environmental risks, and health systems innovation. Through keynote lectures, flash sessions, and thematic panel discussions, the conference highlights evidence-based research conducted by early- and mid-career women researchers and demonstrates the transformative impact of structured mentorship, skills-building, and funded research opportunities.

Senior leaders from AKU and partner institutions—including academic deans, global health experts, and national programme leaders—will deliver keynote addresses exploring women’s leadership in science, research equity, and the future of women-led innovation. The conference will also feature a special closing session honouring mentors who have contributed to strengthening women’s participation in STEM across regions.

The SWIS Conference offers a unique opportunity to engage with emerging women scientists, explore cross-regional research insights, and strengthen networks committed to advancing gender equity in science and public health.

EventDetail:
Rapidly identifying and managing life-threatening conditions with focused ultrasound is vital in emergency and critical care. This hands-on, full-day workshop equips you with the skills to master Point-of-Care Ultrasound (PoCUS) and make life-saving decisions.

Through a combination of interactive presentations, hands-on sessions, and case-based discussions, this workshop provides a unique and practical approach to skill development.


Who Should Attend?
Adult and pediatric physicians, working in Emergency, ICU, and Acute Medicine. Students and interns are not eligible to attend.


Workshop Modules
  • Basic orientation of ultrasound machine (Knobology and Image interpretation)
  • Approach to a patient with undifferentiated shock (inferior vena cava assessment, abdominal aortic aneurysm, intraabdominal free fluid, cardiac tamponade, left ventricular dysfunction, & massive pulmonary embolism)
  • Approach to a patient with shortness of breath (tension pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, pleural effusion, & pneumonia)
  • Role of PoCUS in cardiac arrest (cardiac standstill, pseudo PEA, & PoCUS pulse check)
  • PoCUS-guided central venous catheter (CVC) insertion

Learning Outcomes
  • Understand the basic knobology and ultrasound image interpretation
  • Apply PoCUS to rapidly assess patients with undifferentiated shock (cardiogenic shock, septic shock, hypovolemic and obstructive shock)
  • Acquire the skills to use PoCUS in the assessment of patients with undifferentiated shortness of breath (Pneumothorax, Pleural effusion, Pulmonary edema, & Pneumonia)
  • Gain confidence in utilizing PoCUS as a valuable diagnostic tool in cardiac arrest (H's and T's and PoCUS Pulse Check)
  • Gain proficiency in using PoCUS for central venous catheter insertion

Workshop Director
Dr Noman Ali, Assistant Professor & Consultant, Department of Emergency Medicine, AKUH

EventDetail:
About the talk

Climate change is expected to significantly increase the frequency and intensity of heatwaves in Malaysia, with major consequences for public health and the economy. There is thus a pressing need to reduce heat in urban areas where modern buildings and the reliance on air-conditioning have increased heat and carbon emissions. This session examines the impact of rising temperatures in Penang and the “urban heat island” effect, where surface temperatures are higher in the UNESCO World Heritage Site of George Town. It looks at how traditional building techniques and materials can reduce heat and carbon emissions and improve well-being.

About the Speaker

Dr. Jeff Tan is a Professor of Political Economy at the Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations (ISMC), Aga Khan University. He holds a PhD in Economics from the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS), University of London. Dr. Tan’s research focuses on the intersection of governance, economic policy, and infrastructure, examining how states, private sectors, and communities interact in shaping development outcomes. His current research investigates the use of traditional building techniques and materials for climate mitigation by reducing carbon emissions and reducing the transmission of heat into homes.

EventDetail:
Tracing its roots to a project in Mozambique in 2014, the Aga Khan Foundation’s Learning Hub, an award-winning digital learning platform, is transforming how some of the world’s poorest and most remote communities with little or no access to the internet or digital technology – as well as people development practitioners, civil society organisations (CSOs), educators, government officials and others working to improve their quality of life – access and share knowledge across Africa, Asia, and the Middle East. This lecture will share the story of how a Human-Centred Design process conducted in Mozambique, which aimed to solve a local problem led, several years later, to the development of a digital learning platform sharing hundreds of high-quality highly localised learning materials in 25+ languages.

Following ten years of testing, iteration, scaling, and partnership, today, teachers, farmers, entrepreneurs, government officials, and parents across Africa, Asia, and the Middle East can all find practical, relevant, high-quality learning content in their own language or dialect on The Learning Hub, all produced locally using a low-cost approach. By removing barriers to access, including developing a custom-build learning management system (LMS) using open source technology, The Learning Hub is able to share all learning content for free, as a public good.

By fostering collaborative learning design and prioritising equitable access, The Learning Hub offers a scalable model for inclusive lifelong learning – on that has already been recognised and adopted by 150+ partner organisations globally. Its community-driven, multilingual ecosystem demonstrates how digital platforms can democratise knowledge, empower local practitioners, strengthen education systems – and pave the way for decolonising digital learning.

Ana Barfield leads the Aga Khan Foundation’s Global Practice function. As such, her role is to stimulate an inclusive culture of learning, sharing, innovation, and collaboration across AKF and to amplify AKF’s best practice across the development sector. Ana oversees the implementation of AKF’s learning strategy, including through the design, development, and dissemination of high quality, innovative, digitally enhanced learning and knowledge assets, platforms, and solutions, including AKF’s Learning Hub (akflearninghub.org).


This event will be held at the Aga Khan Centre - London and will also be streamed live via Zoom.
